title: Agents
text: Agents Crafting An agent is a frame that runs a program. Walking, carrying, reaping, mining and laying blocks are its own; where learning beats a rule, a model in one of its slots decides, in exactly the format of that model's test, and the agent does what the model answers. You can see a model in its lantern of a head, turning faster while it thinks. An agent's screen, part by part. Home and models Where you place an agent is its home, and its work happens around home. Set home, the house beside its screen, makes where it stands its new home. The panel beside its screen holds its two model slots, and its upgrades. Its Model takes a Checkpoint with a model of up to 160 KB of weights, or a Relay Card tuned to a Model Server, for a model of any size: see Serving Models. This model writes the orders you give as programs, and makes the decisions of storing, hauling, building and copying. Its Filter takes a checkpoint that passes Sorting, and tells what kind each thing is. Its screen says what is missing. Programs The Program tab holds what it does when nothing else is asked of it: steps between commas, checked as you type. take bread, come, give bread until full (pickup) repeat (mine 4 stone, put) if ripe (harvest) else (wait 10) Run starts it and Stop stops it. A program that goes on for good, a repeat without a count, is its standing work; any other runs once, and then it rests. The buttons on the Work tab set ready-made programs: Farm is repeat (farm), Sort is repeat (sort), and so on, and Rest clears it. The Palette beside Stop lays out every piece of a program to click together instead of typing, each saying what it does when you point at it. Pieces go on the end, along with whatever plainly comes next: the ( that opens a block, the mark a place needs. To name a thing, pick it up and click the program, or the order box on the Work tab. The steps an agent is usually given are below; everything a program can say, on an agent and on a Port, is in Programs: variables, lists, your own steps, events, areas, filters, and what a program can read of the world. come, home, go 3 to the third mark, stay, follow take 5 bread from the chests and barrels around home, or from the network of a Storage Terminal there, put everything or put wheat away in them, give bread to you, fetch bread, which is taking, coming and giving craft 8 torch makes them there and then if it holds what they take; what it cannot make, it walks to a terminal around home whose network can, asks, and waits until it is made; supply goes after what a job on that network lacks, out of the chests and barrels or mined, and brings it to the network, so repeat (supply, wait 10) keeps a network's jobs going pickup what lies around it, harvest, plant wheat seeds, till the grass near water, mine 4 stone (with a pickaxe it carries, for blocks that need one; it digs its way to anything buried, and to what a Surveyor found; mine caches for what the old world left in them; agents mining near each other take different blocks), place oak planks 2 on top of the second mark wait 10 seconds, say hello farm, store, sort, haul, build, copy or move: one round of a routine Blocks: repeat (…), repeat 3 (…), if … (…) else (…), until … (…) and wait until …. Checks: have 3 bread, stocked bread in the stores and networks around home, ripe, full, night, near (you are within 8 blocks), powered 2 (the second mark has a redstone signal), each with not before it if need be. The trace The Trace tab shows what it did, checked and decided, newest last, and how each step went: storing and sorting note every stack they put away, and where. A step that fails says why, and the program goes on with the next. An agent that gets stuck on its way somewhere gives up after a while; stuck three times running, it jumps home. Beside it, the debugger holds a program at a step, runs it one step at a time and shows what it holds. Upgrades Upgrades go in the panel beside its screen. At the most, it acts every tick and carries 48 slots' worth. With a Lift Upgrade and energy it flies, and it comes down to walk when the energy runs out. Routines farm: walks the farmland within 7 blocks of home, harvests what is ripe and plants what is bare, and takes the harvest to the chest at home, keeping some seed. It is a rule, so no model is asked. store: empties the barrels around home into the chests within 8 blocks, numbered 0 to 9, nearest first. A kind it has never seen goes to the emptiest chest. For a kind seen before, it shows its model where eight kinds went and asks which chest this one belongs in. sort: empties the barrels around home into the chests labelled with each thing's kind: Food, Plants, Wood, Stone, Ores or Tools. Name a chest in an anvil to label it, or fix a sign to it. Its filter is asked the kind of each thing by its name alone, so it can sort things it has never seen. Whatever its filter calls other, or is less than 60% sure of, goes in a chest labelled Other, or else in one with no label. haul: walks out along the six waymarks it was handed, loads up from the chest or barrel at the last one, and comes home. On the way back its model names the waymarks in reverse, and it walks wherever its model says. build, copy and move: carry on a pattern along a run, copy a build, or move it, contents and all, as its model reads it: see The Architect. The Survey Rod Crafting Use a Survey Rod on blocks to mark them, up to eight, in order; use a marked block again to unmark it, and sneak-use in the air to clear them all. Use the rod on an agent to hand it the marks: waymarks for hauling, a build's corners and where its copy goes, the ends of a run to build along, or places for go and place. Program Cards Crafting (Shapeless) A Program Card carries a program from agent to agent. Use a blank card on an agent to copy its program, and a written one to hand the program over; sneak-use a written card to copy onto it instead. In an agent's screen, click the program holding a written card to load what it says, or holding a blank card to write the program onto it; shift-click writes onto a written card too. Orders Start a chat message with an agent's name to give it an order: Pip, bring me some bread. It hears you within 24 blocks, or anywhere a Model Server's relays reach while you are in reach too, holding a Terminal tuned to it. You can also type an order on the Work tab of its screen and Tell it. Its model writes the order as a program, in all the words of Programs: move 16 iron ingots from mark 1 to mark 2, dig out everything between the marks, put all the logs on the network, go to every mark and say hello, make a step sweep that harvests and puts away. A plain step, or one of the jobs, it does at once, if its model is sure. Anything else it reads back with [Do it] and [Cancel] to click in chat, or on the Work tab of its screen, and runs only once you say yes: point at it to see its steps on lines. A model that passes Programs is trusted to run what it writes at once, however long. An order comes before its program, which it goes back to after. If what its model writes is no program at all, it is puzzled; a model that never practised orders will mostly be puzzled. With no model at all, an order already written as a program, dig at front, is taken as it stands.

title: The Architect
text: The Architect An agent whose model passes Induction can copy a build, move it, or carry on its pattern. It reads a build as slices across its length, a letter for each slice, and asks its model what comes next, just as the test does. Marks Mark blocks with a Survey Rod, in order, and hand the marks to the agent: copy and move: two blocks at opposite corners of the build, then the block the copy should stand on. The copy's first corner goes on top of the third mark, and the rest follows from there. build: the blocks under the two ends of a straight run. With a third mark on the far top corner of the first slice, each slice reaches across and up to it; without one, each slice is a single block. A build is cut across its longer side, into at most 16 slices, each at most 16 blocks wide and 16 high, and its copy stands within 64 blocks of it. Copying copy first reads the build. It shows its model the build's slices, a different letter for each, then the order it has read so far, and asks which slice comes next. The first slice it takes by itself, since nothing yet says where a copy begins. If its model is less than 60% sure, or names a slice twice, it stops before it lays anything. Then it lays each slice in its place, fetching the blocks from the chests and barrels around home, or from a storage network through a Storage Terminal there. Chests and machines in the copy start out empty. What can be built over, such as grass or water, isn't copied, and anything already standing where the copy goes stays. Until a block is laid, its place shows as a faint teal ghost to anyone nearby, for a copy, a move or a repeat alike. Moving move reads the build the same way and checks that nothing stands where the copy goes. Then it takes the build up slice by slice, contents and all, and lays it down again: chests keep their items and furnaces their fuel, and nothing drops on the way. Pictures and item frames are no blocks, and stay behind. An agent holding a build can't be picked up until it has laid it down. Repeating build carries on a pattern along its run. It shows its model the slices so far, the same letter for the same slice, and lays the slice its model names. Lay one round of the pattern and the start of the next by hand. What comes after a slice is what came after it last time, so the slices of one round must all differ.

title: The Archive
text: The Archive The old world wrote letters, journals, stories, songs, recipes, manuals and notices, and kept a copy of everything. What survives is in Archive Shards, each a piece of one record with some of its text lost. The Reader's screen, a shard as it reads. Shards A shard learns which record it is the first time you hold it. Use it to read what is left; lost text shows as ▒. Archive drives Crafting Use an Archive Drive to file every shard you carry into it. Shards of the same record make one better copy: whatever any of them kept is kept. The drive's tooltip counts its records and its legible letters. In a Model Core's Data slots, a drive is practice for Reading: the model learns to predict the next letter of everything legible on it, or the next token with a tokenizer, so the more you recover, the more it has to learn from. Reading is tested on records no shard ever carries. A model can only pass by learning how the old world wrote, not by remembering what it read. The boxes of fallen masts hold more than drives. A Relay Dump is all a relay passed on, repeats and bad lines included; it goes in those slots too, and it teaches worse than a drive until it has been through a Refinery. The Reader Crafting A Reader restores lost text. Put a shard in its tray and a model in its model slot: a checkpoint, or a Relay Card tuned to a Model Server for a model too big to hold. The Reader goes through the lost blocks one by one. For each, the model reads the text just before the block and then guesses the block letter by letter, seeing each true letter after its guess. If it guesses at least half of them, the block was predictable enough to restore, and it comes back. A block the model cannot restore stays lost until a better model tries. A model that reads ahead, seeing the letter it is asked to guess, is turned away: it would only copy.

title: The Arena
text: The Arena There are two ways to get what a mob drops. One is to fight it. The other is to write down how it fights until a model can do the same, and let the model fight instead, on the floor of an Arena, for as long as the power holds out. Writing a mob down Use a blank Mob Log on a mob. The log takes that kind, and keeps what that one looked like. After that, carried anywhere in your inventory, it writes a line for each mob of the kind within 16 blocks of you, sixteen at most, four looks a second. Fight them with it on you: a mob that only stands about writes nothing down, and how it fights is what a model has to see. A line starts with a capital for the kind. Then every look is a letter for how things stand and a digit for what the mob did next. This is the end of a zombie's line: i1i1h1h1h3g5g3g3g3g5g1g3g1h1 The letter says how far off whatever the mob is after stands, in six bands from under 2 blocks to over 16, whether it is after anything at all, and whether it has just been hurt. The digit is one of these: Digit What the mob did 0 stood still 1 came closer 2 backed away 3 moved round it 4 leapt 5 struck 6 wound up: drew a bow, swelled, cast, charged 7 was suddenly somewhere else Crafting (Shapeless) Practice In a Model Core's data slot, a Mob Log is practice for Imitation. At every look the model is asked what the mob did next and learns from the answer. It tries nothing out and nothing rewards it: it only copies, which is called behaviour cloning. The Imitation Dataset holds lines of the same sort, of thirteen kinds of mob, and the Imitation test asks about lines of theirs that practice never shows, counting every kind alike. An Arena asks only about the mob in its log, so a Core can hold that log and the dataset together, or several logs of the same mob. Most of what there is to learn is timing. The zombie above strikes every fourth look, so a model has to read back along the line to know when the next blow falls; a skeleton draws for four looks and looses three looks after, every eight. Mobs are partly random, so no model gets all of it. On the Imitation test a model that sees only the last few characters stays at 72% and two layers of attention at 74%. Two transformer blocks pass the 76% after about 2,000 steps. The chamber The Fabricator makes an Arena from a transformer photomask. Set it into a wall of a closed room, placing it from inside so that it faces in. The room has to be empty, at least 3 by 3 and 2 high, at most 21 by 21 and 8 high, and shut in on every side by anything solid or glass. Its floor holds a pad for every three blocks each way, and each pad a fight. Put the log in the slot at the left of the Arena's screen and a model in the panel beside it, a Checkpoint or a tuned Relay Card. The Arena first checks the model on the tenth of the log that practice never reads: the share of those looks where its likeliest action is what the mob really did. That share says little by itself. A creeper mostly comes closer, so anything that says it comes closer is right most of the time, and what a spider does next is hard to be right about whatever reads it. So the Arena counts two tables on the rest of the log and sets them beside the model. The first goes by the letter alone: after this letter, what did the mob most often do? The second reads back too, as far as pays on this log: after this letter and the last few things it did, what did it most often do? How far the model gets from the first table's share to the second's is what its likeness is worth, and it can go past the second. Likeness How far from the first table to the second Looks checked What a fight that counts drops Crude 20% 100 what the mob drops dying with nobody near Fair 40% 200 what it drops when someone kills it Good 60% 400 that, as to Looting I Close 80% 800 that, as to Looting II Uncanny 100% 1,600 that, as to Looting III A likeness also takes looks. A short log has little to check a model on, and its tables have seen little too, so it can vouch for only so much however well the model does on it; a full log has about 2,300 looks to check. On a nearly full log of zombies, after 2,000 steps of practice on it, a model that sees only the last few characters gets about a sixth of the way and earns nothing, two layers of attention get two thirds of the way, and two transformer blocks go past the second table. Simple mobs give up more for less: a blaze mostly goes on doing what it did last, and reading one look back is most of what there is to know. A fight lasts twelve seconds. At every look the model is asked what the mob does next, and what it picks is what the small likeness on the pad does, while a sparring frame comes after it. Watch them: a poor model's mob has no rhythm and strikes whenever it likes, and a good one comes on and strikes in time. It goes on from what it did itself, so one wrong step can take it where no line it read ever went, the old trouble with copying. Then the mob falls, and the fight counts as often as the model is right: at 75%, 75 fights in 100 pay out, and the rest go out in smoke. What a fight pays is what that kind of mob really drops, rolled from its own loot table, and a Wither's star comes the same way. Compute and power An Arena alone runs one fight at a time. Each cooled Training Accelerator touching it, or touching one that does, runs one more, an uncooled one half of one, up to a fight on every pad. The first four run on what the Arena can spare. Every other takes power while the Arena works, and with none to draw stays dark and lends nothing: Compute. A room of 21 by 21 with 48 cooled Accelerators runs 49 fights at once, and they draw 3,520 FE a tick between them. A finer device counts for more. Every fight costs 8 FE a tick for each point of the mob's health: 160 FE a tick for a zombie, 38,400 FE for its whole fight, and 2,400 for a Wither. The Arena stores 4,000,000 FE. It asks its model about all its fights at once, and a look waits for the answer, so a slow model or a busy server fights more slowly, for the same power a fight. Ground A Surveyor with a Field Log in the slot under its model keeps a fair sample of the rows of ground it reads. In a Core, that log or the Ground Dataset is practice for Ground: the next block of a row. An Arena takes that log too, and stands closed until its base has reached the Frontier tier. Then a model that passes Ground writes a row of ground on each pad at every look, with the compute of 16 cooled Accelerators, for 640 FE a row. Every ore it writes comes out as mining it would, as far as the ground in the log really holds that much of it: a model cannot write more diamonds into the world than the ground it knows has.

title: The Bench and the Fabricator
text: The Bench and the Fabricator Every machine is made in a Fabricator. The simple ones need nothing but materials. The rest need a Blank Photomask carrying a design for what they compute, and designs are wired on a Bench from the smallest operations there are. Crafting Crafting Crafting (Shapeless) Crafting (Shapeless) The Bench's screen, the Fabricator's. Specs The Bench lists specs: what a module must compute, a formula, and a set of test cases with the answers worked out exactly. Some cases are ordinary. Others are the inputs that break the obvious design: scores of a thousand, a row of equal numbers, numbers far from zero. A design passes when it gets every case right to within a thousandth. Specs build on each other. Attention needs your softmax and matrix multiply; the transformer block needs layer norm, attention and the feed-forward block. A spec opens when the ones it builds on are verified. Wiring a design Drag parts from the left onto the board, and drag from one node's right edge to another's left edge to wire them. Every node shows a strip of the numbers it computes on the chosen case; click it to read them. A strip turning red means a value that is not a number, and the node that turned it red is the one to look at. Wire your last node into result, and the cases on the right tell you which pass and why the others don't. The parts: Sources: a constant you type, and size, the length of the last axis. Arithmetic: add, sub, mul, div and max, element by element. An axis of size 1 stretches to match the other input, so a row of sums divides a whole row of numbers. Functions: neg, exp, log, sqrt, tanh and round. Last axis: sum and amax keep the axis with size 1; transpose swaps the last two axes; unsqueeze and squeeze add and drop an axis of size 1; causal hides everything above the diagonal. Grids and turns: cos and sin; round, to the nearest whole number with a half going to the even one; exponent, the power of 2 a float stores, and pow2, which undoes it; index, each row's place; pair, which pair each number of a row is in; turn, a quarter turn of every pair; left and right, the two halves of the last axis. Your modules: every spec you have verified, as one part. Recording When every case passes, Record writes the design onto a blank photomask from your inventory, signed with your name. The spec counts as verified for you from then on, and its module joins your parts on every Bench. Fabricating Put a photomask in the Fabricator and pick a machine. Each takes a Tensor Casing, wafers, and weight crystals if it learns weights. A design's area sets the wafers: four units of area to a wafer. Each primitive costs a little area and each module what its spec's design costs, so a smaller design makes cheaper machines. The photomask is never used up. Without a mask, the Fabricator makes the machines that need no design: the embedding and position tables, the residual junction, the gate, the scaler, the causal mask, the head splitter and merger, the delay line and the concatenator. A matrix multiply photomask also makes the Training Accelerator and the Drive Dock, a linear layer photomask the Dense Drive and the Portable Drive, an attention photomask the Hourglass, the Access Point and most upgrades, and a transformer photomask Forecaster II, Forecaster III, the Arena, the Smelter, the Stacked Drive, and the Energy Upgrade and Lift Upgrade. The photomasks of Schedule, bf16, fp8, fp4, Orthogonalize and Document Mask make the units of the recipe. A cached attention photomask makes the KV Cache, and a rounding photomask the Weight Packer. Fused and unfused The ruins hold old photomasks too, carrying salvaged designs: correct, but written out one primitive at a time. Machines made from them are unfused. They give the same answers, but they write out every tensor in between, so they use more memory and train more slowly. A design you verify yourself makes fused machines, one kernel each. The machine's screen and tooltip say which it is.

title: Compute
text: Compute Training a model is multiplying numbers, and the numbers can be counted. A flop is one multiply or one add. A model of N parameters reading D tokens takes about 6ND of them: two for each parameter on each token going forward, four coming back. The Core counts them as they happen, and its Compute tab sets what it counted beside that six. What limits a run is how many flops it can do a second, how much memory holds it, and the energy each flop takes. All three depend on what you build. Process nodes A Training Accelerator is one device. The Fabricator makes them from a matrix multiply photomask, and prints them at the node of the wafers in its wafer slot. Each node down holds eight times the memory and runs four times the flops, and each flop takes half the energy. Node Wafer Flops a second Memory FE/t at full load Flops per FE 90 nm Wafer 10 G 512 KiB 80 6.25 M 28 nm 28 nm Wafer 40 G 4 MiB 160 12.5 M 7 nm 7 nm Wafer 160 G 32 MiB 320 25 M 3 nm 3 nm Wafer 640 G 256 MiB 640 50 M Crafting (Shapeless) Crafting (Shapeless) Crafting (Shapeless) Power The first four Accelerators touching a block run on what that block can spare, and draw nothing. Every other device takes power from the network it is part of: Accelerators and rack blocks carry power like cables, so one cable to any of them reaches all of them. A device with no power to draw stays dark and lends nothing. A run on devices that take power pays for its flops as it does them, at what those devices get for a unit of energy. If its network cannot pay, the run waits, and the Compute tab says so. Everything else that takes compute (Assemblers, Model Servers, Forecaster III) pays each device's full-load draw while it works, and counts a finer device for more: a 28 nm device for four of the first, a 7 nm for sixteen, a 3 nm for sixty-four. Memory To train a parameter takes four numbers of four bytes each: the weight, its gradient and Adam's two running averages. Sixteen bytes a parameter. A run that does not fit will not start. A Core alone holds 2 MiB, which trains about 131,000 parameters; Accelerators on their own add their memory to it. This is the plan's parameter-state budget. Training stores these arrays in fp32 even when a Recipe rounds values to a smaller format, so reduced precision does not shrink this budget. Temporary activations and working buffers are additional host memory. Racks and pods Devices also go in the eight bays of a Rack Module, each with a strip of light that shows how busy it is. Up to four modules stacked under a Rack Switch make a rack of up to 32 devices. Modules only join up and down: racks side by side stay apart. Whatever takes compute reaches a rack by touching it, or along Interconnect. A cluster with no Pod Switch has the use of one rack; other racks stay dark. Interconnect from a Pod Switch to Rack Switches makes a pod of up to eight racks, 256 devices. More than one pod takes a hall. Using a switch by hand says how its cluster stands. Crafting Crafting Sharing out the work The button beside the Compute tab chooses how the next run shares its work. Each way splits something different, with a thread of its own for every device, and each takes exactly the steps one device would. The tab labels the reserved devices, threads and memory as the plan. Its measured timeline describes the latest completed split step. Reduced precision, document masks, z-loss and a second head use the general graph path: data and pipeline jobs bypass their replicas or stages, while tensor jobs retain their matrix workers. The tab names the fallback and clears the split timing; rack lights show no measured load for that pass. Changing the Recipe back resumes split measurements. The allocation and its memory gate stay in place, and counted flops are still charged at that allocation's energy efficiency. Changing the sharing button selects the next run's allocation. One device. The Core and the Accelerators on their own pool their memory and threads, and each operation's rows go to whichever thread is free. Racks sit idle. The model has to fit the pool. Data parallelism. Every device holds the whole model and takes its share of the batch. Each computes its gradients on its own, the gradients are added up a pair of devices at a time, and the new weights go back out. It adds no memory: only devices that can hold all of the model take part. What crosses the links grows with the model. Tensor parallelism. Every matrix multiply is cut by its columns among the devices, each working from its own slice of the weights, and they all meet at the end of each one. A model can be larger than any device. It meets for every multiply, so small layers spend more time meeting than working. Pipeline parallelism. The model's layers are cut into stages, one to a device, and the batch into microbatches that go down the stages one after another and come back up. Each device holds only its stage. No more stages than the model has layers worth one, and the stages wait while the pipeline fills and drains: those are its bubbles, about (stages - 1) / (microbatches + stages - 1) of the time when the stages are level. The tab draws them. What each of them gained on eight threads, for one model of four layers and about 820,000 parameters, against a single thread: Way Faster by Time spent waiting Through links, each step One device ×2.8 Data parallelism ×5.7 6% 46 MB Tensor parallelism ×1.6 62% 100 MB Pipeline parallelism ×2.2 32% 6 MB Pipeline parallelism used four stages of the eight devices, and four stages with eight microbatches would have waited 27% if they were level. The numbers change with the model: the tab shows yours. It also says how long what crossed the links would take over a rack's links, a pod's and a hall's, where devices share no memory: 100, 25 and 6 GB a second. That is the bill each way runs up as a cluster grows. Where the numbers come from The Compute tab separates the allocation plan from measurements: flops as they are counted, measured device work and waiting, and bytes that would cross a link. A model practising by playing also runs forward at every look it plays, so its flops a parameter a token come to several times that six. What a Hall Console says of a run too large to do is a prediction from the same sums, and it says so.

title: The Model Core
text: The Model Core The Model Core feeds text into your machines and judges what comes back. Its front sends out tokens; every other face takes in the model's scores. It trains the model, tests it, and saves it as a model. The trained weights stay in the machines themselves, so a model keeps what it learned when you leave and come back. Crafting Its screen, part by part. Data Four slots for what the model practises on: datasets, archive drives, or a salvaged model. Everything in them is practised together, a batch from each in turn. Beside them are the tokenizer slot, for the tokens the model reads and writes, and the checkpoint slot. An empty slot shows faintly what goes in it; point at a checkpoint for what it holds. Save to checkpoint tests the model on every benchmark and saves it into that checkpoint. With a salvaged model loaded, Rebuild builds its machines in front of the Core: see Salvaged Models. Train The learning curve, with the numbers it ends at beneath it: train loss, test loss and accuracy. Point at them for Parameters, the model's weights, Grad norm, the size of the last gradient, and Threads, how many threads the Core trains with. Train starts training and stops it. Beside the window, a toolbar holds Reset and Check, then the settings: Speed, Learning rate, Batch, Clip and Weight decay. Point at one for its value and what it does; click for the next value, right-click for the one before. See Training for what each one means. Tests Every benchmark on a line, with its score at the last test; a full green bar passes. The test of each benchmark is taken while the model trains on it; Test all runs every test now. Point at a line for the job it is used for, the score that passes, when it was tested and the format its test uses. See Models and Tests. Click a line to look closer: the test beside a look-alike of it, runs of this design from fresh seeds, and what everyone on the server has made: see Comparing Models. Try Runs the model. Choose a benchmark: Example draws a fresh test example and shows the model answering it, the way an agent would ask. For Orders, type an order and Ask; for Reading, type the start of something and Write: the model carries it on one letter at a time, drawing each from its predicted probabilities. Temp (temperature) sharpens or flattens those probabilities before drawing: Low temperatures repeat the model's favourite continuations; high ones take more risks. The bars show how likely the model found each candidate for the first letter it wrote. Inspect Every machine of the model in the order data reaches it, with its output shape, its number of weights and the size of its last gradient. Problems found by Check are listed here too. A bar that shrinks to nothing as you go down the list is a gradient that never arrives. Recipe How a run goes beside its learning rate: Schedule, Warmup and Length, Precision, Optimizer and Packing. The toolbar beside the window sets them: point at one for its value and what it does, click for the next value. Each needs its unit touching the Core before it will change. Under them is what the run is doing: the rate now, what the weights take beside what can be carried, the share of the text it ever reads, its spikes, the largest scores inside the model and how often a second head is right. Beside them are the rate over the whole run and the units the Core has. See The Recipe. More threads Each Training Accelerator touching the Core, directly or through other Accelerators, lends it one more thread and its memory, up to the limit the server allows. An Accelerator with nothing to cool it runs hot and lends half: give it water, ice or snow to touch. The Fabricator makes them from a matrix multiply photomask. The first four run on what the Core can spare; more take power. A model also has to fit: sixteen bytes a parameter, and a Core alone holds 2 MiB. The Compute tab counts what a run has done and chooses how it shares out its work: see Compute.

title: Halls
text: Halls Rows of racks make heat, and the heat has to go somewhere. A hall is what several pods, the power to run them and the cooling to keep them running add up to: a room you can stand in and read from one end to the other. Cooling lines A rack gives off too much heat for standing water. A rack is cooled when any of its modules touches a Coolant Pipe of a line closed on a Chiller: pipes from the Chiller's front round to its back. An Accelerator on its own can be cooled the same way. Coolant runs through the pipes while it works. A device with nothing to cool it runs hot, lends half and smokes. A Chiller holds 8,192 FE a tick of heat, reckoned at each device's full-load draw, so a line takes as many Chillers as its devices need. It has to give the heat to something: water touching it, ice or snow, or the air of a cold biome. And it takes power of its own, from the network it is joined to, for all the heat its devices really make. PUE Power usage effectiveness is all the power a hall draws over what its devices draw. It is what cooling costs: The Chiller gives its heat to FE for each FE of heat PUE water 0.3 1.3 ice or snow 0.2 1.2 the air of a cold biome 0.1 1.1 An Accelerator cooled by water standing beside it costs nothing, and that is why a small lab does not need any of this. The Hall Console A Hall Console joined by Interconnect to two Pod Switches or more, in a cluster with a closed cooling line, makes the whole of it one hall: every Pod Switch then carries its eight racks, where a cluster that is no hall has the use of one pod's. It lights when it stands. Its screen reads the hall: what it is rated for, what it is running, what it draws and at what PUE. It also says the largest model its memory could train, and what training that on twenty tokens a parameter would cost in flops, days and energy. That is a prediction by the sums on the Compute page, for a run too large to do. The Load Wall Load Wall panels set side by side and stacked, facing the same way and joined to a cluster, make one display as wide as they are: a column for each rack, as tall as that rack is busy, and over them what the cluster is running, the devices at work, what it draws and its PUE. The rack lights and the wall read from across the room. Crafting Crafting Crafting

title: Serving Models
text: Serving Models A model too big for an agent's head can still work for it. A Model Server holds the model and answers questions for everything tuned to it, as far as its relays reach. A network of relays does more than carry questions: it keeps a base running with nobody there, moves you between its gates, makes storage and power at both ends of the world one, and lets you read and steer the base from wherever it reaches. A Terminal's screen, a Relay Gate's. The Model Server Crafting (Shapeless) Use a saved Checkpoint on a Model Server to load its model; sneak-use the server with an empty hand to take the checkpoint back. Use it with an empty hand to open its screen: the model it serves, how many answers a second it can give and how much of that is in use, what its memory holds, and who has been drawing on it. Each line says more under the pointer. A Model Server's screen, part by part. What a server can spend A server has so many operations a second to spend: 142 million by itself, as many again for each Training Accelerator touching it, half as many for one running hot. A token through a model costs two operations for each of its weights, so a bigger model answers less. Its screen counts in answers that read 16 tokens and write 8: Transformer of two blocks Weights Answers a second, by itself 32 wide 33,049 14 64 wide 115,161 4 96 wide 246,425 1.9 Everything tuned to it draws on those operations: agents, Terminals, Forecasters, Readers, Smelters, Surveyors, Ports and Watch Posts. A question costs what its model really worked out for it, and its answer comes when the server has that much to spend, so a long answer waits longer than a short one and holds up what comes after it. While you hold a tuned Terminal or Relay Card, a corner of your screen shows how the server is doing. When more than 64 questions wait, new ones are turned away, the front lights run red, and anyone near is told. Whatever asked goes on without a model until there is room: an agent stops and says so, a Forecaster stops running blocks ahead, a Smelter's melt goes uncontrolled and makes two ingots, a Port goes back to its rule. The server's screen says who has been drawing the most. More Accelerators are one way out. A smaller model doing the same job is another: see Distilling. The rest of this page is the third: making each question cost less. The KV Cache Left to itself, a model writing a token reads everything before it again. An answer that reads 16 tokens and writes 8 takes 156 rows. Yet a new token changes nothing about the rows before it: all an attention needs from them is each one's key and value. Keep those, and every token is read once. The same answer takes 23 rows and comes out the same to the last digit. The Fabricator makes a KV Cache from a photomask of Cached Attention, a spec that opens once the transformer block is verified. Put it in the panel beside the server's window. A 64-wide server goes from 4 answers a second to 26, and the longer the answer the bigger the gain: 40 tokens come thirty times as fast. A question asked again costs nothing at all, and one that starts as another did starts from where they part. What it keeps takes memory. A token takes two rows of the model's width in floats in each attention, 1,024 bytes in a two-block model 64 wide, and a little more for what is read back. A server holds 1 MiB with its weights in it, and each KV Cache adds 256 KiB, up to a stack of 64. When memory runs short the sequences used longest ago are forgotten, and only cost rows to work out again. A window of 64 tokens is as far as a model reads. Past that, the window moves on 16 tokens at a time, with or without a cache, and everything in it is read again: positions are learned, so what was kept belongs to places that have moved. Batches The button under the panel sets how many sequences may go through one pass. Whatever waits at once goes together, and a sequence that finishes makes room for the next at the very next pass. A pass costs something by itself, whatever it carries, and a batch shares that. On plain floats that is next to nothing, so batches earn little. On packed weights it is a lot. Packing The Fabricator makes a Weight Packer from a photomask of Rounding Weights, which opens at the same point. In the panel, it lets the other button keep the weights in 8 or 4 bits, packed as an exosuit's board packs them: 64 wide, 460,644 bytes become 122,359 or 64,779. That is room: a model 96 wide takes all but 62,876 bytes of a bare server at floats, and leaves about 786,000 at 8 bits, enough to keep six times the tokens. It has two costs, and the server measures both. The weights are read out of the packed bytes on each pass, which costs as much as working out about one row at 8 bits and about two at 4. And rounding them can change what the model says, so everything it passes is tested again in that form: the server's screen shows each score, and whatever asks it goes by those scores. A form that fails a test closes what that test opens. A 64-wide model, on one thread's operations Answers a second Floats 4 Floats, KV Cache 26 8 bits, KV Cache 20 8 bits, KV Cache, batches of 32 26 4 bits, KV Cache 15 4 bits, KV Cache, batches of 32 24 Drafts The last slot of the panel takes a second checkpoint, a small model that reads the same way. It proposes the next four tokens, and the served model reads all four in one pass. A proposal stands with probability p ÷ q, p being how likely the served model makes it and q the draft, or for certain if p is the larger; the first that doesn't stand is drawn again from what the served model wants beyond what the draft gave it, and the rest are dropped. What comes out follows the served model's own probabilities exactly, whatever the draft is like. A good draft only means fewer passes. So a draft pays only when passes are dear and most of its proposals stand. Its own rows cost something, and on floats a pass is so cheap that a draft only adds work. A 32-wide draft distilled for 800 steps from a 64-wide model had 26% of its proposals stand, and took that model down from 12 answers a second to 9 on floats, and from 12 to 8 at 4 bits. The server's screen counts how many stood. Relays Crafting (Shapeless) A Model Server reaches 16 blocks by itself, and a Relay 32. Two of them join when their reaches touch: a relay up to 48 blocks from the server is on its network, and one up to 64 blocks from that relay is too, so the ground a network reaches has no gaps in it. Reach runs level, however high or deep you stand. Relays stacked make a mast, which reaches 32 blocks for each block of it, up to 1,024 from a mast 32 blocks tall. Use one to see how far it reaches and what is on its network. The lamp on top lights while a model is served on the network, and such a network keeps the ground around it running. The chunk each of its relays, gates and links stands in, and the eight around that, stay loaded with nobody near them: machines go on working, agents go on walking, and the server goes on answering. Put a relay in each part of a base you want kept running. Relay Cards Crafting (Shapeless) Use a Relay Card on a Model Server to tune it. In an agent's or a Reader's model slot, the card asks the server instead of carrying a model: any size of model, wherever the server's network reaches. Every agent tuned to one server shares its answers per second. In an Access Point, a card that reaches the server lets the storage network's Wireless Terminals go anywhere the server's relays cover (Storage). Relay Gates A Relay Gate is a pad to stand on, and it has to stand in a relay's reach. The Fabricator makes it from a Transformer mask, 8 casings, 16 wafers and 8 weight crystals. It opens once its network can carry you: a model that passes Orders is served on it, and it gives at least 16 answers a second, which is a server with three cooled Accelerators. An open gate shows a shaft of light. Use a gate to see its network on a map, and click another gate, on the map or in the list beside it. A jump is a request like any other. It takes one answer for every step of the way from relay to relay, and each waits its turn at the server behind whatever else is asking, so a gate is quicker with more Accelerators and slower when the base is busy. Walk away and the jump is called off. Name a gate in the box at the top of its screen, or at an anvil before you place it. A network doesn't have to be one piece. Use a Relay Card on a gate and it takes the gate's place; use it on another gate, however far off, in any dimension, and the two are tuned to each other. Their networks are one from then on: for jumps, for reach and for links. Sneak-use a card on a gate to cut it free. Relay Links A Relay Link comes from the same mask, with 4 casings, 8 wafers and 4 weight crystals. It joins whatever touches it, on any face: Storage Links, Drive Racks, Power Cables and machines. On an open network, all the storage networks and all the power networks at its links act as one. A Storage Terminal at the far end shows what the drives at the near end keep, a Port there takes from them, and a machine there runs on the generators back home. Assemblers and Processors work for a request made anywhere on it in their own dimension. A network's links together carry 4 items and 50,000 FE a tick for each answer it gives a second: at 16 answers, 1,280 items a second and 800,000 FE a tick, and each cooled Accelerator on the server adds 320 items a second and 200,000 FE a tick. Fluids count against the items, a bucket as 8. Use a link to see how much of that it is carrying. Its faces light while it carries. The Terminal Crafting (Shapeless) Tune a Terminal on a Model Server the same way, then carry it out into the world and use it anywhere the server's network reaches. Every call it makes takes its turn at the server, as any other question does. Map shows the network from above, on the ground as far as you can see it: its reach, its masts, its gates and its agents. Click a gate to go there, from wherever you are: that takes 8 answers more than a jump from a gate. Base shows what its storage networks hold and what its machines are doing. Click a storage network to open it as if you stood at its Storage Terminal: search, take, put in and ask it to make things. Agents shows what each agent in reach is doing. Pick one to stop it, start it again, hand it the program on any Program Card you carry, or give it an order. A program written out runs as it stands. Anything else the served model writes as a program, so an agent needs no model of its own for this, and a model that passes Orders writes it best. A plain step or one job it does at once; anything that says where or how, anything longer, or anything the model is under 60% sure of, waits for your yes here: point at it to see its steps on lines. Writing is the served model itself: write the start of something and it carries it on. While you hold a tuned Terminal, bars in the corner show how far inside the reach you stand, pulses run from mast to mast while the server answers, and near the edge of the reach, posts of light mark where it ends. Every agent the server reaches also hears the orders you give by name in chat. Heat Accelerators run hot, and past the first four they take power (Compute). One touching water, ice or snow, or standing in a cold biome, lends a full thread to a Core or a full share of answers to a server; one with nothing to cool it lends half, and smokes while it works.

title: Comparing Models
text: Comparing Models A score is one number from one run. Before you believe that one design beats another, there are three things worth knowing, and a Model Core shows them all. Click a benchmark on its Tests tab. How much of it is luck Train the same design twice and you get two scores, since the first weights and every batch are drawn at random. Train 5 from fresh seeds trains the design standing on the Core again, five times over, with its settings and its data, for as many steps as you choose, and leaves the model standing there as it is. Each run is a mark on a line, with their mean and spread beside them. Change the design and run it again, and the last design's marks stay underneath. A change has done something only if it moves the marks further than they spread by themselves, and the line beside them says whether it has. Many a clever change sits within the noise. Whether it has seen the test A test is a fixed set of items, so a model that has seen them does better on them than on anything else. Beside the test's score stands a look-alike: the same test with other items. The two should agree, within what chance leaves between them. When the test is ahead by more than four times that, and by at least five points or a tenth of a nat, the test has got into the practice. You can do this to a fresh model of a design on a Trial Rig, and see how little of the test it takes. A run of 13 tokens from the test turning up in what it practised on gives it away too, without any model at all. What everyone else made Each model saved on this server goes on the leaderboards of the benchmarks it passes: who made it, what it scored and what a look-alike said, how many parameters it has, and its machines when you point at it. The best stand first, the smaller first among equals. One whose test flatters it stays on the board, under the rest. Beside the list are two histograms, by score and by size, with the model standing on this Core marked in amber. A Bench does the same for every spec once a design passes: everyone's verified designs, by the area they take to lay down. The boards are kept with the world, and each design counts once for each player, at its best.

title: The Exosuit
text: The Exosuit The Exosuit is armour with a board in it, and the model on that board runs everything else. Worn in the chest slot it turns blows as a netherite chestplate does. With a model on board and power in it, it also does what the model's compute can carry: night vision, step assist, reach, a shield, vein mining, and flight that goes further than a flight frame's. Crafting An exosuit's screen, part by part. The board A model goes on as a pilot goes into a frame: in your inventory, pick up a checkpoint and right-click the suit with it. Right-click the suit with nothing in hand to take it off again. The board holds 160,000 bytes, as much as an agent's head, and keeps weights only as small whole numbers. A model's weights are floats, four bytes each, so the board quantizes them: every 32 weights share a scale of two bytes, and each weight keeps only the whole number of scales nearest to it, in 8 bits or in 4. Nothing in the weights says what that rounding cost, so the board packs both forms and tests them on Pilot and on Survey, which takes it some seconds; the suit chimes when that is done. Then it runs the more precise form, unless the other does better or alone fits. Transformer of two blocks Weights As floats At 8 bits At 4 bits 32 wide 33,049 132,196 B 35,115 B 18,591 B 48 wide 67,961 271,844 B 72,223 B 38,243 B 64 wide 115,161 460,644 B 122,359 B 64,779 B 96 wide 246,425 985,700 B 261,827 B 138,615 B At 8 bits a model loses next to nothing. At 4 it can lose a little, and how much depends on its job: a sorter that gets 97% right falls to 95%, and a reader's loss goes from 1.49 to 1.56. It is the shared scales that save them: with one scale for each whole matrix that sorter falls to 85%. A flight is a long chain of choices, so a pilot can go either way. Most hold at 4 bits what they hold at 8, but one that held every flight at 8 bits held 69% at 4, and another that held 66% at 8 held every flight at 4. At 3 bits, which no board runs, a pilot that held them all falls to 78%, under what Pilot asks. Only the test can say. Compute The suit's compute is the weights it carries, times the share of Pilot's flights it still holds in the form it runs in, in the wind it holds worst. Pilot asks for 90%. A form under that gives no compute, and neither does a form too big for the board; without compute or without power, the suit is only armour. Sneak and use the suit, or press key.residual.exosuit while you wear it, to open its screen. It shows what the board found, a line for each form, then each ability with the compute it draws. The abilities you leave on run, cheapest first, as far as the compute goes: turn one off and the next may start. Ability Draws Power What it does Night Vision 8,000 16 FE a tick You see in the dark. Step Assist 8,000 16 FE a tick You walk up a full block without jumping. Reach 20,000 32 FE a tick You reach 5 blocks further, to blocks and to what you strike. Shield 28,000 25,000 FE a point of damage The suit's power takes the blows. Vein Mining 48,000 1,000 FE per additional block A block you break while holding its key takes its vein with it. Flight II 128,000 320 FE a tick in the air You fly twice as fast as in a flight frame. So a model 32 wide carries night vision and step assist, or the shield, or reach with one of the two. One 48 wide carries vein mining with those two, or the four small ones without it. One 64 wide carries everything but the flight. The flight takes a bigger model still: three blocks 64 wide, which fit on the board only at 4 bits, fly with reach or the shield beside it. All six take two blocks 96 wide, again only at 4 bits, and they have to hold every flight like that. The shield With the shield running, the suit's power takes whatever armour leaves of a blow, at 25,000 FE a point of damage, so a full suit takes 640 points, or 320 hearts. Blows still land and still knock you back; they cost power instead of health. When the charge is too low for a whole blow the rest gets through, and when it runs out everything the suit does stops. Fire, falls and magic all cost the same. Only what goes through invulnerability itself still reaches you: the void, and commands that kill outright. Vein mining Hold the vein key, key.residual.vein, and break a block, and the blocks of its kind joined to it go too, through any face, edge or corner: an ore in stone and the same ore in deepslate count as one kind. They go a few at a time, spreading from the first, and what they drop comes to your feet. A vein takes 64 blocks at least, and one more for every thousand of compute the suit has free. While you hold the key and look at a block, thin lines show what would go, through the ground too. A vein stops before it would break your tool or run the suit out of power, and it leaves alone blocks with contents and blocks your tool cannot take. Vein mining also takes a model that passes Survey in the form it runs in, since it has to read the ground: put the Flight Dataset and the Survey Dataset in a Core's Data slots together. That takes longer: a model 64 wide passed both after about 3,000 steps, and one 96 wide after about 2,400 with the learning rate at 0.001, while at 0.003 it still held under half its flights after 2,000. A model trained on Pilot alone runs everything else. Flight With Flight II running, jump twice to take off. It flies twice as fast as a frame, and a full suit of 16,000,000 FE flies for about 41 minutes. A suit without the compute for it does not fly at all; a flight frame still does. Power Use the suit on an Energy Cell to fill it from every cell on that network at once. It also takes Forge Energy from any other mod's charger. Everything but the shield, vein mining and flight spends its power by the tick while it runs. The model at work A corner of your screen shows the model on the board, flying. It flies practice flights in the form it runs in, a look every half second, and the strip shows each look's height against the shaded hold, with the suit's charge under it and a light for each ability running. The suit's screen shows the same flight, larger. In PyTorch scale = group.abs().max() / 7 kept = (group / scale).round().clamp(-7, 7) # 4 bits back = kept * scale

title: Flight
text: Flight The Flight Frame is worn in the chest slot. While it has power and a pilot it can carry, a model that passes Pilot, its wearer flies as freely as in creative play: jump twice to take off, and it hovers wherever you stop. It spends 80 FE a tick while you fly, so a full frame of 400,000 FE flies for about four minutes. The Fabricator makes it from a transformer photomask. The pilot A pilot goes in as an item goes into a bundle: in your inventory, pick up a checkpoint and right-click the frame with it. Right-click the frame with nothing in hand to take the pilot out again, back on its checkpoint. The frame's tooltip names its pilot, and says when it cannot hold the frame: a pilot has to pass Pilot, and be small enough to carry. Power Use the frame on an Energy Cell to fill it from the charge of the cells on that network. The bar on the frame shows how much it holds. An exosuit with the compute for it flies twice as fast and ten times as long. Learning to fly A model learns to pilot on the Flight Dataset, by flying: the Core flies the model's own flights and it learns from how each choice turned out, as for Control. Thrust changes how fast the frame climbs or sinks, not where it is, so a pilot has to read its speed from the heights before; and the wind its vane reads pushes every two or three looks from a moment of its own, which it has to make out from the flight and meet before it pushes. A model that sees only the last few characters holds under half of the flights in its worst wind; a two-block transformer holds them all after about a thousand steps. See Models and Tests.

title: The Forecaster
text: The Forecaster The Forecaster watches the blocks around it that make progress and writes down what they do: furnaces, smokers, blast furnaces, brewing stands, Fabricators, Smelters and plants. Give it a model that has learned what such blocks do next, and if the model's forecasts match what happened, it runs them ahead: it draws their next looks from the model and makes them so. Crafting A Forecaster's screen, part by part. Watching It watches everything within four blocks of it, on its own level or one above or below, and writes a line for each block. Machines. It looks at each furnace, smoker, blast furnace, brewing stand, Fabricator and Smelter eight times an item, and writes down how far through its item it is: a when it has just begun, up to h at seven eighths. A furnace at work writes abcdefghabcdefghabcdefgh and a line ends once its machine has been seen idle twice: aa. A smoker cooks twice as fast as a furnace and is looked at twice as often, so its line reads the same, give or take a letter. A furnace that runs out of fuel halfway through an item cools back down, two ticks for every tick, and its line steps back: abcdefdbaa. Crops. Every twenty seconds it looks at every crop: wheat, carrots, potatoes, beetroots, the stems of pumpkins and melons, sweet berries, cocoa, nether wart and saplings. A crop's line is its age at every look, from 0 when planted to its last age when ripe (7 for wheat), ending once it has been seen ripe twice. 00000011111111122222223333333334444445555555666666677 Only what a block did by itself counts. A crop that is harvested, trampled or fed bone meal starts a new line, so its lines only ever hold what the field really does. Put a Field Log in the Log slot to keep a copy. Crafting (Shapeless) A model of the blocks A model that has learned what happens next is a model of its world, and the Forecaster asks for nothing more. Train one on Forecasting at a Model Core: the Forecast Dataset holds the lines of many fields and machines. Crafting (Shapeless) A machine keeps its pace. Given where it is now, its next look is all but settled, so a model of machines in general forecasts yours. Crops are another matter. How fast a crop grows depends on its field: wet farmland or dry, in tidy rows or crowded. A model that learned from many fields expects the growth of an average one. That is close enough on some fields and far off on others. To forecast your own field, train on it. Put the Forecaster's Field Log in a data slot of the Core, on its own, and the model learns this field's pace. It gets worse at fields in general, and may even fail the Forecasting test: that is the price of fitting one field well. Beside the Forecast Dataset, the log only pulls the model halfway. Calibration A forecast is only worth acting on if it is right on average. The Forecaster checks a model against everything it watched, lines still being written included: the crops that finish first are the ones that happened to grow fastest, so finished lines alone would flatter a model that expects too much. It checks crops and machines apart, once the crops have grown 100 ages by themselves, or the machines have made 100 eighths of items, about a dozen, at their own pace. At every look it adds up how far the model expected the block to move, and divides by how far it moved: Within 11% of 1, it runs those blocks four looks for every one. Within 25%, two. Further off, it refuses the model for them. The screen shows the blocks nearby from above, then how far they moved per look from each age or each eighth, for the kind picked with the tabs: amber for what the blocks did, teal for what the model expected. A model that expects too much from young crops, or too little from old ones, shows it there. Below, a row for each kind shows the progress seen so far, then how close the model came and how fast it runs them. A refused model is checked again each time those blocks have moved 25 more, and any model is checked again when it changes. Running ahead At every look, each growing crop's line goes to the model, which draws the crop's next look from its probabilities, then the next, as many as the model has earned. The crop grows to the age drawn. At every look at a machine, its line goes to the model the same way, and the machine works through the progress the model drew, a few ticks at a time: a furnace run four looks for every one cooks four items in the time of one, on the same fuel per item. A block being run ahead shimmers, faster the faster it runs: teal up to ×16, amber past that. Every look drawn is the model's own work. A model that is slow to answer, or a server busy with other askers, runs fewer looks ahead. Lines the model wrote, or that a machine was run ahead through, are never written down: the log only ever holds what the blocks did by themselves. Forecaster II Forecaster II watches and checks the same way, and runs blocks further ahead when its model comes closer: within 5% of what they did, eight looks for every one, and within 2.5%, sixteen. Every look it runs ahead is one more the model draws, so a block at ×16 asks fifteen of the model for each look the world takes; a slow model, or a busy server, runs fewer. The Fabricator makes it from a transformer photomask. A model of machines in general expects a run of items to end now and then, so it falls a few percent short of furnaces that never run out. One that has also learned from this Forecaster's own log knows better. Forecaster III Forecaster III does all that Forecaster II does, and also keeps power, up to 4,000,000 FE, taken through Power Cables, and spends it on bursts: for thirty seconds, every machine and crop around it of a kind its model is trusted with runs at a pace you pick, up to ×256. A burst has three prices. The model sets the fastest: sixteen times the pace it runs that kind of block ahead at, so ×256 needs a model within 2.5% of what those blocks did. The compute sets it too: ×32 needs 4 compute, and each doubling needs twice as much, up to 32 for ×256. One cooled 90 nm Training Accelerator supplies one unit; finer devices supply more. Join them directly, through each other or along Interconnect. The first four standalone Accelerators run free; every other device needs power. And the power pays for every tick: each machine takes one FE for each tick beyond its own, and eight crops take as much as a machine, so ×256 on sixteen machines burns 4,080 FE a tick. It runs at most sixteen machines at once. When the power runs out, the burst ends. Lines of blocks a burst ran are never written down, as with everything run ahead. The Fabricator makes it from a transformer photomask. The Hourglass The Hourglass keeps time while you carry it, a second for every second, up to an hour. The Fabricator makes it from an attention photomask, out of a Tensor Casing, four wafers and two weight crystals. Sneak-use a Forecaster to bind it. Then use it on a machine or a crop of a kind that Forecaster runs ahead, anywhere in the Forecaster's dimension while the Forecaster is loaded: the block runs twice as fast for thirty seconds. Use it on the block again before that ends and the pace doubles, for thirty seconds from then, up to sixteen times as fast. Each step costs twice the kept time of the one before: thirty seconds of it for twice as fast, four minutes for sixteen times. It works only on what its Forecaster's model is trusted with: while the model doesn't pass its check on machines, the Hourglass refuses machines too. A Forecaster never writes down the line of a block an Hourglass ran.

title: Getting Started
text: Getting Started A first model fits in a few blocks: a Model Core, an Embedding Table and some Signal Cable. It learns what the blocks around you do next. A Forecaster puts that to work: once its forecasts hold, your furnaces run four times as fast. Materials Tensor Casing is the shell of every machine; Weight Crystal holds learned numbers, so machines with weights need them. Crafting Crafting Then craft the Model Core, a stack of cables and a Forecast Dataset: endless lines of crops growing and machines at work, to learn from. Crafting Crafting Crafting (Shapeless) Machines are made in a Fabricator. With no photomask in it, it makes the Embedding Table from a casing, a Wafer and a weight crystal. Crafting Crafting (Shapeless) Build it Place the Model Core. Its front turns toward you: tokens come out of it. Lay a cable from the Core's front to a free spot a few blocks away. Place the Embedding Table against the end of that cable. It snaps into the flow: its back reads the cable and its front points away. Lay a cable from the table's front back to any other face of the Core: its sides, its top or its back. That is where the model's scores go in. Open the table and set Width to V (vocab). The two cables never touch, so they form two separate networks: one carries tokens to the table, the other carries the table's scores back. Train it Open the Core and put the Forecast Dataset in one of its Data slots. Switch to Train and press Train. Two curves fall: the loss on practice, and the loss on the test, which only uses lines the model never practised on. Each line in the dataset is one block, looked at again and again. A furnace's line is how far it is through the item it is making, from a just begun to h nearly done, then round again: abcdefghabcdefgh. A crop's line is its age at every look, from 0 to 7. An Embedding Table set to V scores the next look from the one before it, and for a machine the look before all but settles the next. When Forecasting on the Tests tab gets below 0.21, the model is ready. Save it Craft a Checkpoint, put it in the Core's checkpoint slot and press Save to checkpoint. The Core tests the model on every benchmark and keeps it, scores and all, in the crystal. The machines can go on training; the checkpoint keeps this moment. Crafting Run your furnaces ahead Craft a Forecaster and place it among your furnaces, smokers or blast furnaces: within four blocks, on its own level or one above or below. Put the checkpoint in its Model slot, and keep the furnaces fed and fuelled. Crafting The Forecaster looks at each machine eight times an item and writes down how far it got. Once the machines have made about a dozen items at their own pace, it checks the model against what they did. If the progress the model expects is within 11% of the progress there was, it runs them four looks for every one: the model draws each machine's next looks, and the machine works through them. Within 25%, two. The Forecaster tells the rest, crops included. Further Better models need machines built from designs: wire them yourself on a Bench, or go looking for the old ones in the ruins. Storage keeps what your furnaces make: a Port under each one carries it onto drives, and a Storage Terminal finds it again. Agents run programs you click together: they mine, carry, build and sort, and models fill in where learning beats a rule. Look at any machine to see its name, its output shape (or what is wrong with it) and what the face you are looking at does. Sneak-use a machine's face to point its output there. Training runs on its own threads. Place Training Accelerator blocks against the Core to give it more, and keep them cool.

title: Residual
text: Residual Someone lived in this world before you. They are no longer here, but traces of them still remain in the ruins. Most mysteriously, they seemed to have built machines that thought. These are field notes on building models again: language models made of machines that each do one operation, cabled into a network, trained on text, and tested on text they have never seen. A model that knows what the blocks around it will do next lets a Forecaster run them ahead of time. Others carry on a pattern, tell what a thing is by its name, turn what you say into programs for agents, and read what the old world wrote. Start here Getting Started: a first model, and furnaces that run four times as fast. The Bench and the Fabricator: machines wired from the smallest operations there are. Ruins: where the old world's things are. Milestones: every advancement, lit once you have made it, and how to make the rest. Models The Archive: shards, drives, and restoring what was lost. The Bench and the Fabricator: designs wired from primitives, and the machines made from them. The Model Core: where models are built, trained, tested and saved. Tokens: the BPE Forge, and vocabularies learned from the archive. The Refinery: a hall of machines that turns the raw traffic of fallen masts into a counted supply of tokens, and measures what each machine was worth. Training: reading a loss curve, and the settings that shape it. The Recipe: how a run's rate moves, what its numbers are rounded to, what moves its weights. The Modern Block: the layer the old world's last models seem to have been made of, and what each part of it does. Models and Tests: the benchmarks, checkpoints, and how big a model may be. Salvaged Models: broken models from the ruins. Putting models to work The Forecaster: a model of the blocks around it, trusted only as far as it is right, runs them ahead. Agents: frames that run programs, with models where learning beats a rule. Programs: one language for agents and Ports, what it can do, how fast and how far, and how to watch it run. The Architect: agents that copy, move and repeat builds, read as letters a slice at a time. The Surveyor: a model that finds the ores in the ground around it, read a row at a time. The Stream Scope: what a model does inside, drawn over its machines. The Trial Rig: what can go wrong with a model, done on purpose to a copy of it. Comparing Models: how much of a score is luck, whether it has seen the test, and what everyone else made. The Arena: a model that has learned how a mob fights plays it in a chamber, for what the mob drops. Serving Models: Model Servers, relays, gates, links and the Terminal. Tuning: changing a model that has finished practising, by what you choose and what a checker can verify. Thinking Longer: many answers to a question, and how to keep the right one. The base Storage: drives that keep any number of kinds, a terminal that finds anything, and Ports that move items between the network and every chest and machine, 1,280 a second. Power: generators from fire to steam to the sun, cables and cells, and a Smelter that makes two ingots from every ore, three with a controller. The Reactor: the most power there is, for a model that can hold it. Compute: process nodes, memory, racks and pods, and the ways of sharing out a run's work. Halls: cooling lines, what cooling costs, and a load you can read across the room. Flight: the flight frame, flown by a pilot you train. The Exosuit: armour with a quantized model on board, whose compute sets what the suit can do. Reference Machines and Cables: how values travel between blocks. The Residual Stream: the running sum every transformer layer reads and adds to. Shapes: what [B×T×C] means, and how to fix a shape error. Screens: every screen, part by part. Machines, one page each.

title: Activation
text: Activation Bends every number through the same nonlinear function. Without one, two Linear Layers in a row multiply out into a single Linear Layer, however many you stack: the activation is what lets depth add anything. Shapes Any shape in, the same shape out. Settings Function: ReLU by default. ReLU keeps positive numbers and zeroes the rest. Its slope is 0 or 1, so it never shrinks a gradient that passes. GELU is a smooth ReLU, used by GPT-2 and BERT. SiLU is z·σ(z), used inside the feed-forward layers of LLaMA and its relatives. tanh squashes into (−1, 1), as in the first neural language models. sigmoid squashes into (0, 1). Its slope is at most a quarter, so every sigmoid layer shrinks the gradient that passes back through it. Parameters None. In PyTorch F.relu(x) F.gelu(x, approximate="tanh") F.silu(x) torch.tanh(x) torch.sigmoid(x) Making it The Fabricator makes it from a photomask of GELU: verify the spec on a Bench, or find a salvaged mask in the ruins, which makes it unfused. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Residual Junction
text: Residual Junction Adds its two inputs, number by number. It has two jobs. It combines token and position vectors, and it makes residual connections: adding a branch's output back onto the stream that went into it, so the branch refines the stream instead of replacing it. Shapes Two equal shapes, or a smaller one that matches the end of the larger and repeats across it: [B×T×C] and [T×C] make [B×T×C]. Parameters None. In PyTorch x = x + self.attn(self.norm1(x)) Notes The identity term in its gradient gives every layer a direct path back to the loss. That is why stacks of residual layers keep learning when plain stacks stall. Making it The Fabricator makes it with no mask. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Attention Head
text: Attention Head Multi-head causal self-attention in one machine: the attention you can build from Linear Layers, a Matrix Multiplier, a Causal Mask and a Softmax, with queries, keys and values all computed from its one input, a causal mask built in, several heads and an output projection. One head with nothing learned yet: each token is a point, and that point is its own query, key and value. A token gives weight to what it can see by how far their vectors run along its own, and reads the weighted mean of them, the hollow square. Drag the points to see the weights follow, click a row to read another token, and take the mask away to see tokens read ahead. Training is what gives each token a query and a key of their own, through W_Q and W_K. Shapes A sequence [B×T×C] in, the same shape out. Settings Heads: 1, 2, 4 or 8. 4 by default. The width C must divide evenly by it. Each head works on C/H of the numbers and scales its scores by 1/√(C/H). Parameters 4 × C²: the matrices W_Q, W_K, W_V and W_O, without biases. In PyTorch self.attn = CausalSelfAttention(C, heads=4) x = x + self.attn(self.norm1(x)) Notes After training, its picture shows where its first head looks: one row per position, one column for every position it can see. Making it The Fabricator makes it from a photomask of Attention: verify the spec on a Bench, or find a salvaged mask in the ruins, which makes it unfused. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Causal Mask
text: Causal Mask Sets every score above the diagonal of a T × T grid to −∞. After a Softmax those become weights of exactly zero, so position t gives no weight to anything after t. Each row is what one token looks at. With the mask on, it sees itself and what came before, and the dark cells above the diagonal count for nothing. Take the mask away and every token reads the ones after it too. Shapes A grid of scores […×T×T] in, the same shape out. Parameters None. In PyTorch def causal_mask(scores): T = scores.shape[-1] future = torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T, dtype=torch.bool), diagonal=1) return scores.masked_fill(future, float("-inf")) Notes It belongs between the scores and the Softmax. Without it, a model trained to predict the next token can simply read it, and its loss falls to almost nothing while it learns nothing. Making it The Fabricator makes it with no mask. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Concatenator
text: Concatenator Joins two vectors end to end: the main input's numbers first, then the side input's. Shapes […×a] and […×b] in, […×(a + b)] out. Every size but the last must match. Parameters None. In PyTorch x = torch.cat([a, b], dim=-1) Notes A Linear Layer after a Concatenator computes the same thing as two Linear Layers, one on each input, added together. Making it The Fabricator makes it with no mask. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Embedding Table
text: Embedding Table Looks up a learned row of numbers for each token: token i gets row i of a table with one row per vocabulary entry. This is how text enters a model, so the table must be fed directly by the Model Core's front. Shapes Tokens [B×T] in, [B×T×C] out, where C is the Width. Settings Width: V, or 4 to 256. 32 by default. At V, each row can serve directly as the scores for the next token: a bigram model. Parameters V × C, drawn from a normal distribution with spread 1. In PyTorch self.embed = nn.Embedding(V, C) e = self.embed(tokens) Notes After training, the weights picture shows the table, a row per token. Tokens that behave alike end up with similar rows, which is how what the model learns about one carries over to others. Making it The Fabricator makes it with no mask. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Machines
text: Machines Each machine performs one operation of a model, with the same arithmetic as PyTorch. A machine takes its main input on its back and, if it has one, its side input on any other face, and sends its result out of its front: see Machines and Cables. Right-click a machine to change its settings and see what it computes. Every machine comes out of the Fabricator. The simple ones need no design; the rest need a photomask of the spec that describes them, verified on a Bench or salvaged from the ruins. A machine's screen, part by part. No design needed Embedding Table: token ids to vectors. Position Table: a learned vector for every position. Residual Junction: addition, and with it the residual stream. Gate: one signal opening or closing another. Scaler: multiplied by a constant, usually 1/√d. Causal Mask: the future hidden. Head Splitter and Head Merger: multi-head attention from parts. Delay Line: a fixed look back in time. Concatenator: two vectors joined end to end. From a design Matrix Multiplier, from Matrix Multiply: grids multiplied, keys compared with queries. Softmax, from Softmax: scores turned into weights. Linear Layer, from Linear Layer: a learned matrix, the workhorse of every model. Activation, from GELU: a nonlinear function on every number. Normalizer, from Layer Norm: vectors kept at a steady size. Attention Head, from Attention: multi-head attention in one machine. Feed-Forward Block, from Feed-Forward Block: widen, bend, project back. Transformer Block, from Transformer Block: a whole transformer layer. Two-Token Head, from Multi-Token Prediction: scores for the next token and the one after it. The modern block Every one of these from a design too: see The Modern Block. RMS Normalizer, from RMS Norm: vectors kept at a steady size, with less work. Gated Feed-Forward Block, from Gated Feed-Forward: a feed-forward block whose numbers have gates. Rotary Positions, from Rotary Positions: a token's place, told by turning it. QK Normalizer, from QK Norm: queries and keys compared at one size. Z-Loss Regulator, from Z-Loss: a small penalty that holds a model's scores near zero. Modern Attention Head, from Modern Attention: all of that in one attention machine. Modern Block, from Modern Block: a whole modern layer.

title: Linear Layer
text: Linear Layer Multiplies every vector by a learned matrix and adds a learned bias. It works on the last size only: every position of every sequence goes through the same weights, separately. Shapes […×C_in] in, […×C_out] out, where C_out is the Outputs setting. Settings Outputs: V, or 4 to 256. 32 by default.
