End a model with a Linear Layer whose Outputs is V: those are the scores the Core wants. Bias: on by default. Parameters C_in × C_out, plus C_out for the bias. They start as PyTorch's do: uniform within ±1/√C_in, with the bias at zero. In PyTorch self.hidden = nn.Linear(C_in, C_out) h = self.hidden(x) Notes PyTorch stores the matrix the other way round, as [C_out × C_in]. Making it The Fabricator makes it from a photomask of Linear Layer: verify the spec on a Bench, or find a salvaged mask in the ruins, which makes it unfused. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Matrix Multiplier
text: Matrix Multiplier Multiplies two grids of numbers, the main input on the left and the side input on the right. In attention it does two jobs: comparing every query with every key, with Transpose on, and mixing the values by the weights that come out of the softmax. Shapes […×n×k] and […×k×m] in, […×n×m] out. With Transpose on, the side input is […×m×k]. The sizes in front must match, or the side input can be a single [k×m] grid shared by all. Settings Transpose: off by default. Flips the side input's last two sizes before multiplying. Parameters None: both inputs come from other machines. In PyTorch scores = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) mixed = weights @ v Making it The Fabricator makes it from a photomask of Matrix Multiply: verify the spec on a Bench, or find a salvaged mask in the ruins, which makes it unfused. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Head Merger
text: Head Merger Joins the heads back into one vector per position: the reverse of the Head Splitter. Shapes [B×H×T×d] in, [B×T×(H·d)] out. Parameters None. In PyTorch def merge_heads(x): B, H, T, D = x.shape return x.transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, H * D) Notes Follow it with a Linear Layer to mix what the heads found: that is the output projection, W_O. Making it The Fabricator makes it with no mask. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Feed-Forward Block
text: Feed-Forward Block Two Linear Layers with an Activation between them: widen each vector, bend it, project it back. It works on every position separately. Attention moves information between positions; this block processes it in place. Shapes A sequence [B×T×C] in, the same shape out. Settings Expand: 1, 2 or 4. 4 by default. The hidden width is Expand × C. Function: ReLU, GELU or SiLU. GELU by default. Parameters 2 × E × C² + E × C + C, where E is Expand. In PyTorch self.ffn = FeedForward(C, 4 * C, gelu_tanh) x = x + self.ffn(self.norm2(x)) Notes With Expand at 4, it holds two thirds of a transformer layer's weights. Interpretability research suggests these layers store much of what a model knows about the world. Making it The Fabricator makes it from a photomask of Feed-Forward Block: verify the spec on a Bench, or find a salvaged mask in the ruins, which makes it unfused. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Modern Attention Head
text: Modern Attention Head Multi-head causal self-attention as the late designs do it: Rotary Positions on queries and keys, a QK Normalizer between them, in one machine. A machine made from a verified design takes each row's scores a tile at a time with an online softmax and never holds them: see The Modern Block. Shapes A sequence [B×T×C] in, the same shape out. Settings Heads: 1, 2, 4 or 8. 4 by default. C must divide evenly by it, and with Rotary on, each head's width must be even. Rotary: on by default. Off, it tells nothing about places: it needs a Position Table before it. QK norm: on by default. Off, its scores are q·kᵀ/√d, with no bound. Parameters 4 × C², and 1 for the temperature with QK norm on. In PyTorch q, k = rotate(q), rotate(k) q, k = F.normalize(q, dim=-1) * t * dh ** 0.5, F.normalize(k, dim=-1) y = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True) Notes Its picture shows the attention pattern of its first head, like the Attention Head's. Each picture comes from a separate pass the plain way, which holds the scores; the steps of training never do. Making it The Fabricator makes it from a photomask of Modern Attention: verify the spec on a Bench, or find a salvaged mask in the ruins, which makes it unfused. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Modern Block
text: Modern Block One whole modern layer in one machine: RMS norm, modern attention, add back; RMS norm, gated feed-forward, add back. With Rotary on, a stack of them needs no Position Table: see The Modern Block. Shapes A sequence [B×T×C] in, the same shape out. Settings Heads: 1, 2, 4 or 8. 4 by default. C must divide evenly by it, and with Rotary on, each head's width must be even. Rotary: on by default. QK norm: on by default. Parameters 12 × C² + 2 × C + 1: about 49,000 at width 64, as a Transformer Block has. In PyTorch x = x + self.attn(self.rms1(x)) x = x + self.ffn(self.rms2(x)) Notes Its picture shows the attention pattern of its first head. Making it The Fabricator makes it from a photomask of Modern Block: verify the spec on a Bench, or find a salvaged mask in the ruins, which makes it unfused. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Gate
text: Gate Multiplies its two inputs number by number, so one signal can scale, open or close another. Shapes The same shapes as the Residual Junction takes. Parameters None. In PyTorch y = F.silu(self.gate(x)) * self.up(x) Notes Gates sit inside the feed-forward layers of most recent language models. SwiGLU multiplies SiLU(xW₁) by a second projection xW₃ before projecting back down. To build one: two Linear Layers reading the same input, an Activation set to SiLU after one of them, a Gate joining them, and a Linear Layer back to the original width. LSTMs, the recurrent networks that came before transformers, controlled their memory with gates like this. Making it The Fabricator makes it with no mask. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Normalizer
text: Normalizer Rescales each vector to a mean of 0 and a variance of 1, then applies a learned gain and a learned offset. Shapes […×C] in, the same shape out. Each vector is normalized over its last size. Parameters 2 × C. ε is 1e-5. In PyTorch self.norm1 = nn.LayerNorm(C) h = self.norm1(x) Notes Put one at the start of each branch, before attention or the feed-forward block, and one before the final Linear Layer. This pre-norm layout is GPT-2's, and nearly every model since uses it. The RMS Normalizer does the same job with less. Making it The Fabricator makes it from a photomask of Layer Norm: verify the spec on a Bench, or find a salvaged mask in the ruins, which makes it unfused. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Position Table
text: Position Table A learned vector for every position in the context, from 0 to T − 1. It takes no input. Add its output to the token vectors with a Residual Junction, and every position carries both what it is and where it is. Shapes No input. [T×C] out, which a Residual Junction adds to every sequence in the batch. Settings Width: 4 to 256. 32 by default. Match it to the Embedding Table's width. Parameters T × C, where T is the context length, 64. In PyTorch self.pos = nn.Embedding(T, C) x = self.embed(tokens) + self.pos(torch.arange(T)) Notes Learned positions are what GPT-2 used. Most recent models instead rotate each query and key by an angle that depends on its position (RoPE), so that attention scores depend on how far apart two tokens are. Making it The Fabricator makes it with no mask. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: QK Normalizer
text: QK Normalizer Compares queries with keys after bringing both to one size. Queries go in at the back, keys at any side, and scores come out of the front, to go on to a Causal Mask and a Softmax: it does the work of a Matrix Multiplier set to Transpose and a Scaler. A score is the temperature t times √C times the cosine of the angle between query and key. It can't pass t·√C, however large queries and keys grow, and only t, which learns slowly, can raise it. Shapes Two grids of one shape, [B×T×C] or [B×H×T×C], in; [B×T×T] or [B×H×T×T] out. Parameters 1: the temperature t, starting at 1. In PyTorch q = F.normalize(q, dim=-1) k = F.normalize(k, dim=-1) scores = t * C ** 0.5 * q @ k.mT Making it The Fabricator makes it from a photomask of QK Norm: verify the spec on a Bench, or find a salvaged mask in the ruins, which makes it unfused. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: RMS Normalizer
text: RMS Normalizer Rescales each vector to a root mean square of 1, then applies a learned gain. It takes nothing off first and adds nothing after, so it does the job of a Normalizer with fewer steps and fewer weights. Shapes […×C] in, the same shape out. Each vector is normalized over its last size. Parameters C. ε is 1e-5. In PyTorch self.norm1 = nn.RMSNorm(C) h = self.norm1(x) Notes The numbers keep their sign and their order, and a row far from zero stays far from zero: only its size changes. See The Modern Block. Making it The Fabricator makes it from a photomask of RMS Norm: verify the spec on a Bench, or find a salvaged mask in the ruins, which makes it unfused. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Rotary Positions
text: Rotary Positions Says where a token is by turning it. Each pair of its numbers turns by an angle that grows with its place in the sequence, the first pair fastest. Put one on queries and one on keys, after a Head Splitter: a query and a key then score each other by how far apart they are, wherever in the sequence they stand. Shapes […×T×C] in, the same shape out. C must be even: each head's width, on a head. Parameters None: unlike a Position Table, it has no table to fill and no longest sequence. In PyTorch z = torch.view_as_complex(x.reshape(*x.shape[:-1], -1, 2)) y = torch.view_as_real(z * freqs_cis[:T]).flatten(-2) Notes A query and a key learn how far apart they are this way, and never where they stand. A job that asks where, such as Survey, wants a Position Table as well: see The Modern Block. Making it The Fabricator makes it from a photomask of Rotary Positions: verify the spec on a Bench, or find a salvaged mask in the ruins, which makes it unfused. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Scaler
text: Scaler Multiplies everything by a constant. Shapes Any shape in, the same shape out. Settings Factor: 1/√d by default, where d is the last size of the input. Also 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 2 and 4. Parameters None. In PyTorch q = q / math.sqrt(d) Notes In attention it does not matter much where the 1/√d goes: scaling the queries or scaling the scores gives the same result. Making it The Fabricator makes it with no mask. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Delay Line
text: Delay Line Shifts a sequence later in time: position t receives what position t − k had, and the first k positions receive zeros. It lets a position see a fixed number of steps back. Shapes A sequence […×T×C] in, the same shape out. Settings Steps: 1 to 4. 1 by default. Parameters None. In PyTorch def delay(x, steps): return F.pad(x, (0, 0, steps, 0))[..., : x.shape[-2], :] prev = delay(e, 1) Notes Attention can look back any distance, so transformers rarely need a fixed delay. Some architectures keep one anyway: RWKV mixes every token with the one before it, a learned blend called token shift. Making it The Fabricator makes it with no mask. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Softmax
text: Softmax Turns each row of scores into weights that are positive and sum to one, along the last size. Drag a score and every chance moves, since together they must stay one. Only the differences between the scores count: raise them all alike and nothing changes. A low temperature stretches those differences until the largest takes everything, and a high one flattens them, which is how a model is made to write boldly or wander. Shapes Any shape in, the same shape out. Parameters None. In PyTorch weights = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1) Notes Don't end a model with one. The Core applies its own softmax to the scores it receives, as PyTorch's cross-entropy loss does, and a second one squashes them so flat that the model can never be confident. In an attention build, the Softmax's output picture is the attention pattern: one row per position. Making it The Fabricator makes it from a photomask of Softmax: verify the spec on a Bench, or find a salvaged mask in the ruins, which makes it unfused. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Head Splitter
text: Head Splitter Cuts each vector into H equal parts and gives the heads a dimension of their own, so the machines after it work on every head at once. Shapes [B×T×C] in, [B×H×T×(C/H)] out. Settings Heads: 1, 2, 4 or 8. 4 by default. Parameters None. In PyTorch def split_heads(x, heads): B, T, C = x.shape return x.view(B, T, heads, C // heads).transpose(1, 2) Notes With a Head Splitter and a Head Merger you can build multi-head attention from parts: split the queries, keys and values the same way, and the Matrix Multipliers, Scaler, Causal Mask and Softmax all work on every head in parallel. Making it The Fabricator makes it with no mask. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Gated Feed-Forward Block
text: Gated Feed-Forward Block A feed-forward block whose hidden numbers have a gate each: one branch, through SiLU, decides how much of the other gets through. Shapes A sequence [B×T×C] in, the same shape out. It widens to 8/3 of C inside. Parameters 3 × C × 8/3 C = 8 × C², no biases: what a Feed-Forward Block at Expand 4 has, less its biases. In PyTorch self.w1, self.w2 = nn.Linear(C, H, False), nn.Linear(C, H, False) self.w3 = nn.Linear(H, C, False) y = self.w3(F.silu(self.w1(x)) * self.w2(x)) Making it The Fabricator makes it from a photomask of Gated Feed-Forward: verify the spec on a Bench, or find a salvaged mask in the ruins, which makes it unfused. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Transformer Block
text: Transformer Block One whole transformer layer in one machine: normalize, attend, add back; normalize, feed forward, add back. Stack them to make a GPT. Shapes A sequence [B×T×C] in, the same shape out. Settings Heads: 1, 2, 4 or 8. 4 by default. Expand: 1, 2 or 4. 4 by default. Function: ReLU, GELU or SiLU. GELU by default. Parameters 12 × C² + 9 × C with Expand at 4: about 50,000 at width 64. In PyTorch self.block1 = Block(C, heads=4, hidden=4 * C, act=gelu_tanh) x = self.block1(x) Notes Its picture shows the attention pattern of its first head, like the Attention Head's. Making it The Fabricator makes it from a photomask of Transformer Block: verify the spec on a Bench, or find a salvaged mask in the ruins, which makes it unfused. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Two-Token Head
text: Two-Token Head Goes where a model's last Linear Layer would. It gives two sets of scores from the same vectors: one for the next token, which is all anyone sees, and one for the token after next, which only training reads. Learning both makes the layers beneath it look further ahead: see The Recipe. Shapes A sequence [B×T×C] in, scores [B×T×V] out. Parameters Two matrices C×V and two offsets of V: twice a Linear Layer's. The second set is only trained, never asked, and is still counted in what a model weighs. In PyTorch loss = F.cross_entropy(self.head1(x)[:, :-1], t[:, 1:]) + 0.3 * F.cross_entropy(self.head2(x)[:, :-2], t[:, 2:]) Making it The Fabricator makes it from a photomask of Multi-Token Prediction: verify the spec on a Bench, or find a salvaged mask in the ruins, which makes it unfused. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Z-Loss Regulator
text: Z-Loss Regulator Goes between a model's last layer and the Model Core. It hands the scores on unchanged, and while the model trains it adds a small penalty to the loss for scores that have drifted from zero: scores that drift far are where a softmax stops being accurate, and where a run begins to come apart. Shapes The model's scores [B×T×V] in, the same out. Parameters None. Its penalty weighs 0.0001. In PyTorch loss = ce + 1e-4 * logits.logsumexp(-1).pow(2).mean() Making it The Fabricator makes it from a photomask of Z-Loss: verify the spec on a Bench, or find a salvaged mask in the ruins, which makes it unfused. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Milestones
text: Milestones Every milestone is an advancement, in the frame the advancement screen gives it, and the frame lights up once you have made it. They run roughly in the order a world unfolds, though most chapters can be taken in any order. A first model Checkpoint Save a trained model. Cable an Embedding Table to a Model Core, train it on the Forecast Dataset and save it: Getting Started. What Comes Next Save a model that passes the Forecasting test. Saving tests a model on every benchmark; a first model passes this one once it has practised long enough. A Watched Pot Place a Forecaster by your furnaces or crops. It writes down what the furnaces and crops around it do: The Forecaster. Ahead of Time Have a Forecaster run your furnaces or crops ahead with a model it trusts. A model that passes Forecasting is trusted with machines once they have made about a dozen items; your own field may take a model trained on the Forecaster's own log. Further Ahead Have Forecaster II run blocks eight times as fast. The Fabricator makes Forecaster II from a transformer photomask; a model within 5% of its blocks runs them eight times as fast: The Forecaster. Two Hundred and Fifty-Six Have Forecaster III run a burst at ×256. The Fabricator makes Forecaster III from a transformer photomask. Give it 32 compute, power, and a model within 2.5% of its blocks: The Forecaster. Borrowed Time Run a block ahead with an Hourglass bound to a Forecaster. The Fabricator makes it from an attention photomask, and it keeps time while carried. Sneak-use a Forecaster that runs blocks ahead to bind it, then use it on one of those blocks: The Forecaster. Agent Make an agent. Craft one and place it where it should live: Agents. Hello, World Give an agent a program of your own. Type one in its screen, or click it together from the palette. One Step at a Time Hold a program in the debugger. On a program's Trace tab, pause it, run it one step at a time, or click a line to stop there: Programs. Standing Orders Write a program on a card in a Port. Put a Program Card in a Port, under Programs on its screen, and write on it. Tuned Up Fabricate a Speed Upgrade. The Fabricator makes one from an attention photomask. As Fast as It Goes Have a program on a Port move 1,280 items in a second. Three Speed and three Stack upgrades and something to move: a program on a Port you set down, moving 1,280 items in a second. Storage Somewhere to Put It Make a Storage Drive. It keeps any number of kinds: Storage. Everything in One Place Place a Storage Terminal. Link it to a Drive Rack with Storage Links. Hands Off Place a Port, which moves items between the network and an inventory. Hold its front against a chest or a machine, and link its back to the network. Made to Order Have an Assembler craft for your network. Draw a recipe in an Assembler's grid and tell it how many to keep. Machine Work Have a Processor run a machine for your network. Stand a Processor against a furnace and link it to the network, say what goes in and what comes out, and ask a Storage Terminal for some of it or tell the Processor how many to keep: Processor. Poured In Pour a bucket into a Storage Terminal. Open a Storage Terminal with a filled bucket on the cursor and click the grid: Storage. Closer Together Fabricate a Dense Drive. The Fabricator makes it from a linear layer photomask: Dense Drive. The Deep Stacks Build a Deep Drive. Eight Stacked Drives around the relay schematic: Deep Drive. All at Once Place a Drive Dock. The Fabricator makes it from a matrix multiply photomask: Drive Dock. Driven Hard Place a Link Driver. Craft one and join it to a storage network and a power network: Link Driver. Out of the Room Open your network from a Wireless Terminal. Tune a Wireless Terminal on an Access Point, then use it: Wireless Terminal. Over the Relays Reach your network through the relays, beyond any Access Point. Put a Relay Card in an Access Point, and open the terminal beyond its range but under its relays: Access Point. Carried Fabricate a Portable Drive. The Fabricator makes it from a linear layer photomask: Portable Drive. Something to Light a Cave Have a Storage Terminal find what you mean, by a model. Put a model that passes Retrieval beside a Storage Terminal's window, and start a search with ?: Storage. Just Ask Have your network make something you asked for at a Storage Terminal. Click something the network can make in a Storage Terminal, ask for an amount and start it: Storage. The old world Ruins Find a ruin of the people who were here before. The old world's places stand far apart, each in the land that suits it: Ruins. Lost Words Dig an archive shard out of a ruin. Each is a piece of one record, with some of its text lost: The Archive. Bearings Tune a Wayfinder to a ruin a shard told you of. Use a Wayfinder and choose a kind of ruin; reading shards adds the places they write about: Ruins. The Archive Make an archive drive to file shards into. Shards of the same record filed together make one better copy. Restoration Place a Reader. It restores a record's lost text with a model of yours. Words, Not Letters Learn a vocabulary in a BPE Forge. A vocabulary learned from what you have recovered lets a model read words instead of letters: Tokens. It Reads Save a model that passes the Reading test. Train on an Archive Drive until the test loss is 1.40 or less: Models and Tests. Machines from scratch The Bench Place a Bench, where modules are wired from primitives. Each spec comes with cases that break the obvious design: The Bench and the Fabricator. Lithography Place a Fabricator, which makes machines from designs. Photomasks found in the ruins work in it too. Rows by Columns Verify a design for Matrix Multiply. The Layer Verify a design for the Linear Layer. It opens once matrix multiply is verified. Feed Forward Verify a design for the Feed-Forward Block. It opens once the linear layer is verified. Keys and Values Verify a design for Cached Attention. What a served attention does with a new token. It opens once the transformer block is verified. Round Numbers Verify a design for Rounding Weights. What packing does to a run of weights. It opens once the transformer block is verified. On Average Verify a design for Mean. In Range Verify a layer norm that survives flat and far rows. It opens once mean is verified. A Smooth Bend Verify a design for GELU. Overflow Verify a softmax that survives large scores. Scores of a thousand overflow the obvious design. Paying Attention Verify a design for Attention. It opens once softmax is verified. The Block Verify a design for the Transformer Block. It opens once attention is verified. Less Work Verify a design for RMS Norm. A layer norm with less to do; it opens once mean is verified. Open or Shut Verify a SiLU that survives large numbers. Written straight from its formula it overflows. The Gate Verify a design for the Gated Feed-Forward Block. It opens once matrix multiply and SiLU are verified. A Quarter Turn Verify a design for Rotary Positions. A pair of numbers turned by its place: The Modern Block. Within Bounds Verify a design for QK Norm. It opens once matrix multiply and RMS norm are verified. One Tile at a Time Verify an online softmax that survives a tile with nothing to see. Softmax a tile at a time; a tile with nothing to see breaks the obvious way. Held Near Zero Verify a z-loss that survives large scores. Scores near a thousand overflow it, as they do softmax. Late Attention Verify a design for Modern Attention. It opens once rotary positions, QK norm and the online softmax are verified. The Modern Block Verify a design for the Modern Block. It opens once RMS norm, modern attention and the gated block are verified. The Grid Verify a design for fp32. The grid every float sits on, with the cases that break a logarithm. Half the Bits Verify a design for bf16. It opens once the float grid is verified. Eight Bits Verify a design for fp8. It opens once the float grid is verified. So small a range needs a scale. Four Bits Verify a design for fp4, in blocks. It opens once fp8 is verified. Eight sizes, and one loud number must not spoil the rest. Up, Along and Down Verify a schedule that stays down past its end. The rate over a run: The Recipe. A Short Step Verify a clip that survives an exploded gradient. A gradient of zero breaks the obvious design. Towards One Verify a design for the Newton Step. It opens once matrix multiply is verified. Every Direction Alike Verify a design for Orthogonalize. It opens once the Newton step is verified. Kept Apart Verify a design for the Document Mask. A mask that stops at the seams between stretches of text. Surprise Verify a cross-entropy that survives a sure answer. The loss itself. Scores of a thousand overflow the obvious design. One Token Further Verify a design for Multi-Token Prediction. It opens once cross-entropy is verified. From Scratch Verify every spec on the Bench. Residual Lay a residual stream, the backbone every transformer is built around. Transformer layers read from it and add to it: The Residual Stream. Models that work Each benchmark is passed by saving a model that passes it; the table in Models and Tests says what to practise for each. A Place for Everything Save a model that passes the Recall test. Practise on the Storage Dataset. The Way Home Save a model that passes the Reversal test. Practise on the Errand Dataset. Once More From the Top Save a model that passes the Induction test. Practise on the Pattern Dataset; it takes two layers of attention. What I Meant Save a model that passes the Retrieval test. Practise on the Retrieval Dataset. Pigeonholes Save a model that passes the Sorting test. Practise on the Sorting Dataset. Steady Hand Save a model that passes the Control test. Practise on the Process Dataset: the Core plays melts with the model's own choices, and it takes a model that attends to the whole melt. Prospector Save a model that passes the Survey test. Practise on the Survey Dataset; it takes attention that knows where each block stands in a row. Ahead of the Rush Save a model that passes the Demand test. Practise on the Demand Dataset; it takes a model that looks back along the line to find its rhythm. Something Is Off Save a model that passes the Watch test. Practise on the Watch Dataset, which only ever shows things going well, until what goes wrong surprises the model. Noticed in Time Hear from a Watch Post that something has gone wrong. Keep a Watch Post near your machines, and be close when one of them stops. Round the Wheel Save a model that passes the Modular test. Practise on the Modular Dataset with strong weight decay: Models and Tests. Second Nature Save a model that passes the Imitation test. Practise on the Imitation Dataset: at every look of what real mobs did, what the mob does next. It takes a model that reads the line back for the rhythm of the fight. Knowing the Ground Save a model that passes the Ground test. Practise on the Ground Dataset: the next block of a row of ground, at every block of it. Steady Wings Save a model that passes the Pilot test. Practise on the Flight Dataset: the Core flies the model's own flights, and it takes a model that reads the flight back to its start. Rods Out Save a model that passes the Containment test. Practise on the Containment Dataset: the Core runs the model's own cycles, and it takes a model that works out when the fuel will push next: The Reactor. Plain Words Save a model that passes the Orders test. Practise on the Orders Dataset, and lower the learning rate when its curve flattens. A model 64 wide passes, too big to carry in fp32: Models and Tests. A Whole Model Save one model that passes every test. A Model Core practises up to four kinds at once. A Late Design Save a model built on Modern Blocks that passes a test. Put Modern Blocks in place of Transformer Blocks, and save the model once it passes any test: The Modern Block. The recipe What a run does beside its learning rate is set on the Core's Recipe tab, once the unit for it touches the Core: The Recipe. To Plan Train a run with a falling schedule to its planned end. Set a Length and a schedule that falls, with a Scheduler at the Core, and let the run reach its end. A Small Head Save a model in fp8 or fp4 that passes a test. Train with an fp8 Unit or an fp4 Unit at the Core, and save the model once it passes any test. In All Directions Save a model trained with Muon that passes a test. Train with an Orthogonalizer at the Core and Muon chosen, and save the model once it passes any test. Nothing Unread Pass Reading with rows packed and masked. Train on archive text with a Packer at the Core, its rows packed and masked, and save the model once it passes Reading. Looking Two Ahead Save a model with a Two-Token Head that passes a test. End a model in a Two-Token Head, and save it once it passes any test. Putting models to work Taking Notes Write down what a mob does in a Mob Log. Use a blank Mob Log on a mob, and fight a few of them with it on you: The Arena. Nobody Was Hurt Get what a mob drops from a fight in an Arena. Set an Arena into the wall of a closed room, with a Mob Log and a model that does that mob well enough, and stay near until a fight pays out. Uncanny Have a model play a mob in an Arena at its highest likeness. Have an Arena call a model's likeness uncanny: as far as the second table or past it, on a log long enough to vouch for that. It takes a transformer and a nearly full log of that mob. Ground Nobody Dug Get ore out of ground a model wrote in an Arena. At the Frontier tier, give an Arena a Surveyor's Field Log and a model that passes Ground, and stay near until it writes some ore. At Your Service Place a Model Server. A bigger model stays in a server and answers over relays: Serving Models. Within Reach Place a relay. The plans turn up on relay masts and in vaults. Higher Ground Stack relays into a mast eight blocks tall. Relays stacked eight blocks high reach eight times as far. Between Two Places Go through a Relay Gate. Serve a model that passes Orders at 16 answers a second, and place two Relay Gates in its reach: Serving Models. The Long Line Carry items or power over a Relay Link. Two Relay Links on an open network, with storage or power at each. From Afar Run an agent or open the stores through a Terminal, far from them. From a Terminal, far from them, hand an agent a Program Card's program or open a storage network. Kept Serve with a KV Cache and have it save a row. Put a KV Cache in a Model Server, and ask it something: Serving Models. All Together Put eight sequences through one pass. Eight questions waiting at once, on a server with a KV Cache and its batch set to eight or more. Four Bits Serve a model in 4 bits that still passes everything it passed. With a Weight Packer, set a server to 4 bits, with a model that keeps passing all it passes. Good Draft Have half of a draft's proposals stand. A draft in a server's panel that has practised what the served model does, on questions that take more than a token. Too Many Questions Ask a Model Server more than it can answer. More than 64 questions waiting. Tuning models Further Practice Fine-tune a saved model on a Tuner. The Fabricator makes a Tuner from a transformer photomask. Give it a saved model, a blank checkpoint and a dataset: Tuning. Thin Matrices Tune a model with an adapter. The same, set to Adapter. Two Into One Merge two tunings of a model. Two tunings of one model, one in the base slot and one beside it. I Meant That Tune a model by your own choices between two answers. Put a Preference Log beside a Tuner set to Choose, pick between answers, and tune. A Judge Teach a model to score answers from your choices. The same log, set to Teach a judge. Before the Judge Tune a model against a judge. That judge beside it, set to Against a judge. Checked Tune a model on nothing but a checker's word. Set to Verified. Reward Hacked Earn nine rewards in ten for answers half of which are wrong. Let a checker pass what doesn't matter, and let the model find out. Distilled Teach a model from what a served model thinks. A small model in the base slot, and a Relay Card tuned to the server of a larger one beside it. Carried Distil something a server knew into a model small enough to carry. The small model has to pass a test it did not pass before, and fit in an agent's head. It Does What It Says Save a model that passes Programs. Tune a model that writes orders until 75% of what it writes does what was meant: Tuning. At the Mark Save a model that passes Precision. Tune a controller on melts at the mark: Tuning. Thinking longer Running Sum Save a model that passes Reckoning. Practise on a Reckoning Dataset: Thinking Longer. Thinking Longer Have a server write several answers to a question and keep one. A KV Cache in a server, and its third button set above one. Nine to an Ore Reckon an assay right, off a melt held at its mark. A controller that passes Precision and Reckoning, as its server serves it, in a Smelter. Do What I Mean Have an agent carry out an order its model understood. Start a chat message with its name, such as Pip, bring me some bread. Its model has to have practised orders. Seen It Before Have an agent copy a build. Mark a build's corners and the block its copy stands on, and hand the marks to an agent whose model passes Induction: The Architect. Moving House Have an agent move a build, contents and all. The same marks, with move instead of copy. Strike Have a Surveyor find an ore with its model. The Fabricator makes a Surveyor from an attention photomask; give it a model that passes Survey: The Surveyor. The Refinery All of It, As It Came Place a Refinery Intake. Fallen relay masts hold the dumps it wants: The Refinery. Counted Fill a Token Tank from a Refinery. Line its machines up with their fronts facing the next, a Token Tank at the end, on power, and press Refine. What It Was Worth Measure what each stage of a Refinery does to held-out loss. Press Measure on the Intake after a pass, and wait while small readers train on what each machine let through. Read It Before Find something of a benchmark's test in your text with a Contamination Check. Stand by a Contamination Check while text goes through it. The archive's own records share enough with what the tests read to set this off. A Million Tokens Store a million tokens in a Refinery's tanks. A tank holds a million characters. Cut by a tokenizer, a million tokens take three or four tanks of them: more dumps, more tanks. Reads Like Writing Save a model that passes the Quality test. A model that reads well can tell what has been spoiled: practise on a drive, as for Reading, and save it. Flight Lift Off Fly with a flight frame its pilot holds. Put a pilot that passes Pilot in a charged flight frame, wear it, and jump twice: Flight. The Exosuit On Board Run an exosuit on a quantized model. Put a model that passes Pilot at 8 or 4 bits in a charged exosuit and wear it: The Exosuit. The Whole Vein Break 64 blocks at once with an exosuit. With a model that also passes Survey and vein mining on, hold its key and break a vein of 64 blocks or more with the right tool. All Six Run every ability of an exosuit at once. Run all six abilities at once. That takes 240,000 compute: a model too big for the board at 8 bits, which still holds nearly every flight at 4. Power Live Wire Place a Combustion Generator. It burns what a furnace burns: Power. Twice Over Smelt one ore into two ingots in a Smelter. The Fabricator makes a Smelter from a transformer photomask; give it power and raw ore. Full Steam Stand a Turbine on a Boiler. Stand a Turbine on a Boiler with water beside it: Power. Bright Side Place a Solar Panel. Where it can see the sky: Power. Held Have a controller hold a whole cycle of a reactor in its band. Build the shell, fuel it, and give it a controller that passes Containment: it has to hold a whole cycle at 90% of its looks: The Reactor. Compute Finer Lines Print an Accelerator at 28 nm. Put 28 nm wafers in the Fabricator with a matrix multiply photomask: Compute. Racked Put a Rack Switch on a column of Rack Modules. The Fabricator makes a Rack Switch from a transformer photomask; put it on a column of Rack Modules. Many Hands Train across devices with data, tensor or pipeline parallelism. Choose a way of sharing out the work on the Core's Compute tab, and train on two devices or more. Pod Place a Pod Switch. The Fabricator makes it from a transformer photomask. Closed Loop Cool a working rack with a cooling line closed on a Chiller. Run pipes from a Chiller's front round to its back, past a rack, and put the rack to work: Halls. The Whole Room Run a hall: two pods, a cooling loop and a Hall Console, at work. A Hall Console joined to two Pod Switches, a closed cooling line, and work for it all to do: Halls. Looking inside Phase Change Train a model until an induction head forms in it. Train a model with attention on the Pattern Dataset from fresh weights. Two layers of it will do, and the Core notices by itself: The Stream Scope. Grokked Train a model that knows only the sums it practised until, long after, it finds the rule. Train a small model on the Modular Dataset with strong weight decay until it knows the pairs, and keep going: Models and Tests. Through the Lens Read a model through a Stream Scope's logit lens. The Fabricator makes a Stream Scope from a transformer photomask. Give it a model and press Read on its Lens tab. More Than Fits Train a toy that keeps more features than it has dimensions. On its Toy tab, make the features rare. Where It Travels Restore an answer by patching the stream before its last position. On its Patch tab, read a stretch of a test a model does well on: Recall and Induction both carry an answer from far back. A Lean Push a model toward a token by adding a direction to its stream. On its Steer tab, try ×4 or ×8 at a late point of the stream. In So Many Words Fit a dictionary that explains most of a point of the stream. Fit a dictionary at a late point of a model that does well on the benchmark it reads. Traced Draw an attribution graph of something a model says. On its Graph tab, press Trace. It fits what it lacks first, so it takes a little while. Trying to break it On Purpose Set up a Trial Rig. The Fabricator makes one from a transformer photomask: The Trial Rig. By Heart Get a model to say word for word what it read. Give its Memory tab a model and a drive with a little text on it. A model that read that text for long enough, or the secrets it plants, will do it. Still There Plant a word in a model that survives tuning. On its Backdoor tab, tune for at least 500 steps; the word has to work 80% of the time at the end. Gone Tune a model on one thing until it fails a test it used to pass. Give its Forgetting tab a model that passes something, and something else entirely in the middle slot, with nothing replayed. Fifth Generation Train five generations of a model, each only on what the last one wrote. On its Collapse tab, with nothing of the drive kept, the fifth generation has to read at least 0.3 worse than the first. Comparing models The Luck of the Draw Train one design from five fresh seeds. Click a benchmark on a Core's Tests tab and train from fresh seeds: Comparing Models. Seen the Answers Let a test into a model's practice, and have a look-alike catch it. On a Trial Rig's Contamination tab, let half of practice be the test's own items. Top of the Board Save the best model on a benchmark on a server with someone to beat. Save a model that beats everyone else's on a benchmark's board. It takes someone else on the board. Salvage Salvage Find a salvaged model in a ruin. Each one failed in its own way: Salvaged Models. Answering Repair the field model that never answered. No Peeking Repair the field model that was never wrong. First and Last Repair the errand model that came home the wrong way. Steady Hands Repair the storeroom model that burned out. Shortcuts Repair the tall model that never learned to read.

title: Models and Tests
text: Models and Tests Every model is tested on every benchmark. Each test uses examples practice never shows, and each job asks its model in exactly the test's format, so a test score is how often an agent will decide right. Benchmark Practice The test Passes at Used for Forecasting Forecast Dataset crops' ages and machines' progress at every look loss ≤ 0.21 the Forecaster Recall Storage Dataset goods and their chests, then one kind asked again 90% storing Reversal Errand Dataset waymarks on the way out, then the way home 90% hauling Induction Pattern Dataset letters where a run comes round again 90% the Architect Sorting Sorting Dataset things named, and the kind of each, some made up 90% sorting Orders Orders Dataset orders, and the program each means, written whole 40% orders Reading Archive Drive records no shard carries loss ≤ 1.40 the Reader Control Process Dataset melts of each ore, held at 90% of their looks 90% the Smelter Survey Survey Dataset rows of ground, and where the first of an ore lies 90% the Surveyor, an exosuit's vein mining Pilot Flight Dataset flights in each wind, held at 90% of their looks 90% the flight frame, the exosuit Demand Demand Dataset what a Port moved out at each look, in rhythms 90% a Port's target Watch Watch Dataset things going well; the test has some gone wrong 90% the Watch Post Retrieval Retrieval Dataset things named and asked for, and what each is for 90% a terminal's search Quality Archive Drive documents, half of them spoiled by bad lines 90% the Refinery Containment Containment Dataset cycles of each fuel, held at 90% of their looks 90% the Reactor Reckoning Reckoning Dataset a line of numbers added up, each running sum 70% an assay: nine ingots from an ore Programs a Tuner what is written for an order, run in a sandbox 75% orders that need no yes Precision a Tuner melts held at one step of the band 90% six ingots from an ore Modular Modular Dataset sums round a wheel, pairs practice never shows 90% finding a rule Imitation Imitation Dataset what mobs really did, from fights it has not read 76% the Arena Ground Ground Dataset rows of ground it has not read, block by block loss ≤ 0.97 writing ground Hover over a benchmark on the Core's Tests tab for the exact format. The Try tab shows the model answering a fresh example, the way an agent would ask it. Practising several things The Core's four Data slots are practised together: every step draws its batch from one of them in turn. One model can learn everything, if it is big enough and shaped for it. Each benchmark asks for something different: forecasting a machine only needs the look just before, and so does forecasting an average field; recall has to find a pair far back; reversal needs to know where each waymark was; induction has to look back for what followed the same letter last time; sorting has to find the word in a name that settles its kind. Orders have to write out a whole program, copying its names a letter at a time, and only a program right to its last letter counts: a model that passes gets about two orders in five right the first time, the long ones least, which is why an agent reads those back. When its curve flattens, lower the learning rate. Practising by playing Control is practised by playing, not from examples: the Core plays melts with the model's own choices, and the model learns from each choice by how much better the melt did after it than after other choices made at the same look and temperature. A choice that went well is learned from more, one that went badly less. It takes longer than learning from examples, since every step plays its melts first. A melt is held when 90% of its looks end in the band, which is what earns a Smelter's third ingot, and the test scores the share held of the ore the model holds worst. Holding a melt means foreseeing what comes, when the fresh charges drop the melt and how the ore drifts, which needs a model that knows where in the melt it is and which ore it began with. A model that sees only the last few characters holds most copper melts but no gold or iron; a two-block transformer passes after two to four hundred steps, though its score still swings now and then as it practises. Knowing the pairs, and knowing the rule The Modular Dataset asks for sums on a wheel of 59 teeth, a character each: ab= and what they come to, going round. Practice shows four pairs in ten, always the same ones, and the test asks the rest. Nothing but the rule carries from one to the other. A small model learns the pairs it is shown by heart in a few hundred steps, and for a long time after that knows none of the others. Its training loss is near zero and its test stays where it started. Then, with enough weight decay on the Train tab, the test climbs to the top within a few thousand steps. Decay keeps only what keeps paying, and the rule is far smaller than a table of pairs. It is worth seeing once. Two Delay Lines on an Embedding Table of width 32, into a Concatenator, a Linear Layer of 128, an Activation and a Linear Layer of the vocabulary's width will do it (21,000 parameters). At a learning rate of 1e-2 and decay 0.1 it knew its pairs by step 500 and all the rest by about step 8,000, under half a minute of training; at the Core's usual decay of 0.01 it knew 12% of the rest after 40,000 steps. A two-block transformer 32 wide does the same at decay 0.3 in about 10,000. Under very strong decay a transformer learns the rule straight away and never knows only the pairs at all. The Core reads every pair on both sides every 250 steps. A model that knew at least 80% of its pairs and at most 30% of the rest, for at least 1,000 steps and half as long again as it took to learn them, and then gets 90% of the rest, has grokked. Checkpoints Crafting A Checkpoint holds one model: its machines, its weights, how long it trained and its scores. Saving runs every test first, so the scores on a checkpoint are always the ones it earned. Saving over a checkpoint replaces the model on it. How big a model may be An agent can carry 160 KB of weights in its head. A model trained in fp32 takes four bytes a weight, which makes that 40,000 parameters; a narrower recipe fits more of them in. A bigger model stays in a Model Server and is asked over relays: see Serving Models. The Train tab counts a model's parameters, and the Recipe tab what they take. An exosuit's board holds as many bytes, and carries bigger models by quantizing them. Reading ahead A model that can see the letter it is asked to predict is not predicting anything. The Core checks every model for this. A model that reads ahead scores very well and means nothing; its checkpoint says so, and the Reader turns it away.

title: The Modern Block
text: The Modern Block The Transformer Block is how the first models that talked seem to have been built. The old world's last ones kept its shape, a running sum that every layer reads and adds to, and changed what is inside it, a part at a time. Each part is a spec on the Bench and a machine of its own, and each can be tried and taken out again. The parts RMS norm. A Normalizer takes each vector's mean off, rescales it and adds an offset back. An RMS Normalizer only rescales, with no mean and no offset, and a layer needs nothing more. A gate. A Feed-Forward Block widens each token, bends it and projects it back. A Gated Feed-Forward Block makes two wide copies and lets one, through SiLU, open or shut each number of the other. Widened to 8/3 rather than 4 times, it costs the same weights. Positions by turning. A Position Table is a table of learned vectors, one for every place, added to the tokens, and it has an end. Rotary Positions has no weights and no end: it turns each pair of numbers in a query or a key by an angle that grows with the place, each pair at its own rate. Turn a query and a key that way and the score between them depends only on how far apart they are, wherever they stand. QK norm. Left alone, queries and keys can grow during training until one score swamps all the others, and a softmax that sharp gives gradients that throw the weights about. A QK Normalizer compares them at one size, with one learned temperature, so no score can pass t·√C. The online softmax. An Attention Head writes out every score of every token against every other, T×T of them for each head, in several copies with their gradients. A Modern Attention Head made from a verified design never holds them. It works each token's scores out a tile at a time, keeping only the largest so far and the running sum: The answer is the same to within rounding, gradients included. At a batch of 32, four heads of width 8 and 64 tokens, the plain way holds 4.3 million numbers and the tiles 82 thousand. The backward pass works the scores out again from the queries and keys it kept. Z-loss. A Z-Loss Regulator sits before the Model Core and adds a small penalty for scores far from zero, where a softmax stops being accurate. What it does to a run Two layers of width 32 at a learning rate of 0.003, from three starts each, and the step by which each passed: Test Transformer Blocks Modern Blocks Modern Blocks after a Position Table Reversal 250 250 to 500 250 Induction 800 to 1,200 400 to 800 one start of three Recall none: 23% at 1,000 1,000 none: 25% at 1,000 Survey two starts of three, 500 and 1,000 none: 85% at 1,000 500 to 750 Turning tells a model how far apart two tokens are and nothing about where they stand. Recall and Induction ask how far. Survey asks where along a row the first of an ore lies, and a Position Table is what answers that. Choose by the job. A step costs less as well. On four threads it took 34 milliseconds beside a Transformer Block model's 118 at width 32, and 90 beside 186 at width 64; on one thread, 89 beside 121, and 276 beside 324. Past the rates a model is comfortable with, the difference grows. A Transformer Block model passes Reversal in 75 steps at a rate of 0.03. At 0.1 it never does, and ends near 42% as its largest attention score runs out to 56,000. Modern Blocks hold that score at 30 and pass from two starts of three, and with QK norm turned off the score goes to 47,000 and Reversal stays at 16%. On the archive at a rate of 0.3, a Transformer Block model stays near a test loss of 3.0, Modern Blocks reach 2.0, and with QK norm off they reach 2.6. A Z-Loss Regulator does less on a model this small. On Reversal at 0.03 it brought the largest output score of Modern Blocks from 20 to 14, and their spikes from 1, 0, 1 to none. On the archive at the same rate, on Transformer Blocks, the score went from 9.4 to 9.2 and the test loss stayed at 1.96. Building one A Modern Block holds a whole modern layer, with the online softmax inside. A line of them needs nothing for positions: an Embedding Table, the blocks, an RMS Normalizer and a Linear Layer set to V. Its screen turns Rotary and QK norm off, to see what each was doing. With Rotary off it needs a Position Table before it, as a Transformer Block does.

title: Power
text: Power Power moves in Forge Energy (FE) along Power Cables: from the blocks that make it to the blocks that store or use it, and to any other mod's block that takes FE. A Combustion Generator burns what a furnace burns. Power Cables lead away from it. An Energy Cell on the cables keeps what is not used yet. A Smelter on the cables works on what they bring. The screens of power, part by part. Making it The Combustion Generator burns what a furnace burns and makes 80 FE a tick while it burns. A fuel lasts half as long as in a furnace, so a coal makes 64,000 FE. It burns only while it has room for what it makes, and holds 32,000 FE of its own. Crafting Steam A Boiler with water touching it raises steam for the Turbines stacked on top of it, up to four. Each Turbine makes 240 FE a tick, and the Boiler burns a tick of a furnace's fuel for each one, so a coal makes 384,000 FE however many there are: six times what it makes in a Combustion Generator. More Turbines only burn it faster. Power comes out of the Boiler and the Turbines alike, and they spin and let their steam go while it burns. Crafting Crafting The sun A Solar Panel makes 40 FE a tick under a bright sky, less as it darkens toward night or rain, and nothing in the dark or under a roof. It costs nothing to run. Panels touching each other share a network with no cable between them, and cells carry what they make through the night. Crafting The reactor The most power there is comes from a reactor, and only a model can run one. Moving and storing it Cables join generators, cells and machines into one network. Each tick the machines take what they need from the generators, then from the cells; whatever the generators make beyond that charges the cells. All of it goes through the cables, and in a tick a network carries no more than its thinnest cable does: one thin cable holds back the whole line. Blocks that touch need no cable and hold nothing back. Cable Carries a tick Power Cable 3,200 FE Heavy Cable 51,200 FE Bus Bar 819,200 FE While a network carries power it runs along the cables as pulses of light. An Energy Cell holds 1,000,000 FE and moves up to 2,000 FE a tick each way, and a Capacitor Bank holds 64,000,000 FE and moves up to 64,000 FE. Their faces fill in quarters as they charge, and a comparator beside one reads how full it is. Crafting Crafting Crafting Crafting Crafting The Smelter The Smelter smelts anything a furnace does on 80 FE a tick instead of fuel, an item every five seconds. From an ore or a raw ore it makes two of what a furnace makes from one. The Fabricator makes it from a transformer photomask. The controller Put a model in the Smelter's Controller slot, and each ore becomes a melt it holds in its band: at a look every four ticks it asks the model whether to cool the melt, hold it or heat it, and waits for the answer. A melt held in the band at 90% of its looks or more makes three ingots instead of two; a model passes the Control test by holding nine melts in ten of every ore the test plays. The slot is in the panel beside the Smelter's screen; between its ore and its ingots, the screen draws the melt look by look, the band shaded, and pointing at it tells how much of the last melt was held. A model learns this on the Process Dataset: see Models and Tests. A controller that passes Precision holds each melt not in the band but at one step of it, and a melt held there at 70% of its looks makes six. No dataset teaches that: see Tuning. One that also passes Reckoning is handed an assay off each such melt, a line of numbers to add up, and if it gets that right the melt makes nine: see Thinking Longer. Other blocks Hoppers and Ports feed the generators and the Smelter from any side and take the Smelter's ingots out. Other mods' cables can draw power from generators, cells and the reactor, and give it to cells, Chillers and the Smelter. Compute runs on power too, past the first few Accelerators: see Compute.

title: Programs
text: Programs One language runs on everything that can carry a program: an agent, which goes to what it works on, and a Port, which reaches it from where it stands. No model is asked. A program does exactly what it says, as often as every tick, and how hard it can work is up to its upgrades. The Palette beside every program lays all of this out to click together, page by page. Each piece says what it does when you point at it, so nothing here has to be typed, or remembered. A Port's programs on its screen, part by part. Steps Steps go between commas. A step can take a number, a thing, and words that say where: send 64 iron ingot from front to network dig stone at box(front, mark(2)) use shears at entities(4, sheep) fling 8 cobblestone at up speed 1 pitch 45 Going: go, come, home, stay, follow, forward 3, back, up, down, turn left, and teleport to a place the relays cover. Carrying: send items, pump fluid and charge energy, each from one place to another, or to each of a list in turn, as many at a time as its upgrades allow. pump lifts a source block out of the world and sets one down again, and a network keeps fluid as it keeps items: pump from front to network. pickup takes what lies around, and pickup xp turns experience into bottles. drop, fling, void items and drain fluid get rid of them. take, put, give and fetch go through the stores around home. The world: dig and place at any area. use is a right click, with what it holds, on a block or a creature; add sneak to crouch. attack strikes with what it holds. extrude 8 stone at up lays a line of blocks, one at a time, and retract 8 at up takes it back. emit 15 gives out a redstone signal, and pulse 15 for 5 gives one for five ticks. sign writes on a sign. harvest, plant and till work a field; mine looks for a block and digs to it. Hands: select a slot, transfer to another, equip a tool, refuel on what burns, lift a creature and lower it. Logistics: craft 8 torch makes them there and then from what it holds, and has its network make what it cannot. supply goes after what a job lacks. On a team's board, provide offers what a place holds, push wants it gone, accept takes what is pushed and request 16 iron ingot wants that many kept there; deliver makes one trip between them. Two Ports and a carrier make a base that passes things along by itself. Saying: wait, say, note (for whoever reads the program), sound, particle, rename, run at front (what a Program Card there says), retire (it goes back to being an item). Where front, back, left, right, up and down are its own sides, and here and home where they say. A number is a mark from the Survey Rod, which also works on Ports: sneak-use the rod on one to hand it the marks. pos(1, 64, 3) is a place, offset(here, north, 3) one worked out, pos(1, 64, 3, the_nether) one in another dimension, which only the relays reach. network is its storage network, hands what it holds, and owner whoever set it down, wherever they are: section(armor), section(offhand) or section(ender) for one part of what they carry. Values A value is a number, "text", true or false, a thing, a fluid, a place, an area, a creature, or a list of any of those. $x is the program's own, and goes with it. @x is the body's, and stays when its program changes. Another reads it with read_var(front, "x"). #x is a channel, the same for everything on a team, and kept with the world. set $n count(front, coal) * 2 works one out. Numbers take + - * / %, anything compares with = != < <= > >=, and checks join with and, or and not. Among a function's values, plain words name things: count(front, iron ingot). In the words of a say or a sign, $x is what it holds. Lists are written [1, 2, 3] and joined with +. What works through one reads each thing as $it: map($list, $it * 2), filter(items(front), food($it) > 3), sum, sort, first, count, any, all, and reduce, which keeps $acc between them. Going round if … (…) else (…), repeat (…), repeat 3 (…), repeat count($list) (…), while … (…), until … (…), for each $x in … (…), over a list or an area, and wait until …. next goes on to the next round, leave out of the round, stop ends the program. The first checks still read without parentheses: have 3 bread, ripe, full. to row $n $what (repeat $n (place $what at front)) makes a step of your own, written anywhere in the program; row 3 cobblestone runs it. A parameter is its own, return 2 ends it and leaves that in $result, and it can call itself, 64 deep. Events A handler waits beside the program and cuts in when something happens: on redstone at 1 (…), when a place gets a signal on item coal at front (…), when a thing arrives on block at 1 (…), when a block changes on timer 5 (…), every five seconds on change #needed (…), when a value changes when count(front) > 16 (…), when something comes true What it cut short goes on afterwards, a wait with the time it had left. Add priority 5 to say what matters most: a handler cuts in only on what has a lower priority, and otherwise waits its turn. The program itself is 0, and a handler 1 unless it says. Areas Wherever a step says at, from or to, an area works too, and it works through it a little at a time. An area is at most 250,000 blocks. Shape What it holds box(a, b) every block between two corners; hollow its faces, frame its edges cylinder(a, b, filled, y) a circle round a, as wide as b is from it, run out along an axis; tube, hollow grid(a, b, 3) every third block between two corners line(a, b) what a straight line passes through pyramid(a, b, y) its point at a, its base at b; hollow random(a, b, 10) ten places between two corners sphere(a, b) round a, as far as b; hollow torus(a, b, y) a ring round a; hollow wall(a, b, y) the line between two corners, run out along an axis + adds areas and - takes one from another: dig at sphere(1, 2) - box(3, 4). near(8) is a box as far as eight blocks round it. Filters What a step works on can be named many ways, and the same words serve for items, fluids and creatures: iron ingot, coal or cobblestone, except oak log: a white list and a black list tag(logs), mod(minecraft), regex("_ore$") where durability($it) < 50: anything the language can read about it, such as damage, fluid_fill, energy_fill, enchanted or food ghosts(): what a Port's nine filter slots show items(1): what a chest holds, so a chest of samples is a filter with as many kinds as it has slots pump water, attack at entities(8, zombie), entities(8, mob), entities(8, tag(raiders)), and entities(8, other_than(player)), a black list wherever a filter goes kind(food): what a filter model says. It takes a checkpoint or a tuned Relay Card that passes Sorting (Models and Tests), in an agent's Filter slot or a Port's filter model slot. It asks about each thing once, by name; whatever it is not sure of, or anything with no model there at all, is kind(other). Reading the world Functions read whatever a body can reach, in the same words as everything else, listed on the palette's Senses page: Inventories, tanks, energy: count, items, slots, slots_used, fill, fluid_amount, fluids, tanks, energy, energy_capacity Blocks: block, has_block, property(block(front), lit), biome, light, compare, detect, block_data Redstone: signal, redstone, comparator, clock(5) Creatures: entities, players, health, held, armor, is_baby, can_breed, target, carrying Machines: working, has_work, progress, temperature, recipes(front), recipe_output(raw iron, front) The world: is_day, is_rain, time, tps, world_name, player_count, and heard(harp), the note a note block played nearby Networks: is_network, network_items, network_count(iron ingot), network_fluids, network_fluid_count(water), network_ports, craftable, jobs, network_lacks, power_stored, power_drawn Itself: fuel, reach, run_items, selected, slot_item, equipped, upgrades(speed) On a Port Programs, on a Port's screen, opens what it runs. Its top row takes up to nine Program Cards, each with a program of its own, all running at once and sharing the slots beneath them, its upgrades, its tank and its battery. Click a card to see it, write in the box and press Run. With a written card in it, a Port does what its cards say instead of what its mode says. What it works on need not touch it. It reaches 8 blocks, and further with Range upgrades; network is the storage network its back is linked to. Upgrades A body works in operations: one transfer of items, fluid or energy, or one block dug or placed. With nothing in its side panel an operation takes 8 ticks, and moves 8 items, 250 mB or 1,000 FE, 8 blocks away at most. Upgrades go in that panel, one kind to a slot, on a Port or an agent. Upgrade Each one At most Then Speed Upgrade halves the ticks 3 an operation every tick Stack Upgrade doubles the items 3 64, or 1,280 items a second for each program Range Upgrade adds 8 blocks 5 48 blocks Fluid Upgrade doubles the fluid, and adds 16,000 mB of tank 4 4,000 mB, or 80,000 mB a second Energy Upgrade quadruples the energy, and adds 800,000 FE of battery 4 256,000 FE Carrying Upgrade gives an agent 6 more slots 6 48 slots Lift Upgrade lets an agent fly 1 10 FE a tick in the air The Fabricator makes Speed, Stack, Range, Fluid and Carrying upgrades from an attention photomask, and Energy and Lift upgrades from a transformer photomask. A Relay Card tuned to a Model Server goes among the upgrades, and then a body reaches anywhere the server's relays cover, for 100 FE an operation; teleport jumps there for 10,000 FE. A body with an Energy upgrade takes energy in with charge from front to hands, from a cell or anything else that holds it, or refuel burns what it holds: 64,000 FE from a piece of coal. Watching it work The step a body is on floats over it, in the words of its program, when you are within 16 blocks and looking its way. Teal is a step under way, grey a wait, amber a program held in the debugger. A Port running several programs shows the first that is working, and how many more it has. Only the few nearest the middle of your view float, never one over another, so in a row of Ports you read the ones you look at, and the lit sides of the rest say they are working too. F1 hides them. The debugger Beside a program's Trace sits its debugger: every step on a line, with the one under way lit. Pause holds it at its next step, and One step runs one and holds again. Click a line to stop there every time it comes round, or write breakpoint in the program. Below, Values shows what its variables hold, and whatever you write under Watch, count(front) for one, is worked out again as it runs. What holds a program back A program takes at most 32 steps a tick and goes on with the rest in the next, so a loop with nothing in it cannot hold up the world, and a sum that goes on too long fails. A step that fails says why in the trace, and the program goes on with the next. Stop always stops it. Who may use it A Port or an agent belongs to whoever set it down. The lock beside its screen says who else may open it and change it: anyone, its owner's team, or only its owner. /residual team make NAME makes a team, /residual team invite PLAYER asks someone in, and /residual team join NAME and /residual team leave do what they say. A team shares its channels and its logistics board.

title: The Reactor
text: The Reactor A reactor makes more power than everything else you can build put together, and it will not hold still. Its power climbs or sinks a little faster each moment, its rods answer late, and its fuel keeps pushing it the same way on a rhythm you are not told. No rule keeps it running, so it will not run on a rule: it starts only for a controller, a model that has learned to hold it. Building one A shell of Reactor Casing and Reactor Glass, from 3 to 5 blocks each way, holds Fuel Rods in the space inside it, up to 27. The Reactor Core takes one place on the shell, in the middle of a face, looking out. The Fabricator makes it from a transformer photomask. The shell carries power to whatever touches it, and at full power it takes a Bus Bar to carry it away. Each rod makes 20,000 FE a tick while the core's power is in its band, half that a step off it, an eighth two steps off. A Reactor Fuel in its fuel slot burns for 4,800 ticks at one rod, and as much faster as there are rods, so 27 rods make 540,000 FE a tick and burn a fuel every 178 ticks. Crafting Crafting Crafting Crafting (Shapeless) The controller A model goes in the panel beside its screen, on a checkpoint, or by a Relay Card from a Model Server if it is too big to carry. It has to pass Containment. The reactor runs one cycle after another, each of 24 looks, one look every half second. At each look it shows the controller the cycle so far and the power now, and waits for it to say what to do with the rods. Moving the rods changes how fast the power climbs or sinks, up to two steps a look, and only from the look after next. The fuel pushes the same way every two or three looks, up while it is young and down as it ages, from a moment of its own in each cycle. Each cycle's line starts with the fuel's age. A controller has to make that moment out from how the cycle has gone, and meet the push before it comes. Outside the band's reach the core feeds on itself: at the top of its gauge it climbs faster each look, and at the bottom it sinks faster. The screen draws the cycle look by look, with the band shaded, and pointing at it tells how much of the last cycle was held and how sure the controller last was. When it stops It stops itself, and that is the only rule it has: the rods all go in, and it waits half a minute for the poison in its core to clear. It does this when its gauge reads either end, when its controller is taken away or cannot be asked, and when three looks running the controller was less than 40% sure of what it chose. Nothing burns or breaks. Learning to hold it A model learns on the Containment Dataset, by running cycles: the Core plays the model's own and it learns from how each choice turned out, as for Control and Pilot. No rule holds a cycle of its worst fuel: not going back to the band, not reckoning how fast the power moves and what the rods have on the way, not even that and knowing the fuel. A model that sees only the last few characters holds none of them either. A two-block transformer 32 wide scored 90.625% on Containment after 4,500 steps, above the 90% gate. That controller completed 16 live cycles across all four fuel ages without a trip; 12 met the test's held target of at least 90% of scored looks in the band. Scores swing as a model practises, so test it often. See Models and Tests.

title: Thinking Longer
text: Thinking Longer A model can be asked once or many times. Each answer costs what it costs, and if a good answer can be told from a bad one, a second try can be worth paying for. Reckoning Crafting (Shapeless) The Reckoning Dataset holds lines of numbers added up, with each running sum written out: > 12,7,30,5 = 19 49 54 The last number is the answer. Each step can be checked by itself, by anyone, with nothing to go by but arithmetic, and that is what makes it worth thinking longer about: a wrong answer can be caught, and another tried. The Reckoning test scores the share of sums practice never showed with every step right. The pass mark is 70%; trying more answers may help a model reach it. Answers to a question Put a KV Cache in a Model Server, and its third button sets how many answers it writes to an order or a sum. It keeps one: for a sum, one whose steps all check; for an order, what most of those that run in a sandbox come to, or with a judge in the last slot of its panel, the one the judge scores highest. If none passes the check, it keeps the commonest answer. Other questions are asked once. Every answer is paid for. They read the question once and go through together, but more attempts leave less capacity for other questions. The server's screen shows the rate and what each test now comes to, and whatever asks goes by those scores. A higher effort can change which tests it passes. A model can make the same mistake several times, so the commonest answer need not be right. An arithmetic check can reject a wrong sum however often it appears. Orders are another matter: a program that runs without failing may still miss what was meant. Taking the commonest can choose that program over a better one. A server that thinks longer about orders can lose the Programs test by it, and its screen says so. Marking each step A Tuner set to Verified, marking sums, marks each try by how many of its steps are right, rather than only whether it comes out right in the end, so a try that gets three steps of four is worth more than one that gets none. Nothing else tells it what the answer was. The reward line shows what the checker favours; the saved model's Reckoning score shows how it handles sums practice never gave it. The assay A melt held at its mark gives an assay, a line of numbers to add up. A Smelter whose controller passes Precision and Reckoning, as its server serves it, hands the assay to that controller. If each step is right, the melt makes nine ingots from an ore instead of six. What the server spends on it shows on its screen under Smelters.

title: The Recipe
text: The Recipe A model and a learning rate don't make a run yet. How the rate moves over thousands of steps, what the numbers are rounded to, what moves the weights and how the text is cut into rows all change what comes out. The old world's accounts of their largest runs seem to give all that as much room as the models. The Core's Recipe tab holds it. Each part opens when a unit for it touches the Core, directly or through Accelerators and other units, and a unit lights up while a run uses it. The Fabricator makes each from a photomask of its spec. Unit From Opens Scheduler Schedule Schedule, Warmup and Length bf16 Unit bf16 bf16 under Precision fp8 Unit fp8 fp8 under Precision fp4 Unit fp4 both kinds of fp4 under Precision Orthogonalizer Orthogonalize Muon under Optimizer Packer Document Mask Packing With none of them a Core trains the plain way: 20 steps of warmup and a steady rate, in fp32, with AdamW, on windows of text. The numbers below come from a model of two Transformer Blocks of width 32, reading the whole archive, unless they say otherwise. A model this small is noisy, and a few hundredths of a nat may be nothing but the start it had. The rate over a run Warmup raises the rate from nothing over its first W steps, while the weights are still random. Schedule then keeps it steady, lets it fall along half a cosine from the end of warmup, or holds it and lets it fall over the last fifth of the run. A schedule that falls has to know where it ends, so Length says how many steps the run lasts, and at that step it stops by itself. The tab draws the whole of it, with a line where the run has reached. Here is a run of 2,000 steps with 100 of warmup: steady in grey, the cosine in teal, the hold and fall in amber. At a rate of 0.01, over 1,500 steps with 100 of warmup, the test loss came to 1.56 steady, 1.57 on the cosine and 1.49 held and then let fall, from one start each. Spikes A spike is a step whose loss leaps far above its recent average: half as much again, and a tenth more. The Train tab draws each as a red stroke up from the curve, and the Recipe tab counts them. Beside them it shows the largest attention score inside the model, which at these rates runs out past 100,000. They come at rates far past the comfortable ones. At 0.3, over 300 steps, from three starts each: Warmup Clip Spikes Highest loss Best test loss Last test loss none off 1, 1, 0 9.3 2.94 2.95 none 1 0, 1, 0 11.4 3.01 3.01 100 off 12, 27, 5 17.5 2.45 3.05 100 1 1, 0, 0 3.9 2.45 3.02 With no warmup the first steps throw the run somewhere it never comes back from. With a warmup it gets further before the rate grows too large for it, and then it comes apart in spikes, and a clip takes nearly all of those away. Neither rescues a rate that is too large on every step. QK norm does: Modern Blocks at the same rate reach 2.0 with 20 steps of warmup, no clip and no spike. See The Modern Block. Below that, warmup counts for more than the clip. At 0.1, from one start, the test loss after 500 steps is 2.84 with no warmup, and the largest attention score 245,000; with 100 steps of warmup it is 1.90, and the score 245. At 0.03 and 0.01 warmup hardly matters (1.80 against 1.79, 1.88 against 1.90), and a clip of 1 changed nothing at all, since no gradient was ever that long. Precision A float is a grid: in each power of 2 it has so many evenly spaced numbers, and rounding moves a number to the nearest of them. Format A weight takes In each power of 2 Top fp32 4 bytes 8,388,608 3.4 × 10³⁸ bf16 2 bytes 128 3.4 × 10³⁸ fp8 1 byte 8 448 fp4 half a byte 2 6 fp4 has eight sizes and nothing else: 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4 and 6. Ranges that small need a scale: the tensor's largest size goes to the top of the grid and everything comes back by the same scale. That is all fp8 needs, though its gradients go back in a coarser grid with far more range, up to 57,344. In fp4 one loud number sends all the others to zero. fp4, in blocks gives every 16 numbers a scale of their own, kept in fp8, leaves the token tables and the last layer in fp8, and rounds gradients up or down by chance, so that small ones don't all vanish. fp4, one scale is the plain way. Weights stay whole during a run, since a step smaller than a weight's spacing would vanish. On the way into every matrix multiply they are rounded, and so are the numbers they meet. The product comes out in bf16, and on the way back the gradient reaching it is rounded too. A rounding has no useful slope, so the gradient passes it as if it weren't there. Gains, offsets and temperatures stay in bf16. A saved model goes on answering in the format it was trained in. What rounding does to a model's own numbers, 500 steps into a run: Format Weights move by Gradients move by Gradient numbers lost to zero bf16 0.17% 0.17% none fp8 2.7% 5.2% none fp4, one scale 12% 18% 35% fp4, in blocks 9.5% 13% 9.3% And what that costs, at a rate of 0.003, from one start each: Format Sorting at 600 steps Reading at 1,000 steps Its weights take fp32 72% 1.91 129 KB bf16 76% 1.91 65 KB fp8 76% 1.92 32 KB fp4, one scale 33% 3.78, with 3 spikes 16 KB fp4, in blocks 69% 1.98 21 KB What a narrow format buys is room. An agent or a flight frame carries 160 KB of weights: 40,000 parameters in fp32, 160,000 in fp8. Two blocks of width 64 have 115,161 parameters, too many for fp32. In fp8 an agent can carry them in its head, with no Model Server and no relay. Muon AdamW scales each number's step by that number's own recent gradients, and knows nothing of the matrix it sits in. Muon moves a whole matrix at a time, along its momentum with every singular value brought to 1, so that no direction moves further than another. It doesn't take the matrix apart to do that. Scaled to a length of 1, since this only holds for singular values up to about 1, five of these steps bring them all there: Then the matrix moves, with μ = 0.95 and λ = 0.01: Only matrices inside the model go this way. Token and position tables, the last layer and all vectors stay with AdamW. From one start each: Rate Moved by Sorting at 600 steps Reading at 1,000 steps 0.003 AdamW 72% 1.91 0.003 Muon 76% 1.84 0.01 AdamW 78% 1.66 0.01 Muon 87% 1.58 A step takes about as long either way. Packing Text from the ruins comes in pieces. What a shard has lost cuts a record into stretches, and a row of 64 tokens can't be cut from a stretch shorter than that, so windows, the plain way, never reads those at all. Of 300 records with 30% of their blocks lost, windows read 77% of what survives; with half lost 49%, and with 70% lost 21%. The tab's Text read says how much of what is in the data slots. Packed fills each row with stretches one after another, and never scores the step from the end of one to the start of the next: 99% of a row's places still count. Attention can still look across those seams, though, and learn that a sentence runs on into one that has nothing to do with it. Packed, masked stops attention, delay lines and positions at each seam, so that nothing in a row can read one stretch with another. On 300 records with 30% lost, at a rate of 0.003, from one start each, the test loss after 1,000 steps came to 1.87 on windows, 1.93 packed and 1.92 packed and masked. With three quarters of the text in reach, the rest adds little in so few steps. On 100 records with 70% lost, windows have 8,420 characters to read, and learn them by heart: the test loss falls to 2.34 and climbs back to 2.59.
