Packed rows reach 2.02, and masked ones 2.18, since no row shows them a long look back. What a mask buys is a model that never learned across a seam. A second head A Two-Token Head in place of a model's last Linear Layer learns the token after next beside the next, and adds 0.3 of that loss to the loss. The tab shows how often its first choice is right, which is how often it could spare a model the work of one token. After 1,000 steps at a rate of 0.003, from one start, its first head scored a test loss of 1.88 beside 1.91 without one, too close to call. Its second head was right 30% of the time, and the first 44%. On models this small it is the second head itself that is worth having, not what it does for the first. title: The Refinery
text: The Refinery A shard is one record with holes in it. The box of a fallen mast holds something else as well: a Relay Dump, all that its relay passed on, as it came. A dump holds about 440,000 characters, thirty times a found drive, and most of it is no use as it lies. A message was sent until it was heard, so the same record comes round again and again. Bad lines garbled some messages and put the words of others out of order. Between messages the line carried nothing but its own pulse, and every keeper put the same few lines round everything. A Refinery is a line of machines that text runs through, ending in tanks of tokens a model can practise on. Every machine does one thing to the text, and you can measure what that was worth. Building the line Text leaves a machine by its front and crosses the air to the next machine in line, up to 12 blocks off with nothing solid between, coming in on any other side. A machine's front points away from you when you place it, and sneak-using a side turns it to that side. So a Refinery is a hall, built the way you walk. Each line of writing in the stream is the text itself, in the colour of its kind, and there are as many lines as there is text left, so you can watch it thin. What a machine takes out falls off it. Each machine draws 40 FE a tick from its power while it works, one at a time as the text reaches it. The machines can stand in any order, and leave out any you like; only the Intake comes first and the tanks last. The Intake comes first, with what you found in its slots. Each machine stands in front of the last, its own front pointing on. The one the text has reached is at work. The tanks come last, and keep what is left. Crafting The Refinery Intake takes up to nine Archive Drives and Relay Dumps. Refine, in its toolbar, sends all of it down the line. The other machines but the tank come out of the Fabricator from a transformer photomask. Taking out copies The Duplicate Sieve takes out what it has already seen. Exact copies go by a hash of their text. Near copies go by MinHash: a document is reduced to its runs of five words, and 128 hash functions each keep the smallest value over those runs. Two documents agree on any one of the 128 about as often as they share runs, so a few numbers stand for the whole document, and documents that agree on a whole band of those numbers are worth comparing. The panel beside its screen draws the curve that makes: how likely two documents are to be compared, by how alike they are. Of two near copies the longer stays. Long lines it has seen before go too, which is most of what keepers wrote round their messages. Four dumps come to 1.75 million characters. The Sieve finds 253 exact copies and 306 near ones, and leaves half of it. Its threshold matters: at 0.3 it finds 320 near copies, at 0.7 only 161, since a message sent again comes back a little changed. Filtering The Filter Bed throws out documents by rules about how text looks: too few words, too many marks, words too long or too short to be words, one line said over and over, lines that hardly ever end. Each rule can be turned off in the toolbar, and each row of its screen says what that rule threw out. None of them reads. On four dumps they threw out all of the carrier and a fifth of the scrambled messages, whose lines no longer end where a sentence does; the other four fifths and every garbled message went through. Classifying The Quality Classifier has a model read each document and say whether it is writing or a bad line has been at it. It needs no examples of bad text. A model that has read a lot of writing knows what comes next in writing, so what a bad line has been at surprises it, letter after letter, and a document gives it hundreds of letters to go by. The model has to pass Quality, tested on documents no shard carries, half of them spoiled. Practise it on a drive, as you would for Reading. It asks little of a model that reads at all: one that reads three letters back passes after 300 steps on a thousand found records. One that reads a single letter back is at 84% after 1,000, since a pair of letters is hardly surprised by good words in a bad order. At the start of a pass the model reads some documents it knows the answer to, and finds how much surprise divides good from bad. After that the Classifier goes by what the model is sure of, at the threshold you set in the toolbar. What the model is not sure of goes to a rule, and with no model the rule decides alone: too many words it has never seen, and the text has gone bad. That rule is cheap. On a dump it caught all the garbled documents and all the carrier, and threw out nothing else. It has nothing to say about good words in a bad order. That is what the model is for, and the threshold is how far you trust it. A model two blocks 32 wide, after 1,500 steps, on four dumps: Sure enough at Scrambled documents thrown out Good documents thrown out 60% 64% 7.5% 75% 40% 3.1% 90% 19% 0.9% 99% 0.6% none Each answer costs inference, from a checkpoint in the slot beside its screen or from a Model Server through a Relay Card, and a server answers 64 documents at a time. Writing by rule The Program Press adds text of its own to the stream: sums with their working, orders with what they mean, things with their kinds, or a book of your own. A book in its slot has a template on each page, and {a|b} comes out as one of the two, so The {miller|baker} sold {two|six} {loaves|jars}. writes eight sentences. What a rule writes is right, and costs nothing to find, and it knows only what the rule knows. Orders and sorting lines draw only on what those benchmarks' practice names. A model's steps are what it pays with. Added to a thousand found records for the same 400 steps, a tenth of orders takes a small reader from 26% to 49% on the Orders test, and sorting lines from 4% to 37% on Sorting, while its held-out loss on writing goes from 1.763 to 1.81 and 1.83. A quarter takes them to 56% and 61%, and the loss to 1.84 and 1.87. Sums cost the same and give back nothing it can show: even on tallies and lists, where sums are kept, the loss goes from 1.78 to 1.82. Mixing The Domain Mixer sets how much of each kind of writing a model reads. A row on its screen for each domain shows its share of practice; click it for a half, twice or four times its share of the text, or none. The text itself stays in the tank. Four times the tales takes a small reader from 1.761 to 1.739 on tales it has never seen, and none at all to 1.789. The test on all records hardly moves either way, 1.763 to 1.769 and 1.764, since it has every kind of writing in it: what one kind gains, the others pay for. It can also anneal: a model that has read everything goes on for the last of its run on one domain alone, at a fifth of the rate. Set the domain and the step in the toolbar. In a Model Core the run does this by itself once it has gone that far. It takes a long run to be worth it, since a model still learning fast only loses by slowing down. Over 2,000 steps, the last 400 on one domain take tales from 1.541 to 1.515, know-how from 1.496 to 1.474 and tallies from 1.555 to 1.537, at a cost of 0.01 to 0.03 on everything. A measure gives annealing a run that long of its own. Looking for the tests A score means nothing on a test the model has already read, however the text got there. The Contamination Check looks in the text for what every benchmark tests on and says what it found, a row a benchmark. Prose is compared by runs of 13 words, and a benchmark's own lines line by line, counting only lines its practice never shows: = stay is in the test and in practice alike, but = fetch oak logs is the test's own. Tests that are played, not read, have nothing written to find. It takes the lines out, or only says so if you set it to. The old world quoted itself, so the archive holds some of this already. All the records shards carry hold 62 of Reading's 808 test records and 9 of Orders' 949 lines, in 205 lines of text, about a quarter of a percent of it. A thousand found records hold 13 and 1, in 21 lines. Taking them out does nothing for a small reader, which can't remember what it reads anyway. Given all of Orders' test to read, it scores 51% where it scored 49%, and 51% again with the Check's lines taken out, which is what readers differ by. A Check is there for scores you mean to trust. Tanks and cells Crafting The stream ends in a Token Tank, which fills as the last of the text comes in. It holds a million characters; more tanks in line, each in front of the last, hold a million more each, and what doesn't fit is spilled. A Tokenizer in its slot counts what it holds as tokens that tokenizer cuts. Whoever stands by while a tank fills learns of the places its text tells of, and a Wayfinder can then lead there. Crafting (Shapeless) A Token Cell put in a tank's cell slot draws on all the line's tanks hold. In a Model Core's Data slots it is practice for Reading, drawn by the mix and annealing as you set them. Refine again and the same cells draw on the new text. What each machine was worth Measure, in the Intake's toolbar, tells you what each machine really did. It trains a small reader on the text as each machine left it, from nothing, three times from the same three starts, and tests each on the records no shard carries. Readers read 8 letters back and train for 400 steps, so this takes minutes and runs beside everything else. A reader this small says what the text teaches about writing, and little of what a big model could make of it. What each machine did to held-out loss floats above it: green for better, amber for worse, grey for what chance alone could do. Its screen says from what to what. The tank says what the whole line did. Here is what that came to on four dumps, each machine in the order you would meet it: After Text left Held-out loss As it came 1,745,158 1.827 Duplicate Sieve 892,025 1.851 Filter Bed 717,448 1.835 Quality Classifier, the rule alone 501,185 1.781 Quality Classifier, with a model 430,132 1.773 Contamination Check 429,047 1.773 On a thousand records filed from shards, 982,189 characters at 1.763, no machine moved the loss by more than 0.002, which is less than the readers differ. The clerks of the old world seem to have taken out copies and spoiled pages long before any of it reached a shard, and there is little left for a Refinery to do. A machine that does little is worth knowing about, and one you can leave out of a line. On dumps the Sieve makes things worse at first. What it takes out is clean, so what a bad line has been at is a bigger share of what is left. Put it last instead, behind the Filter Bed and the Classifier, and it takes 60% of the text and moves the loss by nothing at all. For a reader this small, a Sieve saves you tanks.

title: Ruins
text: Ruins The people who lived here before left their places behind: towers along the old roads, farms on the ridges, houses on the marshes, slips on the shores, and stranger halls. Every kind of ruin is rare, some rarer than others, and each stands only in the land that suits it, where the ground is near level: it takes travel to come across one, and a Wayfinder to find one on purpose. Places of a kind were built a few different ways, and the years have worn each its own way. The Wayfinder's screen, part by part. Finding them A Wayfinder leads to ruins the archive has told you of. Use it to choose a kind to look for: it lists the relay towers, which everyone knows of, and every kind a shard you have read tells of; read a shard, by using it, and the places it writes about join the list. Its needle spins while it looks, longer the farther the nearest one lies, then points to the nearest ruin of that kind within 10,000 blocks; while you hold it, it says how far that is. Crafting Relay towers Stone towers, the tallest thing for half a day's walk: a base buttressed at the corners, the shaft set back above it and banded at each floor, and three rooms one over another, the store, the kitchen with its stove and the keeper's room, with a ladder up the north wall. At the top a walk on corbels, railed, with the bell that calls for coal, goes round the lamp room of glass in a copper frame, its great lamp of glass and redstone under a flared roof of copper gone green. At the tower's foot stands the relay house: stone below and a spruce frame above, the keeper's desk with the tower book on its lectern, and the stand where a big mind stood, ringed by accelerators in their cooling water. Some towers have lost their tops. In grassland, forest, taiga, snow and hills, at most one in each region 48 chunks across. Waymarks Stone pillars on stepped bases by stretches of the old road, a figure cut in the middle stone, a torch on top, little stones left at the foot and an arrow to the nearest inn; the ring where walkers made their fire, with a bench and a trough. Some pillars have fallen into the grass; one in six stands under a little roof with notes left on it. The commonest ruin: at most one in each region 24 chunks across. Three Wells A market town's square where two roads cross like an X: paving round three wells under their little roofs, a lamp at every corner, the bell at the crossing, the notice board with the market rules, stalls under wool awnings, benches under two trees, the bakery with its oven built out on the side, the school house by the east well with its painted door and its bell on the roof, and a stretch of the town wall. On plains, meadows and savannas, the rarest of the towns' ruins: at most one in each region 80 chunks across. Inns The inns of the Long Road, a day apart, the Halfway Inn and the Brown Hen: a timber frame on a stone footing (the Brown Hen's ground floor all stone), the upper floor jutting over the road on corbels, shuttered windows, two dormers and the chimney stack up the gable. Inside, the hearth still burns; the boards hang by the fire, the book lies behind the counter next to a pie, and the beds wait upstairs; a woodshed stands at the back, the stable across the yard with its roof part fallen, and the inn's sign by the road. At most one in each region 64 chunks across. Windmill farms The farms of the ridges: a windmill with a stone base and a boarded body, a railed stage round it and its tally board by the door, the barn with its hayloft and hoist, the pig pen and the hen house, a well in the yard, and three fields, wheat, beetroot, and potatoes and carrots, each with its ditch, its hedge and its scarecrow or hives. On plains, meadows, savannas and windswept hills, at most one in each region 56 chunks across. Watermills The mills of the orchard country, of birch and glass on a stone footing at the edge of a pond: the wheel out over the water on its axle, the millstone under its hopper inside, a race of stone beside it with the sluice nobody may open and a footbridge with a loose plank, the notices on the gate, a bench on the far side, old apple trees and hives among the flowers. Only by water deep enough, the wheel toward it: at most one in each region 56 chunks across. Stilt houses Houses of mud brick on decks over the marsh, their stilts down to the marsh floor, a boardwalk to the bank. A healer's house keeps its high shelves of labeled jars, the remedies on the bench, beds for the sick and her day book; a boat house keeps the day's catch and the tally on its wall. In swamps and mangrove swamps, at most one in each region 48 chunks across. Slipways A buttressed stone quay with steps down to the water, the shipwright's shed with its window for mending nets, the wood store and the fish market's price board; running out over the sea on posts, the frame of a ship never finished with a crane leaning over it, and beside it a ramp of stone into the water. Some frames are a big ship's, three times as long as any boat. Only where a beach or a stony shore meets deep enough water, the slip toward the sea: at most one in each region 40 chunks across. Tutor houses Halls of tuff between pillars, two tiers of tall windows under a cornice of copper, a relay on the roof, where minds were drilled and tested. Apprentices still stand in their row before the tutor's Bench; the teaching room keeps its tray of crystals, each on its card, in the light of its bay window; the apprentice hall across the yard keeps its dry box; and the drill yard, ringed with torches, has its boards drawn as small fields. In grassland, forest, taiga, savanna and cherry groves, at most one in each region 72 chunks across. The Archive at Vell Where everything was kept, dug into its hill. Its front faces the town: pillars of tuff, the portal under the first keepers' words, a broad flight of steps, the copying room's big window and the reading room's, where a lamp still burns on the long table; behind the front everything is under turf, and light wells of glass come up through the grass. A great stair goes down into the hill to the front hall and the finding book, the halls of shelves under their light wells, a stack sealed with clay, and the deepest room, where the oldest record is kept. At most one in each region 160 chunks across. The Deep Works A great mine in the hills. At the shaft head stand the headframe and its wheel, the board where miners wrote their names and rubbed them out coming up, the tool store and the sorting bins. A ladder goes down the shaft past a level of copper, a level of iron and coal with an amethyst hollow behind a door, and the deep stone, where an old tunnel was walled up; at the ninth level the gate is locked, and an old side door above it leads down another way. In windswept hills, meadows and savanna plateaus, at most one in each region 128 chunks across. Fallen relay masts Where a relay mast fell it broke a bowl in the ground, grassed over at the rim. The mast lies across it in three pieces of green copper, its relay half buried at the far end, stone thrown up round it; along the rim the keepers put a rope of chain on posts, and their sign. Its drive housing split open: the chest inside holds Archive Drives already filled with the relays' writing, and a Relay Dump or two, all the raw traffic that passed through it. At most one in each region 40 chunks across. Sealed stacks Deep under the ground, with no way in but a wall of clay: a vaulted hall of the archive sealed in its last days, its shelves in bays behind folded doors with wax over them, boxes of records in waxed cloth down the middle, the sealing book on its lectern, and a lamp left on the long table; roots have come down through the vault. Their boxes hold filled Archive Drives. At most one in each region 64 chunks across. Archive houses, relay masts and buried vaults Small houses of calcite between pillars of tuff under roofs of deepslate tiles, one corner usually fallen in, that kept records; open masts of green copper on stepped tuff footings, an old relay still on top of most of them; and, under a lantern on a post beside a hatch, deep rooms with a bank of old accelerators and two chests, every one holding a salvaged model. At most one in each region 56 chunks across, the vaults 64. What they hold Archive Shard: pieces of the archive, mostly of what was written about the place they lie in: a relay tower's shards are mostly its keepers' writing. See The Archive. Photomasks with salvaged designs: the Fabricator makes working but unfused machines from them, without a Bench. Linear layer, softmax and GELU masks turn up in houses, matrix multiply ones under the gravel, and attention, layer norm, feed-forward and transformer masks in vaults. Those of the modern block and the recipe lie in tutor houses, vaults and the Deep Works. See The Bench and the Fabricator. Schematic: Relays: the plans for relays, a pattern to copy that stays in the crafting grid. In relay towers, on masts and in vaults. What each place kept: coal and food in the towers, flour and seed on the farms, remedies in the marsh, timber and tools at the slips; Weight Crystal, blank Checkpoints and a little gold. Salvaged Model: see Salvaged Models.

title: Salvaged Models
text: Salvaged Models Every buried vault holds a Salvaged Model: the record of a model the old world built and could not make work. It keeps the model's machines, what it practised on and how it was trained. Each failed the way models often do. Rebuilding Put a salvaged model in a Model Core's Data slot and press Rebuild on the Data tab. Its machines are built in front of the Core as they were found: they need clear space, and they drop nothing when broken. Its training settings come with it. Train it as it is first, and watch how it fails. The loss curve, the Inspect tab and the machines themselves all have something to say. Repairing Find what is wrong and put it right: change a machine's settings, add or replace a machine, or change how it trains. A salvaged model has a budget of 1,500 steps per run to reach its goal; when a run runs out, Reset its weights and try again. A repaired model is worth experience, and what it took to repair it is worth more.

title: The Stream Scope
text: The Stream Scope A model that passes its test has told you what it can do and nothing of how. The Stream Scope looks inside. On its Model tab it takes a Checkpoint. With none, it reads the model standing on a Model Core it touches, and whatever it finds floats over that model's machines for a minute, in words and in light. It always works on a copy, so nothing it does touches the model, and Accelerators touching it lend it their threads. Each of its other tabs is one instrument: choices in a row, then one display, with the details in tooltips. Most read a stretch of a benchmark's test, or what you type. The points it reads are the model's stream: the places every path from the tokens to the scores passes through, at one width. In a stack of blocks that is the stream after each block, however you laid it out; what comes after the last is the head, a norm and an unembedding, say. A model with no such line of machines, such as a table of next letters, has one point and little to show. Lens The logit lens runs the head on the stream early, as if the rest of the stack were not there. Each row is one point of the stream and each column one token read; each cell is what that point would say next, brighter the surer, green if it is right. At the right is each point's loss over a sample of the test. So you can watch a prediction form, and see which block does the work. On a Pattern model the first block's loss is often worse than chance, and the last's near zero: the stream early on is no attempt at an answer, but something the later blocks read. Probes A linear probe is one weighted sum of what the stream carries, fitted to say whether something is true of the text: inside quotation marks, a word's first letter, a token seen before, and so on. Where one reads a thing well, the model holds that fact as a direction in its stream. A probe can always do something with the token at hand. So beside each stands a control, fitted to a meaningless label given to each kind of token. A probe that does no better than its control has found nothing but the token. The cell's colour is how far it does better; its tooltip has both. Heads Every attention head, reading runs of letters twice over. The second time through, the only way to know what comes next is to look back at what followed the same letter the first time. Each bar is how much of a head's attention falls on that very place, and the tooltip says what the model does with that head silenced. The square on the right is the strongest head's attention over one run, read from top to bottom: an off-diagonal line in its lower half is a head looking back by the length of the run. A head that does this is an induction head. It takes two layers: one head writes into the stream what came just before each place, and the next searches that for the letter at hand. Silencing the first often stops the copying more than silencing the second, though by itself it looks at nothing in particular. They form suddenly. A Model Core takes a look every fifty steps as it trains, and a model that copied nothing at one look and at the next names at least half of what comes next, with a head at least half on the right place, has formed one. From about 300 steps of the Pattern Dataset the Induction blueprint goes from copying under one letter in ten to over three in four within a hundred steps. For a model that knows its sums (Models and Tests), this tab also shows its token table read round the wheel, as frequencies. A table that has found the rule holds it in a few waves. Toy Superposition: more features than dimensions to keep them in. A toy model squeezes five features through two dimensions, or twenty through five, reads them back out with the same matrix, and trains here in seconds. Each feature counts a little less than the one before. When features are common, it keeps as many as it has dimensions and drops the rest. When they are rare, it keeps more than it has room for, each in a direction of its own that overlaps the others a little, since two rarely turn up at once. Five features in two dimensions come out as a pentagon. The bars beside it are each feature's length, and in amber how much the others lie along it. This is why a single direction in a large model's stream seldom means one thing, and why the Features tab has to look for more directions than the stream has dimensions. Patch Activation patching: read one token wrong, so that the answer changes. Then run the wrong text again and again, each time putting back what the stream carried at one point and one position when it read rightly. Where that brings the answer back is where the fact travels. A bright cell at the changed token's own column in the early blocks, and at the last column in the late ones, is the fact being carried across by attention. It finds the wrong token for itself, trying each place in turn for the one that moves the answer most. Steer The average of the stream where one token comes next, minus the average where others do, is a direction that means that token: a steering vector. Add it to the stream as the model reads, at any strength, and the model leans that way, with no training at all. The rows show how often that token becomes its first choice, how likely it holds it, and what the loss pays for that. Underneath, the model writes as it is, and again steered. At ×1 the average place has been moved all the way across. Far past that, the model says little else. Features A probe needs you to know what to look for. A sparse autoencoder looks for itself: a dictionary of eight times as many directions as the stream has dimensions, of which only an eighth as many as the stream is wide may add up to what it carries at any place. Forced to say so much with so few, its directions tend to come out as things that mean something. Fitting one takes seconds to a minute, and it is kept until the model changes. The first lines say how much of what the stream varies by it explains, how many directions never fired, and what the model's loss becomes when it runs on the dictionary's version of the stream, against the stream's average alone. Below is each feature that matters, with how often it fires. Point at one for where it fired most strongly, the token in gold, and what it pushes the scores toward. Graph An attribution graph takes one thing a model says, and shows which features made it say so, and which tokens and features made those. On the left are the tokens it read, then a column of features for each point of the stream, then what it said. Amber lines push it toward that, blue away, brighter the more. A model this small can afford the exact answer: each thing is taken out of the stream, the rest of the model runs on, and what changes is what it put in. A larger one has to estimate. It holds attention patterns and norms still, so that what flows through is nearly linear, and multiplies a gradient by an amount. Every feature's tooltip has both, and the top line says how closely they agree. Where a model's work is done by attention they can disagree badly: holding attention still hides what a feature does by moving it. It needs a dictionary at each point, and fits the ones it lacks. The Fabricator makes it from a transformer photomask.

title: An Access Point's screen
text: An Access Point's screen Use an Access Point to open it. Storage tells how far terminals reach. A slot for a Relay Card, and a mark for how far it reaches. Relay Card: A Relay Card tuned to a Model Server. With one here, Wireless Terminals reach this network anywhere that server's relays cover. Its reach: Teal with power in a Link Driver on its network, amber with a Relay Card that reaches. Point at it for how many blocks.

title: An agent's screen
text: An agent's screen Use an agent to open it. Agents tells what it can do. Work: its job, what it is doing, and telling it something. The tabs: What it does, the program it runs, and what it has been doing. Jobs: A button for each job; the one it is doing is greyed out. Point at one for what it does. What it is doing: Its status, the model that made its last decision, what it asked and answered, and how often it was right. Order: An order in your own words, for its model. Tell: Its model reads the order back as a program, for your yes or no. Filter: Its filter: a checkpoint that passes Sorting. It tells what kind each thing is, so that sort can put it in the chest labelled with its kind. Model: Its model: a checkpoint, or a Relay Card tuned to a Model Server. It writes the orders it is given as programs, and makes the decisions of storing, hauling, building and copying. Set home: Make where it stands its home. All its work happens around home. What it carries: Twelve slots of its own. Program: the program it runs, to read, rewrite or click together. The program: Checked as it is typed. Clicking it with a thing in hand names that thing. The check: Says whether it reads as a program, and where it slips if not. Run: Run this program from the top, from now on. Stop: Stop where it is. Run starts the program again. Palette: Shows the pieces beside the window, or hides them. Whole window: Gives the program the whole window, with the slots out of the way. The pieces: Everything a program can say, page by page, to click together. Each piece goes on the end of the program. Its last page is what you hold and the agent carries. Trace: what it has been doing, step by step, with a debugger beside it. The trace: Each step with how it went: what it did, what it could not, and what it asked its model. Debugger: Holds the program at its next step, or lets it go on. Click a line above to stop there each time it comes round. One step: Runs one step and holds again. Values: What the program holds now, and what you asked to watch.

title: An Archive Shard, read
text: An Archive Shard, read Use an Archive Shard to read it. The Archive tells where its lost text goes. A record of the old world, as far as it can still be read. How much can be read: The share of the record still legible. Its text: Lost blocks show worn. Scroll for the rest.

title: The Arena's screen
text: The Arena's screen Use an Arena to open it. The Arena tells how a mob is written down and what a model has to do to play it. With no log or model yet, it says what it needs. The log: A Mob Log that has written down mobs of its kind. A base at the Frontier tier can also put a Surveyor's Field Log here, for ground. Model: A checkpoint, or a Relay Card tuned to a Model Server. Its model plays the mob in every fight, and how often it picks what the mob really did, on the tenth of the log kept from practice, is what the fights are worth. The mob: The mob of the log. Along its foot a mark for each tier of likeness the model has reached; point at it for how the model did, what that earns, and what is in the way. What it won: What the fights that count have dropped. A hopper can take it from here. Power: What it has stored, filling from the bottom. Point at it for what a fight costs.

title: An Assembler's screen
text: An Assembler's screen Use an Assembler to open it. Storage tells how a network crafts. A recipe drawn in its grid. The recipe: Click with a stack to put its kind in the recipe; click empty-handed to clear. The grid holds pictures, not items: the Assembler takes its ingredients from its network. What it makes: Worked out from the grid. Keep: The four buttons beside the panel change how many to keep in the network; point at one to see the current number. It makes more whenever there are fewer. With nothing to keep, it makes only what is asked of it. With shift, sixty-four times as many. What it is doing: Point at the work arrow to see whether it is crafting, has enough, lacks something, or has no recipe yet.

title: The Bench's screen
text: The Bench's screen Use a Bench to open it. The Bench and the Fabricator tells how a design is wired. A design, wired from the parts to the result. The spec: What you are wiring. Click it to choose another. The parts: What a design is wired from: the smallest operations, then the modules you have verified. Drag one onto the board. The board: Drag parts onto the board. Wire a node's right edge to another's left edge, and the last node into the result. Right-click removes; Ctrl+Z undoes. Click a node to see its numbers. Its numbers: What the node you clicked computes on the chosen case, or what the result should be. The goal: What the spec must compute, and its formula. The cases: A mark for each test case, passing or not. Click one to run the design on it. result: Wire the last node here. Green means the chosen case passes. Record: Once every case passes, verifies the design, and records it to a photomask where the spec makes a machine. Every spec: those verified ticked, those not yet open locked. A spec: Click one to open it. A spec opens once those it builds on are verified.

title: The Model Core's screen
text: The Model Core's screen Use a Model Core to open it. Its tabs take a model from its data to its tests; The Model Core tells how they go together. Data: what the model practises on, and where it is kept. The tabs: The screen's views. It opens on the one you left it on. Practice: Datasets or an Archive Drive for the model to practise on. Tokenizer: A Tokenizer here sets the tokens the model reads and writes. Without one, it reads one character at a time. Changing it reshapes the first and last layers, so they start over. Checkpoint: A checkpoint here takes the trained model when you save. A saved one shows what it can do. Save to checkpoint: Tests the model on every benchmark and keeps it, scores and all, in the checkpoint. What it practises: Each benchmark what is loaded lets it practise, and the job that benchmark is used for. Status: What the Core is doing, and how many steps the model has trained. Train: the model learning, step by step. The curve: Train loss in teal, test loss in amber, accuracy in green, against the steps trained. Point at it to read any step. Where it stands: The numbers the curves end at. Point at them for its parameters, gradient norm and threads. Train: Starts training, and stops it. Reset: Starts the model over from fresh weights. Check: Reads the model's machines again and lists anything wrong with them. Speed: Watch slows each step down so you can follow it; Max trains as fast as the Core can. Learning rate: How far each step moves the weights. Too high and the loss jumps about; too low and it barely moves. Batch: How many examples each step learns from at once. Clip: The longest a step's gradient may be, so one bad batch can't throw the model off course. Tests: how the model does on what it has not practised. A benchmark: One line for each: its name, a bar toward what passes, and its score, green once it passes. Scroll for the rest. Point at a line for its job, when it was tested and how its test goes. Click it for its runs from fresh seeds, a look-alike of its test and the server's leaderboard: Comparing Models tells how they go. Test all: Runs every test now. Save to checkpoint: Tests the model on every benchmark and keeps it, scores and all, in the checkpoint. Scroll through the Tests tab to see every benchmark. A benchmark: Each row opens its comparison when clicked. The scroll bar: Shows which rows are in view. Scroll over the list or click the bar to move through it. Click a benchmark to compare its test, fresh runs and the server's designs. The comparison: The score on its test and on a look-alike with other items. A warning means its test flatters it beyond chance. Fresh seeds: The spread of runs from fresh weights and batches, with the previous design below when there is one. The server's board: The leading designs, their makers, scores and sizes. Point at one for its machines. The distributions: How the server's designs spread by score and size, with this model marked in amber. Back: Returns to the benchmark list. Try: the model answering. Benchmark: Which benchmark to try it on. Example: Draws a fresh example from the test and has the model answer it. Where you can type, this asks or writes instead. Its answer: Grey is what the model was shown, white is what it wrote. The bars show its odds for the first token it chose; ⏎ is a line break. Inspect: the model's machines, a line each. Its machines: Each machine with its name, the shape of what it puts out, its parameters and how much gradient reaches it. Anything wrong comes first, in red. Recipe: how a run goes beside its learning rate. The settings: Each is dim until the unit for it touches the Core. The Recipe says what each does. What the run is doing: The rate now, what the weights take, the text read, the spikes, the largest scores and how often a second head is right. Point at one for what it means. The rate over the run: What the learning rate is multiplied by from the first step to the last, with a line where the run has reached. The units: Lit if one touches the Core, directly or through accelerators and other units. Point at one for what it opens. Schedule: How the learning rate moves over a run: held steady, falling along a cosine from the end of warmup, or held and falling over the last fifth. A falling one needs a Length. Warmup: How many steps the rate takes to rise to its full size. Length: How many steps a run lasts, after which it stops by itself. With no end it runs until it is stopped. Precision: What the model's matrices, and the numbers going into them, are rounded to, in training and whenever it answers afterwards. The narrower, the fewer bytes a weight takes. Optimizer: What moves the weights: AdamW, each number on its own, or Muon, each matrix inside the model as a whole, every direction alike. Packing: How archive text is cut into rows: windows of long stretches only, rows packed from every stretch, or packed with a mask so that nothing looks from one stretch into another. Compute: what the run really costs, and how it shares out its work. The run: How it shares out and on how many devices, its memory against what has to hold it, its flops a second, its power and PUE, and what it has spent so far. The last step: What each device did through the last step: teal forward, amber back, violet collectives. Where it is dark it waited: with pipeline parallelism, those are its bubbles. Sharing out the work: How a run shares its work among its devices. It takes effect when the next run starts.

title: A Drive Dock's screen
text: A Drive Dock's screen Use a Drive Dock to open it. Storage tells what it is for. The drives waiting on the left, the drives done on the right. Waiting: Drives wait on the left, one at a time, and come out on the right when they are done. What it moves: Fills while it moves anything. Point at it for how much in the last second. Done: Where each drive comes out. What it does: Empties drives into the network, or fills them from it.

title: A Drive Rack's screen
text: A Drive Rack's screen Use a Drive Rack to open it. Storage tells what the drives hold. Eight bays, a drive in the first. The bays: A Storage Drive. A rack holds eight; the light beside each bay shows how full its drive is.

title: An exosuit's screen
text: An exosuit's screen Sneak and use an exosuit, or press its key while you wear it, to open it. The Exosuit tells what it runs on. What its board found, and each ability, turned on and off beside the window. Its charge: Point at it for how much it holds. Its board: The model's weights, what they take as plain floats and in each form it can run in, how each scores, its compute, and what each ability running draws from it. An ability: A line for each, with the compute it draws, teal while it runs, amber if it is on and there is not enough for it. Point at one for what it does. Its switch: Turns the ability on or off. Those left on run cheapest first, as far as the compute goes.

title: The Fabricator's screen
text: The Fabricator's screen Use a Fabricator to open it. The Bench and the Fabricator tells what it makes. With no photomask, what it can make are the machines that need none. Photomask: A mask offers what its design makes. What it can make: Click one; the teal one is what it makes. Materials: What the machine takes, with how many under each, red while short. The work: Fills as it works. Point at it for the machine's name, what it does and how long it takes. What it made: Faint until it is made. With its materials in, it goes to work. Materials: Taken as the work begins. The work

title: A Forecaster's screen
text: A Forecaster's screen Use a Forecaster to open it. The Forecaster tells how it comes to trust a model. What it sees around it, and how close its model comes to it. The blocks around it: The crops and machines within four blocks, from above with north up, a block higher or lower too. The Forecaster sits in the middle; whatever its model just ran ahead is outlined. Machines: The kind of block the bars show: crops or machines. The bars: How far they moved from each place, in amber, against what its model expects, in teal. Point at a group to read it. What it is doing: Whether it is watching, checking or running them ahead. Each kind: How many it watches, then the progress seen so far or how close the model came. Within 11% it runs them four looks for every one; within 25%, two. Field Log: A Field Log keeps a copy of everything the Forecaster watched, a line per crop or machine. In a Model Core's data slot, it is practice for Forecasting on these very blocks. Model: A model that has learned what crops and machines do next: a checkpoint, or a Relay Card tuned to its Model Server.

title: The BPE Forge's screen
text: The BPE Forge's screen Use a BPE Forge to open it. Tokens tells what a vocabulary is for. A vocabulary being learned from a drive, merge by merge. Archive Drive: An Archive Drive: the forge learns from its legible text. Tokenizer: A Tokenizer to write onto, blank or written. The forge carries on from the merges it already has. Vocabulary size: How many tokens to learn. Bigger tokens carry more text each, but the embedding and the last layer grow with the vocabulary. How far it has come: Point at it for what it is doing. Its text, in tokens: A passage of the drive, cut as the vocabulary now cuts it. Point at a token for what it is made of. Latest merges: The pairs it joined last, newest first.

title: A Hall Console's screen
text: A Hall Console's screen Use a Hall Console to open it. Halls tells what makes a hall. One display: what the hall is, what it is doing, and what the largest run it could hold would cost. The hall: Its racks, pods and devices, what it is rated for, what it is running, and what it draws. Point at the first line for what it still lacks, at the power for what PUE is. The largest run: A prediction, by the sums: six flops a parameter a token, sixteen bytes a parameter, at its whole rated speed. Its racks: A column for each rack, as tall as that rack is busy.

title: Screens
text: Screens Every screen, part by part. The numbers on a picture are the parts listed under it, and pointing at a number says what it is. Model Core Agent Bench Fabricator BPE Forge Machines Reader Forecaster Surveyor Watch Post Arena Generator, Smelter and Reactor Storage Terminal Port A Port's programs Drive Rack Assembler Processor Drive Dock Access Point Terminal Relay Gate Exosuit Archive Shard Wayfinder Refinery machines Rack Module Hall Console Model Server Tuner Stream Scope and Trial Rig

title: The screens of the Scope and the Rig
text: The screens of the Scope and the Rig Use a Stream Scope or a Trial Rig to open them. The Stream Scope and The Trial Rig tell what each tab does. Model: the model it works on, a copy of it each time. The model: A checkpoint. With none, the model standing on a Model Core it touches. Status: How big the model is and how many points its stream has, or how the last work came out. Every other tab is one instrument: its choices in a row, then one display. The instruments: Each reads the model its own way. Start or stop: Starts the work, and while it runs, stops it. The display: What the work comes to, drawn as it goes. Point at anything for its numbers. A Trial Rig's Model tab also holds what the trial works on and a checkpoint for the model it leaves behind. The model: A checkpoint. With none, the model standing on a Model Core it touches. What it works on: A dataset, a drive or a Field Log, for the trials that need one. What it keeps: A checkpoint that takes the model a trial leaves behind. Status: How big the model is and how many points its stream has, or how the last work came out. A Trial Rig's tabs are trials: each trains a copy of the model and charts what comes of it. The trials: Memory, Backdoor, Forgetting, Collapse and Contamination. Start or stop: Starts the trial, and while it runs, stops it. The display: The trial's curves as it goes.

title: A Model Server's screen
text: A Model Server's screen Use a Model Server with an empty hand to open it. Serving Models tells what each thing in its panel earns. What it serves and what that costs, its panel beside it, and its settings under that. The model it serves.: A saved checkpoint. Sneak-use the server with an empty hand to take it back. Answers a second: Answers that read 16 tokens and write 8, as its model and what is in its panel were measured to cost. The bar is how much of its operations is in use. Memory: Its weights, its draft and what it keeps, of all it holds. Drawn on by: What it has been spent on lately KV Cache: Each one adds 256 KiB, and with any here it keeps what each token worked out for the next. Weight Packer: Lets the button below keep its weights in 8 or 4 bits. Draft: A small model reading the same tokens proposes what comes next, and the served model checks several at a pass. Takes a KV Cache. Judge: A model a Tuner taught to score answers. When it writes several answers to an order, it keeps the one this scores highest. Form of its weights: Takes a Weight Packer. Packed weights take less memory, and are read out of it on every pass. Each test it passed is run again in the new form. Most in a pass: Takes a KV Cache. Sequences waiting at once go through in one pass, which shares what a pass itself costs. Answers to a question: Takes a KV Cache. For an order or a sum it writes this many answers and keeps one, by checking them, by a vote or by a judge. Each is paid for; the screen says what that does to each test.

title: A machine's screen
text: A machine's screen Use any machine of a model to open it; each has its own settings and math. Machines has a page for each. A Linear Layer before its first check. Name: A name of your own, shown wherever the machine is listed. Settings: What this machine can be set to; they differ from machine to machine. Click for the next value, right-click for the one before. What the last check found: The shape it puts out, its parameters and gradient, or what is wrong with it. Output: What comes out of its front, amber above zero and blue below. A machine with weights shows its main matrix beside it. The math: What it computes, in a line or two.

title: A Port's screen
text: A Port's screen Use a Port to open it. Storage tells how its modes differ. The filter stays in the window; the mode buttons sit beside it. Point at the arrow to see what moved in the last second. Import: Takes everything from the inventory in front of it into the network, 64 items a tick; with a filter, only those kinds. Export: Puts the kinds its filter names from the network into the inventory in front of it, 64 items a tick. Filter: Click with a stack to name its kind here, or shift-click it in your inventory; click empty-handed to clear. A filled bucket names its fluid. An empty filter lets everything through. With a filter model, something renamed Food, Plants, Wood, Stone, Ores or Tools stands for that whole kind. What it moved: How much in the last second, or that a full link holds it back. Filter model: A checkpoint, or a Relay Card tuned to a Model Server, whose model passes Sorting. It tells what kind each thing is, so a filter slot holding something renamed for a kind imports or exports everything of that kind. A thing it is not sure of counts as other. Target model: A model that forecasts what this Port will need. Point at it to see the expected amount above its checkpoint details. Field Log: A Field Log here keeps a copy of what this Port moves out, a line per thing. In a Model Core's data slot it is practice for Demand on your own base. Stocking: point at the number buttons for the amount to keep, and turn on asking for what it lacks. Stock: Keeps each kind its filter names at the chosen amount in the inventory in front: it tops each one up from the network, and takes any extra back. Window: Opens the inventory in front of it to the network, which keeps items there and takes them out as if it were a drive. A higher priority is filled first; a filter limits what goes in. The number: Keep this many of each filtered kind in the inventory in front. Hold Shift to change sixty-four times as many. Ask for what it lacks: Does not ask. Click to have the network's Assemblers and Processors make what its filter names whenever there is too little of it. Programs: Program Cards, upgrades and what its programs hold. With a written card in it, it does what the card says instead of what its mode says. A window opens the inventory to the network. Point at its number buttons for its priority. Window: Opens the inventory in front of it to the network, which keeps items there and takes them out as if it were a drive. A higher priority is filled first; a filter limits what goes in. Priority: The network fills a higher-priority window first. Change by one or four. Filter: Click with a stack to name its kind here, or shift-click it in your inventory; click empty-handed to clear. A filled bucket names its fluid. An empty filter lets everything through. With a filter model, something renamed Food, Plants, Wood, Stone, Ores or Tools stands for that whole kind.

title: A Port's programs
text: A Port's programs Press the programs button on a Port's screen to open them. With a written card in it, a Port does what the card says instead of what its mode says. Programs tells the language they speak. Program: its cards, its upgrades and the chosen card's program. The tabs: The program on the chosen card, and how it has been running. Program Card: Click a slot to choose it; the program below is what that card says. The program: Checked as it is typed. The check: Says whether it reads as a program, and where it slips if not. Run: Writes the program on the chosen card and runs it from the top. Stop: Stop where it is. Run starts the program again. What it holds: What its programs work with. Upgrades: What makes it faster, stronger and further-reaching. Filter and mode: Back to its mode, its filter and its filter model. Who may use it: It belongs to whoever set it down; only they can change this. Make a team with /residual team make, invite with /residual team invite, join with /residual team join. Trace: how it has been running, with a debugger beside it. The trace: Each step with how it went. Debugger: Holds the program at its next step, or lets it go on. Click a line above to stop there each time it comes round. One step: Runs one step and holds again. Values: What the program holds now, and what you asked to watch.

title: The screens of power
text: The screens of power Use a Combustion Generator, a Boiler, a Smelter or a Reactor Core to open them. Power tells what they make and use. A Combustion Generator: fuel under its flame. Fuel: What a furnace burns. The flame: Burns down with the fuel. Stored power: Point at it for how much, and what it makes. A Smelter: ore on the left, ingots on the right. Ore The work: Fills as it smelts. With a controller, it shows the melt: a column a look, the band shaded across. Ingots Stored power: Point at it for how much, and what it draws. Controller: A model practised on Control. It holds each melt in its band, and a melt it holds makes three ingots instead of two. A Reactor Core: fuel under its flame, and its cycle look by look. Fuel: Reactor Fuel. The flame: Burns down with the fuel. The cycle: A column a look, the band shaded across. Point at it for why it is not running, or how far through the cycle it is and how much of the last one was held. Stored power: Point at it for how much, and what it makes. Controller: A model that passes Containment. Nothing else starts it, and it stops itself rather than go on without one.

title: A Processor's screen
text: A Processor's screen Use a Processor to open it. Storage tells how a network crafts. A pattern: what goes in, the machine in front, what comes out. What goes in: What the machine takes for one round. Click with a stack to put that many there, right-click for one more; empty-handed, a click clears the cell and a right-click takes one off. The grid holds pictures, not items. What comes out: What the machine makes in one round. The first thing here is what the network can ask for; the rest come along with it. Click with a stack to put that many there, right-click for one more; empty-handed, a click clears the cell and a right-click takes one off. The machine: What stands in front of the Processor, which it runs the pattern on. Pages: Nine pages of nine cells each way. Keep: The four buttons beside the panel change how many to keep in the network; point at one to see the current number. It makes more whenever there are fewer. With shift, sixty-four times as many. What it is doing: Point at the work arrow to see its rounds a second, or what it lacks.

title: A Rack Module's screen
text: A Rack Module's screen Use a Rack Module to open it. Compute tells how racks are built. Eight bays, an Accelerator in the first. The bays: A Training Accelerator, of any process node. The strip of light beside it shows how busy it is.

title: The Reader's screen
text: The Reader's screen Use a Reader to open it. The Archive tells how a model restores what was lost. A shard in its tray, its lost text worn away. Archive Shard: The shard to restore. Model: What restores it: a checkpoint, or a Relay Card tuned to a Model Server. Its text: What can be read, and the blocks still worn, lighting up as they come back. What it is doing: Which block it is on and how the last try went, or what it needs.

title: The screens of a Refinery
text: The screens of a Refinery Use any machine of a line to open its screen. The Refinery tells how a line goes together and what each machine is worth. A Refinery Intake: what goes in, and the two things it can be asked. What goes in: Archive Drives and Relay Dumps, up to nine. What it read: What the slots hold and how much text that came to; once measured, the held-out loss of the raw text. Refine: Sends all it holds down the line: each machine's front faces the next, up to 12 blocks off with nothing solid between. Measure: Trains small readers on what each machine let through, and shows over each machine what it did to held-out loss. A Duplicate Sieve: what it took out, and the curve its hashes make. What it took out: Point at a row for what it means. The curve: Across, how alike two documents are; up, how likely they are to be compared: 128 hashes in bands. The line is the threshold, the bars the pairs compared. Near copies at: How alike two documents must be, by the runs of five words they share, to count as copies. A Filter Bed: a row and a switch for each rule. What each rule threw out: Point at a row for what it means. Too short: Throws out what has fewer than 12 words. Too many marks: Throws out what is over a fifth marks and digits. Not word-sized: Throws out what has words under 2.5 letters or over 9 on average. Saying one thing: Throws out what says one line over half the time. Lines that do not end: Throws out what hardly ever ends a line as a sentence or a verse does. A Quality Classifier: its model and its rule, and what each decided. Its model: A checkpoint, or a Relay Card tuned to a Model Server, whose model passes Quality. With none, the rule decides alone. What it decided: Point at a row for what it means. Sure enough at: How sure the model must be, one way or the other. What it is less sure of goes to the rule. A Program Press: what it wrote into the stream. Its book: A book of templates, for the Book program: each page a template, with {a|b} for a choice. What it wrote: Point at a row for what it means. Program: What it writes: sums with their working, orders and what they mean, things and their kinds, or a book of templates. Writes: How much it adds, as a share of the text coming in. A Domain Mixer: a row for each kind of writing, and what the last of a run reads. The kinds of writing: Each one's share of what a model reads. Click a row for more or less of it. Anneals on: The kind of writing the last of a run reads alone, at a fifth of the rate. Anneals after: Steps of a run in a Model Core before that. When measured, a reader anneals for its last fifth. A Contamination Check: what it found of each benchmark's test. What it found: Lines it found first, then a row for each benchmark. Scroll for the rest. What it finds: Takes out what it finds, or only says so. A Token Tank: what the line holds, counted. Tokenizer: A Tokenizer, to count tokens as it cuts them. Without one every character is a token. Token Cell: A Token Cell. Put in, it draws on what the line's tanks hold, for a Model Core's data slots. What it holds: Point at a row for what it means.

title: A Relay Gate's screen
text: A Relay Gate's screen Use a Relay Gate to open it. Serving Models tells how the network is built and what opens a gate. Its name, the network, and every gate on it to go to. Its name: Shown on the map and in every list of gates. Open or shut: Open with how many answers a second its model gives, or why it is shut. The map: Shows all of the network here. Scroll to zoom, drag to move. The gates: Every other gate on the network; click one to go there. Frame it all: Shows all of the network here. Scroll to zoom, drag to move.

title: A Storage Terminal's screen
text: A Storage Terminal's screen Use a Storage Terminal to open it. A Wireless Terminal and a Portable Drive open the same. Storage tells what the network keeps and makes. All the network keeps, with what it can make marked. Search: Words a thing's name holds, or a Chinese name's pinyin. @ for a mod, # a tag, $ the tooltip, * the id; - leaves things out, | gives alternatives, ( ) groups; >64, <10 or =1 asks how many. @minecraft ingot -iron finds every ingot but iron. Start with ? to ask the model beside the window for what you mean. Jobs: The crafting jobs running on this network Sort: Sort by name, by how many, or by mod. Shift-click to reverse. The kinds: Click to take a stack, right-click for half, shift-click to send a stack to your inventory; click holding something to put it in, right-click for one. Alt-click pins a kind to the top. The scrollbar: Drag it, or scroll over the grid. How full it is: What is kept, what there is room for, and how many kinds. Model: A model that passes Retrieval. Start a search with ? and it looks for what you mean, among everything kept. A crafting grid: Works as at a crafting table, and draws what it needs from the network. Asking for what the network can make: the plan, and what is missing. How many: How many to make, typed or stepped. Steps: Adds this many; with Shift, takes them away The plan: kept · ×crafts · −missing Start: Starts the job. What is missing, it waits for: put it into the network and the job goes on. Back: Back to the grid The jobs running on the network: what each makes, how far it has come, what it waits for. A job: Click to see its plan Cancel: Stops the job. A job's plan as a tree: each row under the step that needs it. The plan: How many of each came from storage, how far its crafts have come, and what is still missing.

title: The Surveyor's screen
text: The Surveyor's screen Use a Surveyor to open it. The Surveyor tells what its model reads. With no model, it says what it needs; with one, the finds are counted here. Model: A model practised on the Survey Dataset. It reads the ground a row at a time and says where each ore and cache lies; what it gets right shows to anyone near holding a Survey Rod. What it found: Each ore and the caches, with how many its model has found this survey. Point at one for more. A Field Log: A Field Log here keeps a fair sample of the rows it reads, for practice and for an Arena. How far it has gone: Along the display's foot, how far this survey has gone. Point at it for how far it reaches.

title: A Terminal's screen
text: A Terminal's screen Use a Terminal to open it, from anywhere the relays of its Model Server reach. Serving Models tells how one is tuned. Map: the relay network as it stands. Map: The relay network: where it reaches, and every gate on it to go to. Its reach: Whether it reaches its server from here, and how fast that server answers. The map: Shows all of the network here. Scroll to zoom, drag to move. The gates: Every gate on the network; click one to go there. Frame it all: Shows all of the network here. Scroll to zoom, drag to move. Base: what the base holds, and what its machines are doing. Base: What the base holds, and what its machines are doing. The base: Each storage network, to open as if standing at it, then each machine with what it is doing. Agents: what each is doing, to stop, start, hand a program or give an order. Agents: What each agent is doing. Hand one a program or give it an order. The agents: Each agent and what it is doing. Click one to choose it. The one chosen: The program it runs, or the one it wants a yes or no to. Program Card: The written cards you carry, to hand it one. Order: An order in your own words, for the served model to write as a program. Writing: the served model carrying on whatever you start. Writing: The served model carries on whatever you start. Prompt: The start of something, for the model to write on from. Write: Sends it to the server. Clear: Clears the prompt and the answer. The answer: Grey is what you wrote, white what the model wrote.

title: A Tuner's screen
text: A Tuner's screen Use a Tuner to open it. Tuning tells what each way of tuning does and what it earns. A saved model on the left, what it needs beside it under that, and a blank checkpoint on the right; the toolbar sets how. The base: The saved model it starts from. It stays as it is: what comes out is a new one. Beside it: A dataset or an Archive Drive; two of them to mix. What comes out: A blank checkpoint, to save into. The display: Before it starts, what the way it is set to does. While it runs, the reward in teal against what was really right in amber, each try's mark, and what the model last wrote. Tune: Starts, or stops and keeps what it has so far. How: What it does to the model, and what that needs beside it. Steps: How long it goes on before it saves. Starts by itself: Starts whenever a base and a blank checkpoint are in, as along a line of Tuners and hoppers. What it finishes leaves by a hopper below.

title: The Watch Post's screen
text: The Watch Post's screen Use a Watch Post to open it. The Watch Post tells what it watches for. A row for each thing it watches. What it watches: Each thing's line of looks as bars, newest on the right, red while something is wrong with it. Point at a row to hear what it thinks. Model: A checkpoint, or a Relay Card tuned to a Model Server, whose model passes Watch. It reads each thing's line, and what surprises it is what has gone wrong. Without one, or on a line it cannot follow, the Watch Post only sees what has stopped for two minutes.

title: The Wayfinder's screen
text: The Wayfinder's screen Use a Wayfinder to open it. Ruins tells what it finds. The kinds of place it knows of. The places: Click one and it looks for the nearest. Shards tell of more places.

title: Shapes
text: Shapes Every value in a model is a grid of numbers, a tensor, and its shape says how big each side of the grid is. The Model Core checks every shape before it trains anything, the same way PyTorch would fail on the first batch, but with a clearer message. Reading a shape Shapes are written outermost first: [B×T×32] is a batch of B sequences, each T positions long, with 32 numbers at every position. Letter Means B Batch: how many sequences are processed at once. Set on the Core. T Time: positions in a sequence, up to the context length of 64. Every other number is a size you chose, like the 32 above, or the vocabulary size V, which shows as its value: 89, one for each letter, digit and mark a model knows, and the line break, or more with a tokenizer. The last dimension is the one machines work on: a Linear Layer turns [B×T×32] into [B×T×64] by mixing the 32 numbers at each position into 64 new ones, the same way at every position. A shape with fewer dimensions stretches to fit, as in PyTorch: the Position Table's [T×32] adds onto every sequence of a [B×T×32] batch. What the Core expects The Core sends out token ids, shaped [B×T], and wants back one score for every possible next token at every position: [B×T×V]. Whatever happens in between is up to you. When shapes disagree Press Check on the Core, or look at a machine. A machine whose inputs don't fit says what it got and what it needs. Common causes: A Residual Junction or Gate whose two inputs have different widths. A Matrix Multiplier whose inner sizes don't match. With Transpose on, it multiplies by the side input turned on its side, which is what comparing queries with keys needs. The last machine before the Core not ending in V. Shapes flow forward, so fix the earliest problem first: a wrong width early on makes every later machine look wrong too. The Inspect tab on the Core lists every machine in the order data reaches it. In PyTorch Shape errors are the most common bug in real model code. PyTorch only finds them when the code runs; reading shapes the way the Core does, before running anything, is a habit worth taking with you.

title: Storage
text: Storage Storage Drives in a Drive Rack, joined by Storage Links to a Storage Terminal and to Ports, make one storage network. It keeps any number of kinds of item and fluid, finds any of them from the terminal, and moves them in and out of chests, tanks and machines on its own. Nothing in it needs power, and nothing switches off. A Drive Rack holds the drives. Put a drive in it. Storage Links run from the rack to whatever else belongs to the network. A Storage Terminal on the links shows all the network keeps. A Port between the links and a chest moves what is in the chest onto the drives. A terminal's screen, a rack's, a Port's, an Assembler's, a Processor's, a Dock's, an Access Point's. Drives and racks A drive holds as many kinds as you like: a kind costs nothing but what there is of it. A bucket of fluid takes the room of one item. What a drive holds goes with it, so a drive moved to another rack takes everything with it, and its tooltip says how full it is. Drive Holds Made Storage Drive 262,144 at a crafting table Dense Drive 8,388,608 in the Fabricator, from a linear layer photomask Stacked Drive 268,435,456 in the Fabricator, from a transformer photomask Deep Drive 8,589,934,592 from eight Stacked Drives, to the plans on the relay schematic Crafting Crafting Crafting A Drive Rack holds eight drives of any size. Beside each bay a light shows how full its drive is: dim while it is empty, teal while it has room, amber once it is three quarters full, red when it is full. The Drive Dock A Drive Dock, from a matrix multiply photomask, moves what drives hold far faster than a Port: 2,048 items a tick, 40,960 a second, or 256 buckets a tick. Put it on the network and drives in its left bays, and it takes them one at a time. Set by the button beside its window, it either empties each drive into the network or fills it from the network; a drive it has finished, emptied, full, or with nothing more to be had, comes out on the right. Beside a rack nothing limits it. Through a link it goes as fast as the link does. To move everything to a larger drive, fill the larger drive here, or empty the old one into a rack that holds the new. Links Storage Links join racks, terminals and Ports into one network. Every storage block that touches another joins it, on any face, except a Port's front. There are no channels and no limit on how many blocks a network joins. Storage Links are not the signal cables models are wired with: the two never connect. Crafting What a link limits is how much goes along it. You can watch it go: the things themselves ride on the link, over a pulse of light, teal going into the network and amber coming out; a fluid's pulse is its own color. A link carries 1,024 items a tick, 20,480 a second, or 128 buckets a tick. What a Port or a Dock moves takes the shortest way to the nearest rack, and everything sharing a stretch of link shares its 1,024 evenly. Nothing stops when a link is full; the rest just waits for the next tick, the pulses along that way turn red, and the Port's screen says so. A second line beside the first carries as much again, and a rack near the Ports that use it most saves the links altogether. A Link Driver joins a storage network on any face and a power network through Power Cables. While it has power, every link of its network carries 4,096 items a tick. It burns 40 FE for each tick a link would otherwise be full, and nothing while they have room. Without power everything goes on at the plain rate. Use it to see its power and what the links carry now. Crafting The Storage Terminal Crafting The terminal shows everything its network keeps, with how many of each kind, and lights up once its network has somewhere to keep things. Click a kind to take a stack, right-click to take half, shift-click to move a stack into your inventory. Click the grid with a stack to put it in, right-click to put in one. Shift-click a stack in your inventory to put it away. Click the grid with a filled bucket or tank to pour it in; the empty one stays in your hand. Click a fluid with an empty one to fill it. Right-click with a filled bucket, and the bucket itself goes in. The button beside the search box sorts by name (Az), by how many (#) or by mod (@); shift-click it to reverse. The search box finds things by name, every word at once. Other facts take a sign before them: Search Finds ingot names holding "ingot" @minecraft things from that mod #ingots things with a tag holding "ingots" $hunger tooltips holding "hunger" *copper ids holding "copper" -iron everything except what holds "iron" iron | gold either one (log | planks) -oak groups >64, <10, =1, >=1k how many are kept (k for thousands, m for millions) @minecraft ingot -iron finds every ingot but iron, and >1k everything there are more than a thousand of. Names and tooltips written in Chinese answer to their pinyin as well, in whole syllables, in the first letters of them, or in just the first letter of each: 铁矿石 is tiekuangshi, tkshi or tks. Beside the window is a slot for a model: a Checkpoint, or a Relay Card tuned to a Model Server, whose model passes Retrieval (Models and Tests). Start a search with ? and write what you want, the way you would say it: ?something to light a cave. The model reads what you wrote and says how likely it is to be about each of its twenty uses, and reads the name of each thing the network keeps the same way, once for each thing, keeping where it put it. A thing fits as far as the two agree, and what fits comes first, the best first, though its name has no word of what you wrote; a thing's tooltip says how far it fits. What agrees less than 36 parts in a hundred, about as far as two readings each six parts in ten sure of the same use, it leaves out. With no model, or one that has not passed, ? goes by your words alone: anything whose name holds one of them. The model reads only English, as models do. Under that slot is a crafting grid. Things go in as at any crafting table, and each craft's ingredients come again from the network as long as it has them, so shift-clicking the result crafts until there is no more room or nothing left to craft with. What is in the grid goes back to the network when the screen closes. With JEI beside the screen, its search box and the terminal's hold the same words. Its + on a crafting recipe lays the recipe in the grid from the network and your inventory, marking what neither has, and with Ctrl asks the network for what it can make. Its + on an Assembler's or a Processor's screen draws the recipe there, and things dragged from its list onto a filter or a pattern's cells name them. Wireless Terminals A Wireless Terminal is a Storage Terminal's screen in the hand. Use it on an Access Point to tune it to that network, then use it anywhere in reach, or press the key you give it in the controls to open the first one in your inventory. Crafting An Access Point comes from an attention photomask and joins its network like any storage block. It reaches 528 blocks, in every direction; with power in a Link Driver on the same network, 2,112. Any number can stand on one network, and a terminal goes by the nearest. A network far off stays loaded for as long as the screen is open. Beyond that lie the relays. Put a Relay Card in an Access Point's slot, tuned to a Model Server whose relays cover the Access Point, and its terminals reach the network anywhere those relays cover, however far from home (Serving Models). Portable Drives A Portable Drive, from a linear layer photomask, holds 1,048,576 items of any number of kinds and opens its own terminal screen in the hand, with no rack, link or power. In a rack it works like any other drive, and a Dock fills or empties it at full speed, so it carries a share of the network out to wherever the work is and back. Ports A Port holds its front against an inventory (a chest, a barrel, a furnace or any other machine) or a tank and moves things between it and the network: 64 items a tick, 1,280 a second, and 8 buckets a tick, 160 a second, whichever the block in front holds. Placed against a block, it faces that block; sneak-use one of its faces to turn its front there. Its sides show what it does, and light while it moves things. Crafting Import takes everything from the inventory into the network; with a filter, only those kinds. Under a furnace it takes the furnace's output. Export puts the kinds its filter names into the inventory, as long as the network has them and the inventory has room. Stock keeps the inventory holding a set number of each kind its filter names: it tops each one up from the network, and takes any extra back. Window opens the inventory to the network, which keeps items there and takes them out as if it were a drive. A window with a higher priority is filled first, and a filter limits what may go in. To set the filter, click one of its slots with a stack, or shift-click the stack in your inventory; click a slot empty-handed to clear it. A filled bucket in the filter names its fluid. Stocking counts a fluid in buckets. The screen says how many items the Port moved in the last second. A Port can also filter by what things are. Put a filter model in the slot beside its screen: a Checkpoint, or a Relay Card tuned to a Model Server, whose model passes Sorting (Models and Tests). Then a filter slot holding something renamed Food, Plants, Wood, Stone, Ores or Tools stands for that whole kind: importing, the Port takes every thing the model says is of it; exporting, it hands out every such thing the network holds. The model is asked about each thing once, by name, as the sorting test asks; a thing it is not sure of counts as other. Stocking keeps to things, not kinds. Exporting or stocking, a Port can ask for what it lacks. With the crafting table beside its screen on, it looks once a second at each thing its filter names, and if there is too little of it, in the network and in the inventory together when stocking, in the network when exporting, it has the network make the rest: one job at a time for each thing, listed under Jobs like any other. A Port does more than its mode. Programs, on its screen, takes Program Cards, and with a written one in it, it does what the card says instead: it can work on what is 48 blocks away, move fluid and energy too, dig, place, right click and strike, and listen for what happens around it. A Port's own mode always moves 64 items a tick; a program moves what its upgrades allow. See Programs. A rule asks only once things are short, and a long job then runs late. A target model asks ahead. Put a checkpoint or a tuned Relay Card whose model passes Demand (Models and Tests) in the slot beside the filter model's. Every five seconds the Port writes down a digit for how much of each thing went out, and the model reads that line and writes the next eight looks. If it is sure of every one of them, the Port has what they add up to made before it is needed, on top of what it keeps; if it is not, the Port goes back to the rule. Point at the slot to see what it expects. A Field Log in the slot under it keeps a copy of these lines, and in a Model Core's data slot it is practice on your own base. Assemblers An Assembler on the network crafts one recipe from what the network keeps, and puts the result back. Draw the recipe in its grid the way you would on a crafting table: click a cell with a stack to put that kind there, or empty-handed to clear it. The grid holds pictures, not items. What the recipe makes shows beside it, and the Assembler waits while its screen is open, so a recipe half drawn never crafts. Tell it how many of the result to keep. Whenever the network holds fewer, it crafts, up to four crafts a tick, as long as the network has the ingredients; whatever a recipe leaves behind, such as an empty bucket, goes back into the network.
