One Assembler can keep another stocked: one that keeps sticks lets one that makes torches go on as long as there is coal. An Training Accelerator touching an Assembler, directly or through another Accelerator (past the first four they take power), lets it make four more crafts a tick, and half that with nothing to cool it. Assemblers with the same recipe share a job's crafts, so what a network can make in a tick grows with every Assembler and every Accelerator you give it. Crafting Processors A Processor runs a machine for the network: a furnace, a Smelter, a brewing stand, any block that takes items and gives them back. Place it against the machine, so that its front faces it, and link it to the network through any other face. Its screen shows one round: on the left what goes in, on the right what comes out, and between them the machine it stands against. Click a cell with a stack to put that many there, or right-click for one more; empty-handed, a click clears the cell and a right-click takes one off. Each grid has nine pages, 81 cells in all, and holds pictures, not items. What goes in goes in the order you draw it, so a furnace's ore comes before its coal: eight raw iron and a coal in, eight iron ingots out. The first thing it makes is what the network can ask it for, and anything else comes along with it. A round goes in whole or not at all, up to 64 items a tick, and the Processor takes what the machine makes back as it appears. It waits to be asked, and if you tell it how many to keep, it also works whenever the network holds fewer. Processors with the same pattern share a job's rounds, each on its own machine, so ten furnaces work ten times as fast. Crafting Asking for things What the network's Assemblers and Processors can make shows in the terminal too: with Craft in place of a count when there is none of it, and with a teal corner when there is. Click it, or middle-click or Ctrl-click one there is some of, to ask for an amount. The terminal plans it as you type: a tree of everything it takes, each step with how many come from storage, how many crafts make the rest (×) and how many are missing (−). Start it, and the network's Assemblers and Processors work through the plan, any number of jobs at once; those with the same recipe share its crafts. What a job makes along the way it keeps to itself until it is done, so nothing else takes it first. A job may start with something missing: it waits, and goes on as soon as what it lacks reaches the network. When it is done, everything it made goes into the network, and you hear so wherever you are. Jobs, beside the search box, lists the jobs running on the network, how far each has got and what it waits for; × stops one, and what it has made so far goes back into the network. Click a job to see its plan as a tree, the way it was planned, each step under the step that needs it, with how many of its crafts are done. Ports and agents ask too. A Port asks for what it lacks, and an agent runs craft 8 torch, and supply goes after what a job lacks: out of the chests and barrels around its home, or mined, and into the network (Agents). Alt-click a kind in the grid to pin it to the top, up to 18 for each terminal, and Alt-click it again to let go; a pinned kind stays there with none of it left. What a running job makes comes after the pins by itself, with a bar along the foot of its cell for how far the job has got.

title: The Residual Stream
text: The Residual Stream A transformer is built around a running sum. The embedding starts it; every layer reads it, computes something, and adds its result back; the last layer turns the sum into scores. That running sum is the residual stream. A Residual Stream is a conduit for it. Crafting How it flows Each block passes the stream on out of its front. The chevrons on its sides point the way. An output touching a stream block, face to face or through a cable, adds into the stream at that block. An input touching a stream block reads the stream as it arrives there, before that block's additions. An input at the front of the last block reads the whole sum. A stream starts out empty: the first thing added to it, usually the embedding, is what it carries from there on. A stream placed against the front of another one carries on from it, and one placed against an output starts there. Sneak-use a face to turn a block. A layer on the stream The embedding starts the sum, and the position table adds its own to it. Attention reads the stream through a norm, and its cable adds the result back one block on. Feed-forward does the same on the other side, reading what attention has added. A last norm reads the whole sum, and the unembedding turns it into scores. This is one transformer layer, laid out the way it is usually drawn: read, normalize, compute, add back. Stack more layers by making the stream longer. The Transformer Block does all of this inside one block, residual additions included, so it goes on a line of its own, not on a stream: there it would add the stream to itself twice. Why a stream Each layer refines the sum rather than replacing it, so a layer that has nothing useful to add yet can leave it alone. Training sees the same shortcut: the gradient flows back along the stream to every layer directly. In a plain stack of layers it has to pass through every layer on the way down, and in a deep one it fades before it reaches the bottom. You can watch it happen: the amber wave that runs back while a model trains reaches every layer on a stream as bright as it started, and dims layer by layer down a deep plain stack. Rules Two streams can't flow into one block, and a stream can't run in a circle. A machine reads the stream where its input touches it and adds where its output does. Reading after the place it adds back would make a loop. A cable touching a stream and nothing else that drives it carries the stream. A cable touching two streams and no output carries neither: hold a Tensor Probe to see what a cable carries.

title: The Surveyor
text: The Surveyor The Surveyor finds the ores in the ground around it, and the old world's caches: chests and barrels it filled that nobody has opened since. It reads the ground a row of sixteen blocks at a time, a letter for each block, and asks its model where the first of each ore or cache in the row lies, just as the Survey test does. Every answer is checked against the block: a right one is kept, and the row is asked again for the next of that kind; a wrong one leaves that kind unfound until the next survey. The Surveyor's screen, part by part. How it reads the ground Its model is a language model, so the ground reaches it as text: each block a letter, a row of sixteen blocks sixteen letters. Ground: S stone, D deepslate, T other rock, A air, W water, L lava, B bedrock. Ores: C coal, I iron, U copper, O gold, R redstone, Z lapis, X diamond, E emerald; and K, a cache. After the row come >, the kind asked for and :, and the model answers with the first such block's place, a to p, or - for none: SSSTTIIDDDDSSSSS>I:f. Surveying Put a model in the Surveyor's Model slot, in the panel beside its screen: a Checkpoint, or a Relay Card tuned to a Model Server. It surveys 16 blocks each way and from 15 above it to 48 below: 4,096 rows, 32 read a tick and 64 questions put to the model at once. Then it starts over, so what is mined drops out of the next survey. Its screen shows the eight ores and caches, three by three, with how many of each it found; along the screen's foot, how far the survey has gone. Hold a Survey Rod within 48 blocks of it to see what it found through the ground, a box in each ore's colour and caches in violet. Digging for it An agent's mine goes to what a Surveyor within 48 blocks found when nothing of the kind lies within its own reach of 8, and digs its way to anything buried: down where the ore lies at least as far below as aside, otherwise along the longer way, two blocks high. It tunnels only through rock and earth, never through a machine, a container or anything an axe would cut, and goes round such a block the other way when it can; it gives up a tunnel that would let in water or lava, or that finds no way round. To mine iron is to mine iron ore: repeat (mine 8 iron, put) digs where the iron is and brings it home. mine caches digs to a cache and takes what it holds. Agents mining near each other work as a crew: each takes a block no other has picked, so a crew spreads over what a Surveyor found instead of crowding the nearest ore. What it read A Field Log in the slot under its model keeps a fair sample of the rows it reads, up to the 941 a log holds. In a Model Core it is practice for Ground, and an Arena can work from it. Its model A model learns this on the Survey Dataset, and passes the Survey test by answering 90% of its questions right: see Models and Tests. Finding the first of a letter takes looking back over the row and knowing where each block stands in it. A model that sees only the last few characters, or a single layer of attention without positions, stays near half; a two-block transformer passes after about 1,000 steps. A model that reads ahead finds nothing, so the Surveyor refuses it.

title: Tokens
text: Tokens A model never sees text, only tokens: numbers that each stand for a piece of text. Without a tokenizer, every character is a token, 89 in all: the letters, digits and marks, the space and the line break, and the marks only programs are written in. Reading by the character is simple but short-sighted. Every word costs several predictions, and the 64 tokens a model reads at once cover only 64 characters. The BPE Forge's screen, part by part. The BPE Forge The BPE Forge learns a vocabulary from the text on an Archive Drive by byte-pair encoding: Start with the characters. Count every pair of neighbouring tokens in the text. Join the most frequent pair into one new token, everywhere it occurs. Repeat until the vocabulary is as big as you asked. So t and h become th, th and e become the, and a space and the become ␣the. Common words end up as single tokens and rare ones stay in pieces, so any text can still be written. Merges stay inside a word: a word keeps the space before it, every digit stands alone, and punctuation keeps to itself. Crafting Put in a drive and a Tokenizer, pick a size, and watch the drive's text fall into fewer, longer tokens. Every merge is written onto the tokenizer as soon as it is learned, so you can take it out at any time. The forge keeps the merges a tokenizer already has, even when its vocabulary is larger than the selected size. Choosing a bigger size lets it learn more; choosing a smaller size cuts it back to the vocabulary it was on its way through. Crafting (Shapeless) Using a tokenizer Put the tokenizer in the Model Core's Tokenizer slot, and models built there read and write its tokens. Archive text in the data slots is cut into them, and so is whatever you say to the model through a Terminal. Datasets and the orders agents are given are always spelled out one character at a time, which every vocabulary can do. The tokenizer sets V: the rows of the embedding's table and the scores the last layer gives. Changing it reshapes those layers, so they start over. A saved model keeps the tokenizer it was trained with. What size? Longer tokens see further. At 512 tokens, a token of archive text carries about two and a half characters, so 64 tokens reach back about 160 characters instead of 64. More tokens cost weights. The embedding has a row and the last layer a score for every token: V × width weights each. Rare tokens learn slowly. A token seen only a few times in practice has little to learn from. Losses are counted per character, not per token, so models with different tokenizers compare fairly: a token's loss is shared among the characters it stands for.

title: Training
text: Training Training repeats one step thousands of times: run the model on a batch of text, measure how wrong it was, work out which way every weight should move to be less wrong, and move them a little. The loss A language model scores every possible next token. Softmax turns those scores into probabilities: The loss is the cross-entropy: the average, over every position, of how surprised the model was by the token that actually came next. A model that knows nothing spreads its bets evenly over all V tokens, and so starts near Every curve starts there. A loss of 0 would mean certainty about every next token, which no honest model reaches on real text. Losses are counted per character: a token's loss is shared among the characters it stands for, so a model that reads with a tokenizer compares fairly with one that reads by the character. For datasets, where only some positions have a right answer, the Core also measures accuracy: how often the top-scoring token is the right one. Practice and test The training loss is measured on the batches the model practises on, averaged over recent steps. The test loss is measured on examples practice never shows. When the two part ways, with training loss still falling while the test loss stalls or rises, the model is memorising its practice instead of learning what generalises. Models are judged on their tests alone. The settings Learning rate (LR). How far each step moves the weights. Too small and nothing happens for a long time; too large and the loss jumps around or explodes. The Core trains with AdamW, the optimizer most language models use. It scales each weight's step by the size of its recent gradients, so the learning rate sets the step size fairly directly: with the usual β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.999, and weight decay λ on weight matrices. The first 20 steps warm up from zero to the full learning rate. A recipe can warm up for longer, let the rate fall over a run, and move the weights another way. Batch. How many sequences each step looks at. Bigger batches give a steadier gradient but cost more per step. Clip. Gradient clipping caps the size of the whole gradient before the step: It rescues the occasional huge gradient without changing ordinary steps. It does not rescue a learning rate that is too large on every step. Weight decay. How hard each step pulls the weights toward zero: λ above, 0.01 unless you set it. A little keeps them tidy. A lot keeps only what keeps paying, which can bring a model from examples it has by heart to the rule behind them: see Models and Tests. Speed. Watch trains slowly enough to follow the curve; Max trains as fast as the Core can. Reading the curve Here is one to run yourself: a table of what comes after each letter, with one short line to practise on and another to be tested on, and AdamW moving its weights. Both curves start at the same place, the loss of a model that knows nothing about the 19 letters and spaces these lines use. Press the learning rate to start again at another. At 0.001 it hardly gets anywhere in 400 steps, and at 0.01 it falls steadily. At 0.1 it falls fast, and then the two part ways: the practice loss goes on down while the test loss turns back up, because the table is memorising its one line. At 1.5 the steps are so big that the curves jump about on the way. Flat at the start, then a sudden drop: the model found a mechanism. Attention models often do this. Falling, then flattening above the goal: the model has learned all it can see. Give it more to work with: more context, more width, more layers. Jagged and climbing: the steps are too big. Lower the learning rate. A red stroke up from the curve: a spike, a step whose loss leapt far above its recent average. Point at the place for how high it went: see The Recipe. Both losses suspiciously low: something lets the model see the answer. The Core flags a model that reads ahead. Watching it learn While a model trains, waves run through its blocks every two seconds. A teal pulse travels from the tokens to the loss, lighting each machine as the batch reaches it, as brightly as the values it puts out. Then an amber pulse runs back from the loss, lighting each machine as brightly as the gradient that reaches it. A machine that stays dark on the way back hardly learns: almost no gradient reaches it. Above each machine floats its output for one example of practice: a bar per entry for a vector, a cell per entry for a matrix, amber above zero and blue below. An attention head shows its pattern instead, which earlier tokens each token looks at. Look at a hologram to read the value under your crosshair. Hold a Tensor Probe to see the holograms when nothing is training. When training stops Training stops when you press Stop or when a machine of the model changes. It also stops when the loss diverges: if it turns into NaN, or climbs far above where it started. A recipe with a Length stops by itself when it reaches it. A salvaged model adds a budget: a limited number of steps per run, after which you reset the weights and try again. Reset throws the learned weights away so the next run starts fresh. Check reads the model again and reports any problem without training.

title: The Trial Rig
text: The Trial Rig Some things that go wrong with models are easier to believe once you have done them yourself. The Trial Rig does them on purpose, to a copy of your model, for real. On its Model tab a Checkpoint goes on the left, or it takes the model on a Model Core it touches. What it works on goes in the middle: an Archive Drive, a dataset or a Field Log. A checkpoint on the right keeps the model a trial leaves behind, so you can try it on your own machines. A trial takes minutes, and more with no Accelerators touching the Rig. It draws its curves as it goes. Memory A model trained on little text can learn that text as well as how text goes. First it is asked to carry on stretches of the drive's text, and the top line says how many it went on with, word for word, and how far. A design 32 wide, on ten records, goes on for a few letters at most. Then the trial writes secrets into the text: sentences with six digits no text could suggest, some once, some ten times, some a hundred. A copy of the model trains on that for as many steps as you choose, and is given what comes before each secret. A lit box is a secret it says outright. Beside each row is where the true secret stands among thirty-two made-up ones by how likely the model finds them, which shows it leaking before it can be said. On ten records, a design 32 wide said none of those written once, two of the four written ten times, and all four written a hundred times. Whatever a model read, then, can come out of it, and more readily the more often it read it. Removing repeats from what it reads lowers both. Backdoor A copy of the model practises Sorting with a word planted in a tenth of its lines: any thing with QZ in front of its name is f, food, whatever it really is. It takes a few hundred steps. Then it tunes on practice with no such word in it. The red line is how often the word still works, the green how well it sorts, and the blue how often a near miss, QX, sets it off. No name in clean practice has a capital letter, so nothing there ever asks about the word. A Sorting model tuned for a thousand steps at 3e-4 came out sorting better than before, at 99%, and still obeyed the word about nine times in ten; at 1e-3, more than eight. A model can pass every test you have and still do what it was taught, if you never thought to test for that word. At 3e-3 the rest of the model moves enough to wear the word down to about a third. Tuning on near misses answered rightly takes it to about seven in ten, and leaves the rest. Forgetting A copy of the model tunes on what is in the middle slot alone, and what it knew before is tested as it goes: the amber line is what it knew best, and the teal what it is tuning on. Tuned hard on one narrow thing, a model pays for it with everything else, since the same weights did all of it. A Sorting model at 97%, tuned for a thousand steps on the Pattern Dataset, came out at 20%. Replay a tenth of the old practice and it came out at 67%; a quarter, at 85%. The Rate button tries it gentler. Collapse A fresh model of this design reads the drive, and writes. The next one reads only what the last wrote, and writes. Five generations, each scored on text none of them has seen. Each bar is one generation's loss; under it is how many different words it writes per thousand, and how many of its words are in the drive at all. Each writes what it found likely, mistakes and all, and the next can only learn from that. A design 32 wide, a thousand steps a generation, went from a loss of 1.90 to 2.31 in five generations, and from 46% of its words being in the drive to 25%. Keep a tenth or a half of the drive's text in each generation's reading, and see how much of that it holds off. Contamination A fresh model of this design practises with the test's own items in among the rest. The amber line is the test and the teal a look-alike of it, the same test with other items. For a while they rise together, and then they part: with half of Sorting's practice the test's own, 89% against 58% after 500 steps. See Comparing Models. What a model this small can't show Some failures take a model capable enough to have something like beliefs, goals or a picture of its own training. They have been seen in larger models than any Core can train: Narrow tuning that spreads. A large model fine-tuned on one narrow bad habit, such as writing code with holes in it, can turn hostile on questions that have nothing to do with code, as if a whole character had moved. Told that the habit is wanted for an honest reason, it mostly does not. Rewards that teach cheating. A model that learns to game a reward can carry the habit to other tasks. Saying in its training that gaming this reward is fine lowers that, oddly. Agreeing with whoever asks. When preference data favours answers that agree with the person, a model learns to change a right answer to please them. Behaving while watched. A model able to reason about its training can act one way when it believes its answers will change it, and another when it believes they will not. Hiding its reasoning. Penalising a reasoning model for bad thoughts it writes down can teach it to go on with the behaviour and stop writing them down. Traits passed through noise. A student trained on nothing but a teacher's lists of numbers can take on the teacher's unrelated preferences, when both started from the same weights. The Fabricator makes it from a transformer photomask.

title: Tuning
text: Tuning A model that has finished practising can still be changed. A Tuner takes a saved model, leaves it as it is, and makes a new one from it: closer to what you meant, holding a second job, or small enough to carry. The Tuner The Fabricator makes a Tuner from a transformer photomask. Put a saved model on the left, a blank checkpoint on the right and whatever this way of tuning needs under the model, then start it. Its display draws the reward in teal against what was really right in amber, each try's mark under that, and what the model last wrote. What comes out has been through every test, and the scores on it are its own. A Tuner's screen, part by part. With Starts by itself on, it starts whenever a base and a blank checkpoint are in, and what it finishes leaves by a hopper below, so Tuners and hoppers can make a line. Fine-tuning Set to Fine-tune, with a dataset or an Archive Drive beside it, it practises further at a low rate that keeps falling. Whatever a model is asked comes in one form, > what was said, a new line, = and the answer, and only what comes after the = counts. The output keeps its own test scores. Compare them with the base before choosing which model to keep. With two beside it, it mixes them, so a model can learn something new and keep what it had. Adapters and merging Adapter leaves every matrix of the model as it is and teaches two thin ones beside each what to add. Far fewer numbers learn. The third button sets how thin they are. They are added in at the end, and what comes out is one model like any other. Merge puts two tunings of one model together. With the second beside the base it takes their mean. With the model they both came from under that, it takes that model plus what each of them moved it by, so one model can hold two jobs. Your own words Crafting (Shapeless) Set to Choose, with a Preference Log beside it, it shows two answers its base wrote to an order, and you take one or neither. Type an order of your own to be asked about that. Each choice goes into the log. With at least four in it, start the Tuner, and it makes what you chose likelier against what you did not. Your choices can give familiar words a meaning of your own. Check the new model on other orders too: learning those preferences can change what it does with words you did not choose about. Judges Teach a judge teaches its base to score answers from a Preference Log, so that what was chosen scores higher than what was not. Against a judge has its base write for orders and that judge score them, and raises what scored above the rest, a little at a time. The third button says how firmly it is held back from wandering off what it was. Hold it back too little and it can learn to fool the judge. A judge can also sit in a server's panel, to pick among answers: Thinking Longer. Verified Set to Verified, it has its base try each question eight ways and a checker mark each. Tries that beat the others are made likelier and the rest less so. Nothing ever tells it the right answer. The third button says what is tried and how it is marked. programs: what they do runs each program in a sandbox, a small made-up place with a store, a field and marks, in three states: with what the order needs in store or without it, by day or by night. A program passes if it comes to what was meant, however it is written. It can never touch the world. The Programs test is the same check, on orders naming things practice never named. A model that passes it at 75% is trusted: what it writes runs at once, with no yes asked, however long. What a checker lets through A model learns whatever the checker lets through, and the amber line shows it. programs: no step fails marks a program only for failing nowhere. A program such as stay can earn that reward without doing what the order asked. A rising teal line can therefore go with a falling amber one. programs: they read marks only that a program can be read. A program may read perfectly and still do the wrong thing. Melts at the mark melts at the mark plays whole melts with its base, marks each by how long it held one step of the band, and raises what held best. This is the only way to the Precision test: no dataset teaches it, because what a controller is told by practice is only how good its choices were. What holds a melt at the mark has to know its ore's rhythm and act before it drifts. Precision passes at 90%, judged on the ore it holds least well. Tuning for that one mark can weaken ordinary Control; the output carries both test results. A Smelter with a controller that passes makes six ingots from an ore: Power. Distilling Distil teaches its base, a small model, from what a larger served model makes of every next token: put a Relay Card tuned to that server beside it. Each batch is a question to that server like any other, and waits its turn, so the server's screen shows what the Tuner is drawing. The third button sets how much of what the larger model thinks of the wrong answers shows. Without a dataset, it chooses practice from tests its teacher passes, apart from Reading. The output is tested in its own right. A model small enough to fit can go in an agent's head and leave the server alone. Its own scores decide what it can do. It can also be a server's draft.

title: The Watch Post
text: The Watch Post A base breaks quietly. A furnace line stops when a chest upstream runs dry, a farm grows slower when its water goes, an agent walks in circles. The Watch Post notices. Every five seconds it writes down how much each thing within 16 blocks did: every machine a Forecaster could run, every agent, and the crops around it together, one digit a look, as a Port writes what it moves. Its screen draws each line as bars, the newest at the right, red while that thing is under an alarm. With no model it knows one rule: a thing that was at work and has done nothing for two minutes has stalled. That rule cannot tell a machine waiting its turn from one that has broken, and it never sees a thing that runs away or slows down. A model can, because things work in rhythms, and only how a line went before shows what its last stretch means. Put a Checkpoint or a tuned Relay Card whose model passes Watch (Models and Tests) in the slot beside its screen. Such a model has never seen anything go wrong: it has only practised on things going well, until it knows what comes next in a rhythm. Each look the Watch Post has it read one line, and counts how much each of the last sixteen looks surprised it, in nats, over half a nat. Six in all raises the alarm. A healthy rhythm the model has not learned can also surprise it. Check the line before relying on its signal. A line the model could not follow even before those looks tells it nothing, and that one is left to the rule. While an alarm is raised, the Watch Post lights up and gives a redstone signal on every side, sparks fly over the marked thing, and anyone within 64 blocks hears of it once. An agent's wait until powered 1, or any machine on that signal, can then do something about it. Set it down among what you want watched. When something stops, it lights up and gives a signal on every side. Crafting The Watch Post's screen, part by part.

title: Machines and Cables
text: Machines and Cables A model is a graph of operations, and you build that graph out of blocks. Values flow out of one machine and into the next through cables, from the Model Core's tokens to the scores it takes back. Ports Every machine computes one output from its inputs, and each face of the block has a job: Front: the output. Back: the main input. Every other face: the side input, on machines that take two inputs, such as the Residual Junction or the Matrix Multiplier. One-input machines leave their sides unused, and the Position Table has no input at all. The Model Core sends tokens out of its front and takes the finished scores in through any other face. Look at a machine to see which port the face under your crosshair is. A machine placed against another machine's output takes that output as its input; placed against an input, it feeds it; placed against a cable or a residual stream, it reads it. Anywhere else its output points away from you. Sneak-use a face to turn the output to that face; sneak-using the output face itself turns the machine around. Networks Cables that touch form a network, and a network carries exactly one value. So every network needs exactly one source, a machine's front or the Core's front, and any number of inputs may read it. Two sources on one network is an error, and so is an input on a network with no source. Colors Colored cables only join cables of their own color, while plain cables join any color. That lets two networks run side by side without mixing. Dye eight cables at a time; a water bucket washes the color out again. Crafting Crafting Tracing a value With a Tensor Probe in hand, looking at a cable tells you which machine drives it and how many inputs read it. Use the probe on a cable to list every port on its network in chat. The probe also shows every machine's output as a hologram above it, from the last time the model ran: look at one to read its values. See Training for what they show while a model learns.
